source_terms: The 4 principles of creating effective YouTube video ads are Attention, Branding, Connection, and Direction
Attention, Branding, Connection, Direction
the ABCDs
item.claim: The source decomposes effective YouTube video-ad execution into exactly four named principles — Attention, Branding, Connection and Direction — and presents them not as a menu to choose from but as a set to be factored into each of the many decisions that go into making an ad.

mechanism.text: The source's account is that these principles were observed across video ads that worked effectively for brands, and that "by factoring four simple principles into each decision, your work is more likely to achieve your marketing goals".

scope.conditions: Paid video advertising on YouTube, as the platform and its ad products stood on the pages dated April 2022 and May 2023 and as retrieved on 30 August 2026.

caveats.text: The source nowhere states that the four principles are exhaustive, and reports no result for omitting one. Jointness is asserted by how the framework is written and used, not by any test the source describes.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

source_stated_problems: Making an ad involves many decisions: some big, some small
source_stated_remedies: By factoring four simple principles into each decision, your work is more likely to achieve your marketing goals

positive.description: The 'Fishos' fish-flavoured dog-treat storyboard, revised principle by principle as the source walks the four letters

counter.description: The same Fishos ad before the ABCD principles are applied, which the source presents as the weaker of the pair

intra_source_relations.note: the framework object anchors the system

Branding is one of the four
Connection is one of the four

the source limits the framework to execution

item.question: Under which of the four principles does the source file the fault of doing too much in an ad, and what does that filing imply?
item.answer: Under Connection — not Attention and not Direction. Google Ads Help lists "Focus the message: Avoid doing too much in your ad. Keep messaging and language focused and simple" as a Connection guideline. Think with Google is more explicit about why it sits there: it states the instruction as a brake on the Connection instructions immediately preceding it — lean into humour and surprise, "But avoid doing too much in your ad. Focus the message as you make your connection." So on the source's arrangement an overloaded ad is one that fails to connect, and the focus instruction is the stated limit on how far the engagement devices may be pushed. The source quantifies neither side: no message count, and no test for when an ad is doing too much.
item.support: "Focus the message" is in the Connection row of the core table; the "But avoid doing too much" construction is in the Connection section of the Think with Google page.

item.source_locator: Ch. 'Jo Biwi Se Kare Pyaar…', Airtel passage
item.question: A team wants to use a corpus of Indian television commercials from 2014 as evidence about how common working-woman households were that year. On this source's own position, what is wrong with that, and what would the corpus actually be evidence about?
item.answer: The author blocks the inference himself. Discussing a 2014 Airtel commercial in which a woman manager's subordinate turns out to be her husband, he writes that the ad 'was a depiction of a future, not the current reality', and that in most Indian homes the older division of roles still held. His stated mechanism is that good advertising deliberately runs one step ahead of the consumer, which decouples depiction from prevalence: the depiction is selected for aspirational pull. So the corpus is evidence about what advertisers judged aspirational in 2014, not about how common the arrangement was. Note the author does not say how far ahead is too far, and offers no test.
item.support: 'But I would submit that the Airtel ad was a depiction of a future, not the current reality.'
item.confounders: The same ad drew opposite readings — praised as an ode to the new Indian woman, criticised for still putting her at the stove — and the author declines to adjudicate.

item.label: abcd_four_principle_execution_framework
item.description: The four principles — Attention, Branding, Connection, Direction — as the source presents them: one set applied to each execution decision on a YouTube video ad, with the claimed effectiveness result attached to the set rather than to any member.

whole_system_claim.text: The source treats the four as jointly applied rather than as a menu. Its instruction is to factor all four principles into each decision; its effectiveness figures are stated for "the ABCDs" as a whole and are never decomposed by principle; and its objective table, which is where a menu reading would show up, never drops a principle — where an objective needs no special treatment of one, the cell reads "Apply core principles" rather than being empty.

source_ref.locator: Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", section "Crafting a successful ad" ("By factoring four simple principles into each decision, your work is more likely to achieve your marketing goals"); Google Ads Help, "About the ABCDs of effective video ads", sections "Benefits" and "ABCDs by marketing objectives"

dependencies.nature: The "richly" half of the branding principle, and the see-and-say guideline under it, rest on the source's claim that YouTube audio is almost always heard.
Reinforcing the on-screen call to action with voice-over rests on the same audio premise.

tradeoffs.nature: Engagement devices — humour, surprise, intrigue — against the instruction to focus the message and avoid doing too much. The source states the second as a brake on the first: "Lean into emotional levers ... But avoid doing too much in your ad."

source_ref.locator: Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", section "C = Connection: Help people think or feel something"

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The membership, the joint-application claim and the trade-off between engaging and focusing are all the source's own. What is ours: the decision not to record an ordering. The source always presents the principles in the fixed sequence A, B, C, D, but that is a mnemonic — it never says an earlier letter takes precedence over a later one, nor that the letters map to positions in the ad's timeline. Recording A–D as a priority order or a sequence would assert something the source does not, so the ordering scheme is "none" and that choice is ours. Also ours: the two dependencies on the sound-on claim. The source states the audio premise on one page and the audio-dependent guidelines on others, and never connects them itself.

source_terms: Using real animals in ad films is today highly regulated by the Animal Welfare Board. They can appoint a supervisor to oversee the shoot and more. So before you approve a script featuring a python, a dog or a cat, just find out how you are going to manage the Animal Welfare Board.

television broadcasters too set up two self-regulatory bodies, News Broadcasting Standards Authority (NBSA) and Broadcasting Content Complaints Council (BCCC). These bodies are, by and large, concerned with the content that is broadcast and not the advertising.
item.claim: Beyond the advertising self-regulator, Indian ad production is constrained by other bodies with different remits: the Animal Welfare Board regulates the use of real animals and may appoint a supervisor to oversee a shoot, and the author advises settling that route before a script featuring an animal is approved. Two broadcaster bodies, NBSA and BCCC, exist but address broadcast content rather than advertising. Cinema advertising ran on a separate track: brands made shorts of roughly 100 feet (30.4 m), running about a minute, which required a censor certificate — a practice the author says continues.

scope.conditions: India, as at 2016; the cinema-short practice is described as running from the pre-television era to the present

caveats.text: 'before you approve a script featuring a python, a dog or a cat' is practitioner advice addressed to a reader in the Indian ad industry, not a general production rule
the author's comparison — that cinema censors were 'a lot clearer about what they wanted to stop' than Doordarshan — is his opinion, offered without evidence

item.claim: The source states a two-stage decision rule. The core ABCDs are the starting point for any video ad; on top of them, the emphasis given to each of the four principles is then varied according to the campaign's marketing objective — awareness, consideration, action, or a combination of all three that the source calls full funnel. Across all four objective rows no principle is ever dropped: where an objective calls for no special treatment of a principle, the table's instruction is to apply the core principles for it.

scope.conditions: Four named marketing objectives, with a fourth combined row for full funnel

caveats.text: The observation that no principle is ever dropped is read off the table rather than stated by the source. It is directly checkable: the Google Ads Help matrix has an instruction in every one of its sixteen cells, and three of those instructions read "Apply core principles".

The source gives no evidence for the objective-specific weightings. The headline lift figures are attached to the ABCDs as a set, not to any objective variant, and no result is reported for tailoring against not tailoring.

Think with Google names only three objectives — awareness, consideration, action — and points readers to a downloadable playbook. The fourth row, full funnel, exists only in the Google Ads Help table.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. item.answer: It is a claim about how one named platform was being watched, made once, on the Think with Google page dated April 2022, and offered as the reason to exploit the multisensory nature of the medium. item.question: An ad packs three separate product benefits into fifteen seconds, each with its own voice-over line and its own super, over fast cutting. Which named faults does this source say it hits, under which principles — and which element of the description does the source not object to?
item.answer: Two named faults, under two different principles. "Doing too much" under Connection, from "Focus the message: Avoid doing too much in your ad. Keep messaging and language focused and simple." And "competing elements" under Attention, from "Support the story with audio and supers: Reinforce your message with audio and text. Avoid competing elements." — three voice-over lines and three supers carrying three different messages are not reinforcing one message. The fast cutting is the element the source does not object to: engaging pacing is what it asks for under "Jump in". Neither fault is quantified anywhere — no message count, and no test for when two elements compete rather than reinforce — so the diagnosis is directional and the threshold would be the implementer's.
item.support: Both faults are named at the locators given; "engaging pacing" is part of the Jump in guideline.

item.question: You are asked to build an automated check for the source's "Jump in" guideline. Why can it not be run on individual frames, and what does the source fail to give you?
item.answer: Because what "Jump in" describes is a property of a span, not of a still: how quickly the ad reaches the heart of its story, and whether the pacing and framing across the opening draw the viewer in. No single frame carries any of that, so the unit of observation has to be the opening sequence at least. What the source fails to give you is every number the check would need — no target time to the heart of the story, no definition of what the heart of the story is, and no reference point for "faster", which is comparative with nothing to compare to. The only figure anywhere nearby is a five-second mention in an illustrative caption about when one ad introduced its brand, which is a different guideline and is not stated as a rule. A check built from this can be directional; any threshold in it is the implementer's.
item.support: "Jump in" names pacing and framing over the opening and gives no duration; the five-second figure belongs to the Weekendesk caption under "Show up early and throughout".

item.label: objective_weighted_abcds
item.description: The source's second-stage rule: having applied the core ABCDs, vary the emphasis given to each of the four principles according to the campaign's marketing objective — awareness, consideration, action, or all three combined as full funnel.

whole_system_claim.text: Across the four objectives the membership of the framework is constant and only the emphasis moves. Every one of the sixteen cells carries an instruction; where an objective calls for no special treatment of a principle the cell reads "Apply core principles", which happens three times — Direction under awareness, and Attention under both consideration and action. The full-funnel row is the only one with no such cell, and the only one whose instructions include ordering within the ad.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source publishes the matrix and states the two-stage rule ("Great video ads start when you apply the Core ABCDs, but you can optimize your ads for specific marketing objectives"), but it never characterises the matrix's own shape. The claim that membership is constant and only emphasis varies, and the count of where "Apply core principles" falls, are read off the published table by us. They are directly checkable against it, but they are our reading, not the source's statement.

dependencies.nature: each objective variant presupposes the core principles it modifies

source_ref.locator: Google Ads Help, "About the ABCDs of effective video ads", section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", introductory paragraph

tradeoffs.nature: How directly the ad asks. Consideration is to "plant the seed of urgency"; action is to "present the ask after the context is set"; full funnel escalates directness through the ad. This is the source's whole account of how the ask varies with objective.

conflicts.nature: The action row's "Make the product the ad" pulls against the core Connection guideline to build the story on people's experience of the product. The source publishes both and does not address the tension.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The four objectives, the two-stage rule and the sixteen cell contents are the source's. The characterisation of the matrix's shape — constant membership, varying emphasis, three "Apply core principles" cells — is ours, and so are the trade-off and the conflict recorded above. One extraction note matters: the plain-text capture of the Google Ads Help page linearises the table and loses which cell each instruction belongs to, and two rows carry two bullets in a single Connection cell. The cell-to-column mapping used here was resolved by re-fetching the page and reading the table markup, not inferred from reading order.

item.question: Two teams building an action-objective ad both cite this source: one to justify a cast-led human story, the other to justify cutting the people entirely and shooting the product. Which of them has the source right?
item.answer: Both are quoting it accurately, and the source does not settle it. The core Connection guideline says "Humanize the story: Feature people to help you tell a better product story and relate to your consumer.", which supports the first team. The action row's Branding cell says "Make the product the ad" — the strongest branding instruction in the whole table — and its Connection cell says "Be exact and tangible", not "feature people", which supports the second. The source publishes both and never addresses the tension between them. The only structural guidance it does supply for this objective is about ordering: present the ask after the context is set. An answer that picks a winner is going beyond the source.

source_terms: Deliver as much as a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution
On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution
Source: Google/Kantar, The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, Global, Apr 2021. n=11,000 ads
item.claim: The source attaches two effectiveness figures to the ABCDs as a set — a 30 per cent lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17 per cent lift in long-term brand contribution — sourced to a study it names "The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness", credited to Google/Kantar, global, April 2021, with a sample of 11,000 ads. The publisher's three pages state the same two figures at three different strengths and with three different levels of citation detail.

scope.conditions: Attributed to a global study of 11,000 ads dated April 2021; the source does not state the markets, categories, ad formats, lengths or comparison baseline behind either figure.

caveats.text: The three Google pages phrase the identical finding differently and the difference is not cosmetic. Google Ads Help says "Deliver as much as a 30% lift ... and a 17% lift", which is an upper bound. Think with Google says "On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift ... and a 17% lift", which is a central tendency. The Google for Business resources article prints the two numbers as bare callouts ("30% lift in short-term sales likelihood", "17% lift in long-term brand contribution") with no qualifier at all, above a page-footer line reading "Actual results will vary by advertiser". An upper bound and an average are different statistics. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved; nothing in any of the three pages settles which is correct.

Citation detail also differs by page. Only the Google for Business resources article gives the sample size, "n=11,000 ads". Google Ads Help gives the same study, publisher, scope and month with no sample size. Think with Google cites it as "Google/Kantar Link AI, Global, The Short and the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, 2021" — naming Kantar's Link AI, dropping the month and giving no sample size.

The underlying study is not published on any of the three pages and is not linked. No method, comparison baseline, definition of "short-term sales likelihood" or "long-term brand contribution", confidence interval or dispersion is given. These are reported results, but they are reported by an interested party from a study the source does not let the reader inspect.

The figures are attached to the ABCDs as a set. The source does not decompose the lift by principle, so no figure here supports a claim about Attention, Branding, Connection or Direction individually.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

item.answer: The reason is device coverage: "Ensure visuals are optimized for all devices", and the source's own illustration reduces that to holding visual engagement on small screens. item.question: Google states the same ABCD effectiveness result on three of its own pages. How does the phrasing differ between them, and why does the difference matter?
item.answer: Three different strengths for one finding. Google Ads Help says the ABCDs "Deliver as much as a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — an upper bound. Think with Google says "On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — a central tendency. The Google for Business resources article prints the two numbers as bare callouts with no qualifier at all, above a page-footer line reading "Actual results will vary by advertiser". An upper bound and an average are different statistics, and a reader who meets one page will draw a different expectation from a reader who meets another. Nothing on any of the three pages resolves which is right, and this bank does not resolve it either.

item.source_locator: VERTICAL LINES, converted-PDF pages 76 and 77
item.question: You are processing a facade shot in which the vertical planking should dominate, and your instinct is to even out the tonal range. What did Freeman do instead, and what else did he remove?
item.answer: The opposite. He says he was far from wanting to balance tones and actively wanted strong contrast so that the vertical lines would dominate, and he processed for contrast accordingly. The reason is that contrast is what separates a line from its surroundings sufficiently for the eye to read it as a line rather than as a boundary between two similar tones. He then removed everything competing: he cropped to eliminate anything that would distract from the verticals — naming a window at the left and lit grass below — and shaved the frame at top and bottom. He also offers, conditionally rather than as a recommendation, a further step: if you do not mind altering the geometry in post-production, straightening the roof ridge from diagonal to horizontal would allow an even tighter crop. Note that the picture did not begin as an image about verticals; he was photographing the architecture and redirected when the low sun caught the planking.

source_terms: A grid's orthogonal (90° axis) logic, and all the thinking about how to work with it, derive from the fundamental verbivisual qualities of type.
Stacking horizontal sentences below each other creates a new vertical line—the column—and columns appearing side by side establish yet another horizontal structure.
item.claim: The right-angled logic of the grid is not imposed mathematics; it grows out of the physical form of type. Letters in the Western alphabet are built from vertical strokes; sequenced into words and sentences those verticals form a horizontal line; sentences stacked form a new vertical, the column; columns set side by side establish a further horizontal structure.

mechanism.text: The alternation between vertical and horizontal at each level of assembly is what produces an orthogonal structure. The source states the chain explicitly, level by level.

scope.conditions: Western alphabetic typesetting

source_terms: This represents a dramatic shift in compositional emphasis, from emphatically horizontal—in which the verticality of the columns adds contrast—to overtly vertical, in which row divisions assume an increased level of importance.
it’s important that strong horizontal breaks and alignments of a similar quality as will appear in the small format are built into the large format presentation to ensure continuity
item.claim: Material placed in the rightward columns of a large-screen layout reorients into a single-column vertical scroll when the browser closes to smartphone width. That is a dramatic inversion of compositional emphasis: from emphatically horizontal, where the columns' verticality supplies contrast, to overtly vertical, where the row divisions become far more important. A change this pronounced can disunify a branded experience, so horizontal breaks and alignments of the same quality as those that will appear in the small format must be built into the large-format presentation to preserve continuity.

mechanism.text: Collapsing several columns into one removes the horizontal reading and leaves only the vertical, so whatever the layout's character depended on horizontally has to be carried by the rows instead.

scope.conditions: responsive layouts that collapse to a single column

caveats.text: the remedy asks the designer to compromise the large-format composition in advance for the sake of a small-format one that does not exist yet

item.claim: Where the source wants lines to dominate an image, it works by removing everything that competes and by pushing tonal contrast up rather than balancing it. In the horizontal-lines case it cropped tightly with a telephoto to exclude the sky. In the vertical-lines case it says plainly that it was "far from wanting to balance tones" and actively wanted strong contrast, then processed for contrast and cropped away a window at the left and lit grass below, shaving the frame top and bottom. Both moves are subtractive.

mechanism.text: Contrast is what separates a line from its surroundings sufficiently for the eye to read it as a line rather than as a boundary between two similar tones; anything else in the frame competes for the same attention, so it is removed.

item.claim: The source imports a compositional grammar from a tradition unlike the rest of the book. The Chinese vertical scroll it calls mountain-water differs from Western imagery in two ways it names: long and vertical is not part of the European painting canon, and the aim is to express the essence of the landscape rather than an image of what can be seen. The method it reports is to combine elements from the landscape in general and stack them vertically, almost always leading to an upper peak. item.claim: Spatial zones are regions of a page or spread designated for a function or a kind of content, both to invigorate layouts and to help readers navigate. In a column grid a flowline or two defines horizontal zones and a column or group of columns defines vertical ones; in a modular grid groups of rows or columns do the same. A designer may also add a flowline or vertical guide independent of the grid's basic structure, deliberately interrupting its regularity to emphasise the zone; and modules may be grouped in mosaic-like patterns to make stepped or irregularly shaped zones. In effect, spatial zones add some of the qualities of a hierarchic grid to a grid defined by regular intervals — useful for separating continuous text from recurring sidebars or information graphics, or for correlating the text of a step-based process with the images illustrating each step.

mechanism.text: A zone is not a new kind of part; it is a role assigned to a group of existing parts, which is why it can be added to any regular structure without changing it.

item.source_locator: Ch. 5, 'The Indian Middle Class'; Ch. 10, 'Youth'; Table 10.1
item.question: A dashboard reports that engagement among 'young professionals' rose 12 per cent this quarter, and a budget is being set against it. What does this source require before that number is used, and which of its two worked cases is the closer parallel?
item.answer: It requires two things stated before the number is usable: THE DEFINITION of 'young professionals' and THE POPULATION BASE it was measured on. The book's charge against 'the Indian middle class' is exactly this — the category has no agreed definition, so its size varies enormously with whichever definition is chosen, and a number quoted without its definition is uninterpretable, yet capacity gets built against it. A percentage change makes this worse rather than better, because it hides the base entirely: 12 per cent of a self-selected panel of existing engaged users and 12 per cent of the addressable population are different findings with the same label. THE CLOSER PARALLEL IS THE YOUTH CASE, and it is closer for a specific reason. The middle-class failure is that no definition exists; the youth failure is that a definition exists, is narrow, and is REPORTED UNDER A BROADER LABEL — surveys of the highest social classes in four or five big cities, covering at worst under 1 per cent and at best about 3 per cent of Indian youth, reported as findings about Indian youth. Table 10.1 quantifies the gap: Rich Brats 0.4 per cent and Consuming Class about 3 per cent, all in the top 23 cities, against Rural Marginal Consumers at 71 per cent. A dashboard segment is almost always the second case — a real measurement on a narrow tracked population, labelled with the name of the population you wish you were measuring. The source supplies no threshold for when a base is too narrow; what it supplies is the requirement to state it, and the demonstration that stating it sometimes ends the argument.
item.support: Table 10.1, read directly; surveys covering 1-3 per cent of Indian youth reported as findings about Indian youth.
item.confounders: Both of the source's cases are national-scale and this one is not, so the arithmetic does not transfer. The requirement — definition and base before use — is what does.

item.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
item.source_locator: Ch. 11 "Status, Dominance, and Affiliation", sections "Affiliation and dominion are different ways to measure status" and "Affiliation or dominance is up to the customer, not you" (spine 18)
item.question: Two audiences respond to completely different status signals. Distinguish Godin's two measures, give the questions each asks, and say why the pair is not a segmentation.
item.answer: Dominion is vertical — above or below. Its questions are: who has more power; this is mine, not yours; I did this myself; my side dominating your side. Affiliation is horizontal — who is standing next to me. Its questions are: who knows you; who trusts you; have you made things better; where do you stand within the tribe. They also behave differently under abundance: affiliation admires the network effect, since more affiliation benefits everyone affiliated, while dominion is scarcity-bound because someone must be below. The reason it is not a segmentation is that Godin says the same person switches by situation — his example is a twelve-year-old who cares about nothing but beating the opposition on the field and cares a lot about who sits next to him on the bus. It describes a moment, not a personality. And the priority is stated: which measure applies is the customer's, not yours.
item.support: Affiliation and dominion: the affiliation questions (who knows you, who trusts you, where do you stand within the tribe) against the dominion ones (this is mine not yours, who has more power); dominion is vertical, affiliation horizontal; affiliation admires the network effect, abundance is welcome; the ball-field child who cares only about winning but also about who sits next to him; the way you see the world isn't nearly as important as the worldview of those you seek to serve.
confounders: using it as a persona split, when Godin makes it situational
assuming affiliation is the good one; he presents both as legitimate measures
projecting your own measure onto the audience, the error he names explicitly

item.claim: Desai's most explicitly argued thesis is that the Indian disposition to accept the almost-good-enough — usually deplored as *chalta hai* — encodes a defensible position about time: that solutions are temporary equilibria, that imperfection is a permanent condition conferred by time, and that holding a solution perfect costs ever-increasing effort until it becomes unsustainable. He contrasts this with what he characterises as a Western analytical mode that reduces a problem to components and freezes it in time, taking the individual as the fundamental unit.

source_terms: 'THIS as well as THAT'
continuity with change
high tolerance of ambiguity
item.claim: Bijapurkar argues that the expectation of a zero-sum contest between tradition and modernity, with modernity winning, was wrong, and that the observed pattern is "this as well as that": the new is adopted alongside the old in hybrid forms rather than replacing it. Her worked cases: chocolate makers failed to enter the Diwali sweets exchange with advertising, special flavours and Indian motifs, and succeeded only when small players packed individually wrapped chocolate mounds in the traditional decorated clay lamps used for the festival; ready-to-eat processed food was pre-empted not by changed food habits but by a cottage "kitchen outsourcing" sector supplying idli-dosa batter in plastic packets and home-cooked tiffin, which she analyses as "the best of both worlds — made on a micro scale, as if at home ... ready to cook (all negative labour outsourced!) but home-made (the positive labour retained!)"; and the arranged marriage becoming an "engineered" marriage rather than giving way to dating.

mechanism.text: Where a practice bundles several benefits, only some of which the new offer improves, adoption proceeds by unbundling: the disliked component is outsourced and the valued component retained. The result looks like resistance to the new offer but is actually a more precise version of the demand than the offer addressed, which is why the successful entrant is usually the one that unbundles rather than the one that substitutes.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets post-1991. Bijapurkar generalises it as "the DNA of Indian society", which is a strong culturalist framing and is treated below.

caveats.text: THE UNBUNDLING MECHANISM AND THE CULTURALIST FRAMING ARE SEPARABLE AND SHOULD BE SEPARATED. The mechanism — a bundled practice is adopted by outsourcing the disliked component and retaining the valued one — is a clean and general account. The framing that this expresses an Indian 'DNA' with 'high tolerance of ambiguity', evidenced by avatars in the Hindu pantheon and by Brahmins in Bengal being permitted fish, is essentialist, is not evidenced, and does no work the mechanism does not already do

the cases are told without dates, volumes or sources. The kitchen-outsourcing claim in particular — that it 'succeeded in pre-empting the entry of ready-to-eat processed food' — is a strong causal statement with no evidence offered

Table 9.2, 'Indian and Western Values', which sets out the culturalist framing as a two-column list, appears ONLY as an image in this copy and its content does not appear in the text. It was opened and read. It is a schematic of asserted binary contrasts (patriarchy/egalitarianism, ambiguity/clarity, dharma/individually chosen roles) with no source and no data, and it should be read as the author's summary of her own position, not as a finding

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Cases without dates or figures; the culturalist generalisation is asserted.

item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.claim: Inserting any form into a space, even a solitary one, creates structure: a set of visual relationships between that form's contour and axis and those of other forms. Because of human orientation to Earth, forms are typically perceived as expressing two primary axes, horizontal and vertical — orthogonal, grid structure. But structures may be far more complex than that, and any structure may be fluid and irregular in proportion or interval. That an arrangement presents no perceptible repetition or pattern among its parts does not discredit it as a structure.

mechanism.text: Structure is defined here as relationship between contours and axes, not as regularity. Two forms in one space have relationships whether or not those relationships repeat, so structure is unavoidable and only its kind is chosen.

The source does not reconcile it with its own culturally specific reading claims elsewhere in the chapter.
Read strictly, this definition makes "no structure" impossible and so makes the chapter's title figurative. That is the extractor's observation; the source does not draw it.

item.question: ASCI was a voluntary self-regulator whose rulings members obeyed and non-members often ignored. What single change gave its findings reach over non-members, and what is the general shape of that move?
item.answer: In 2007 the government of India amended the Cable TV Network Rules so that no advertisement ASCI found objectionable could be aired through any cable network. The general shape is that a self-regulator binds only its members, so attaching its findings to a distribution rule that applies to every carrier makes the finding effective against non-members too — the constraint moves from the advertiser, who may not be a member, to the channel that would have to carry the ad, which is bound regardless.

item.question: What does this source say changed after economic liberalisation, and why is this the object in the record most likely to be out of date?
item.answer: She describes a double movement: 'one set of processes creates identifiable symbols of cultural identity while another lays down the universal ground within which these markers of difference operate.' The mechanism she names in the trade is concrete — 'advertising agencies in India — the new Ravi Varmas, if you will — often use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments.' With it comes a narrowing of what 'culture' is taken to mean: circumscribed, globally portable signs of heterogeneity — language, dress, food, music, art, rituals, festivals — grafted onto the protocols of a putatively universal modernity, which relegates cultural difference to leisure and harnesses it to niche marketing. source_terms: Centered-Axis Structure
centering is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualization

because it assumes only one governing alignment axis; because that axis is "buried" within the area of the material, rather than marked by its contours; and because the exterior contours, widths, and depths of centered elements are mutually interdependent
a sense of immediacy, or unfussy directness
item.claim: Centred-axis, or symmetrical, composition arranges elements in response to the format's centre — halfway between left and right or top and bottom edges, and sometimes in response to each other's central axes independently of the format. Although a grid may guide the proportions or positions of centred material, centring is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualisation, for three stated reasons: it assumes only one governing alignment axis; that axis is buried inside the area of the material rather than marked by its contours; and the exterior contours, widths and depths of centred elements are mutually interdependent — driven by their fit and relative proportion as they come into central alignment, not by predetermined intervals. Elements stack sequentially top to bottom or left to right, and the shapes either side of the axis, and the negative spaces beyond them, are identical. The primary visual result is a sense of immediacy or unfussy directness, followed by an appearance of formal simplicity, as the material's quality as a unit dominates perception of its internal divisions.

mechanism.text: A grid works by predetermined intervals marked at the contours of the material; a centred axis works by mutual fit around a line that is not drawn. The two allocate space by incompatible logics, which is why one cannot simply be laid over the other.

scope.conditions: classical or traditional page architecture, print or screen

caveats.text: Samara calls this the classical or traditional page architecture, so the claim is partly a statement about a Western typographic convention rather than about perception.
This is an unusual member of a chapter about breaking grids: the alternative here is older than the grid, not newer.

positive.description: a poster whose typographic and planar image forms situate around the format's central vertical axis while the title reads across both vertical and horizontal axes

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', opening section on paid, owned and earned media (spine 25)
item.question: A client asks for a viral video. What does Sullivan instruct you to say, and what does that imply about how "viral" should be treated in a brief?
item.answer: Politely point out that nobody makes viral videos: it is customers who make things viral, not us. Viral is not a strategy — it is a result of first coming up with a genuinely great idea. The implication is that "go viral" cannot be an objective on a brief, because it names an outcome that is not under the maker's control; what a brief can specify is the idea's quality and its designed shareability. He supports the point with his own counter-example: the creatives behind a print advertisement that became widely shared had no request to go viral on their brief, they simply pushed their thinking to the edge — and his stated lesson is that anything can blow up, including a print advertisement.
item.support: Stated position with one named case. The paid/owned/earned vocabulary he uses around it is a trade taxonomy of the writing period; the substantive claim — that virality is an outcome, not an instruction — does not depend on it.
confounders: accepting 'go viral' as a specifiable objective, which is exactly what he refuses
assuming only video or social formats can spread, which his print example contradicts
confusing the refusal with indifference to earned attention, which he prizes

source_terms: knowing exactly what's going on in every part of your frame
avoid 'passive' areas that don't add much
a little lower, a touch to the left, a couple of steps back

item.claim: A finished composition is one in which every part of the frame has been accounted for, and the instrument for achieving it is a small change of the photographer's position — a little lower, a touch to the left, a couple of steps back — rather than a change of subject. Carroll names the failure as a "passive" area that adds nothing, and gives a set of concrete checks: is a vertical element actually vertical; is a passing object framed rather than cut in two; do the colours balance without one overpowering; is anything creeping into the frame that does not belong. His procedure is to pause before releasing the shutter and look around the frame.

mechanism.text: Elements move relative to one another at different rates as the camera moves, because they lie at different distances. So a small change of viewpoint re-arranges the relationships in the frame without changing the subject, which is why minor adjustment is the right tool.

scope.conditions: any situation with enough time to adjust position before shooting

caveats.text: Explicitly incompatible with the timing-driven work Carroll praises elsewhere: he says pictures like this cannot be snapped, and the decisive moment leaves no time to think. The two disciplines apply to different situations and he does not reconcile them.
"Passive area" is defined only as an area that "doesn't add much" — an aesthetic judgement, not a testable property.

item.source_locator: Introduction
item.question: How does this source bound its own scope, and why does that bound matter more here than in most sources?
item.answer: It bounds itself four ways, explicitly and repeatedly: it examines urban middle-class India from INSIDE that class; it uses 'we' while stating that 'the diversity of India cannot be collapsed into a single undifferentiated "we"'; it declares 'in-built biases' from the author's own experience; and it declines both to prescribe and to judge, stating its purpose is 'to understand what is happening'. It matters more here than elsewhere because the book's most quotable material — the Imperfect Solution thesis, the reading of hierarchy, the essay on Indian traffic — is essayistic generalisation about 'the Indian mind' that reads as a claim about a population, and the Introduction is what forbids that reading.
item.support: 'I am acutely aware that there are many Indias…'; 'the book carries with it in-built biases'
item.confounders: The rhetorical force of the later essays makes it easy to forget the Introduction's disclaimers.

item.question: A colleague cites the 30% lift as independently verified evidence that the ABCDs work. On the source's own presentation, what can honestly be said about that figure and what cannot?
item.answer: It is a reported measurement result, so it is more than an assertion — but it is reported by the company that sells advertising on the platform the research validates, from a study named but not published on any of the three pages. No method, comparison baseline, market coverage or dispersion is given, and neither "short-term sales likelihood" nor "long-term brand contribution" is defined. The independent-reviewer language on the Think with Google page (Ipsos as research partner, Nielsen and Kantar as two independent reviewers) is stated about how the framework was arrived at, not offered as verification of these two numbers. And the figure is claimed for the ABCDs as a set: the source never decomposes it by principle. Third- party involvement moderates the publisher's interest here; it does not remove it.

item.rationale: SPEC-01 carries aspect ratios as a flat list of delivery requirements. This source treats the frame's proportion as a compositional decision with consequences: a square has no direction and pulls the eye inward, a vertical does not by itself produce a sense of tallness, a wide frame is called for by shapes that continue across it. That gives a reason a ratio might be chosen rather than merely required, and a reason a given subject may fail in a required ratio.

applicability.when: a delivery ratio is being chosen, or a subject is being assessed against a required ratio
applicability.limits: Where the ratio is externally mandated the causal direction reverses and this supplies only a warning, not a choice. The square's claimed connotation is undercut by the source's own history — photographers used the square because their film was that shape — so the geometric claims here are better supported than the cultural one.

source_terms: An advertiser of many years' standing, spending as high as $700,000 per year, told the writer he did not know whether his advertising was worth anything or not.
End an ad with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes you that he read the ad through. The scarcity of replies will amaze you.
Men getting back 30 per cent of their cost when they might get 150 per cent. And the facts could be easily proved.
Every line of a big store's ad is charged to the proper department. And every inch used must the next day justify its cost.

Advertising is prima facie evidence that the man who pays believes that advertising is good... So he takes it like some secret tonic which others have endorsed. If the business thrives, the tonic gets the credit.
item.claim: The source proposes a specific cheap diagnostic for advertising whose effect is unknown: end the advertisement with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes in that he read it through, and the scarcity of replies will amaze the advertiser. It is offered in a reported exchange with an advertiser of many years' standing spending up to $700,000 a year who said he did not know whether his advertising was worth anything, and to whom the writer replied that he did know it was utterly unprofitable and could prove it in one week. The diagnosis behind the proposal is that unmeasured advertising survives by default attribution: advertising is taken as prima facie evidence that the man who pays believes in it, like a secret tonic others have endorsed, so if the business thrives the tonic gets the credit and otherwise the failure is put down to fate. The contrast the source draws is with a big store, where every line is charged to the proper department and every inch must justify its cost the next day.

mechanism.text: A payment large enough to be worth claiming converts readership into a countable act, so a quantity that is otherwise invisible becomes observable for the price of the few claims made. The reason it is needed is that a growing business supplies a default explanation for the advertising, and nothing forces the attribution to be tested.

scope.conditions: national advertising running without a key, where no return can be traced

caveats.text: THE PROPOSED TEST WAS NEVER RUN, or at least no run of it is reported. "The scarcity of replies will amaze you" is a prediction of the result, offered in the same sentence as the proposal, in a book whose argument is that predictions must not be trusted. It is recorded as a proposed diagnostic, not as a finding.
The instrument measures reading, not selling, and the source does not distinguish them. Even a run of it would answer a narrower question than the one the $700,000 advertiser asked.

"Men getting back 30 per cent of their cost when they might get 150 per cent" is an assertion about other people's unmeasured advertising, made in the course of arguing that assertions about unmeasured advertising are worthless, and immediately followed by "the facts could be easily proved" — which is a claim that proof is available, not proof. Recorded as the clearest instance in this span of the book applying a standard to others that it does not meet.
The default-attribution diagnosis is the durable content here and is genuinely sharp: a growing business will absorb any expenditure into its success story unless something separates them.

source_stated_problems: those ads are always unkeyed. The money is spent blindly, merely to satisfy some advertising whim
The business is growing through many efforts combined, and advertising is given its share of the credit.
source_stated_remedies: End an ad with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes you that he read the ad through.
Men and methods will be measured by the known returns.

counter.description: an advertiser of many years' standing spending up to $700,000 a year who did not know whether his advertising was worth anything

positive.description: a big store charging every line of its advertisement to the proper department, with every inch required to justify its cost the next day

source_terms: attractions
items
cinema of attractions
item.claim: Dwyer reports Vasudevan's argument that Indian cinema's relationship between narrative, performance sequence and action spectacle is loosely structured in the fashion of a "cinema of attractions" (Gunning and Gaudreault), and describes what the song sequence is licensed to suspend: real time, with the heroine changing costume repeatedly within one sequence; location, which may move from India to Switzerland without any reference to moving in space; and narrative consequence, since love "may be expressed in the song but not necessarily acknowledged in the narrative." She adds that eroticism in the movies is largely contained within the song, which also contains other breaks in continuity such as numerous costume changes and a whole different range of gesture and movement.

mechanism.text: An attraction is a unit the audience accepts as suspending the film's own rules for its duration. Because the suspension is bounded and signalled, material that could not survive inside the narrative — costume changes without elapsed time, continents crossed without travel, eroticism, declarations that leave no trace — can be carried there without damaging the narrative it interrupts.

scope.conditions: Hindi commercial cinema. Dwyer notes that attractions appeared in certain genres of early Indian cinema (the stunt and the mythological), entered the previously middle-class 'social' by the 1950s, were largely eschewed by state-sponsored realism after Prasad's 1970s segmentation, and were "deployed to the full" by the aesthetic of mobilisation. The device is period-differentiated by the source, not constant.

caveats.text: Dwyer expressly tracks the device's uneven presence across genres and decades, so 'Hindi film suspends continuity in songs' as a flat statement is weaker than what she says
the source treats the audience's acceptance of the suspension as given and does not evidence it

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed p. 55 (Chapter 18, 'Negative Advertising')
item.question: Hopkins claims a positive advertisement outpulls a negative one four to one. State the claim exactly as he makes it, including what he attaches to it.
item.answer: He says: compare the results of two advertisements, one negative and one positive, one presenting the dark side and one the bright, one warning and the other inviting — "You will find that the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, IF YOU HAVE OUR EXPERIENCE." The conditional is his and it is routinely dropped in quotation. He reports no comparison at all: no product, no pair of advertisements, no returns. It is an outcome claimed on records he does not show, explicitly conditioned on the reader's records resembling his. Note also that the figure is attached only to the framing claim, not to his separate claims that attacking rivals is bad policy or that assuming compliance outperforms implying neglect.
item.support: p.55: "Compare the results of two ads, one negative, one positive... You will find that the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, if you have our experience."
confounders: Quoting 'four to one' as a measured result — the standard citation of this passage.
Extending the figure to the whole chapter's doctrine rather than the one claim it is attached to.
Reading the prohibition on attacking rivals as evidenced by the four-to-one claim; it rests on policy and on 1923 medium acceptance rules.

item.source_locator: Essay 'The Dhania Factor'
item.question: A researcher observes affluent Indian shoppers still demanding free coriander with vegetables and concludes they are price-sensitive. What does this source argue instead, and how confident is it?
item.answer: That the demand has nothing to do with affordability. The author's claim is that it is made in affluent neighbourhoods and crowded flats alike, and that its function is to make the transaction feel complete — 'sneaking in additional value to make the transaction fulfilling' — so the free extra is a marker of closure whose monetary size is irrelevant. He attributes the disposition to an ingrained cultural memory of scarcity rather than to present need. His confidence is explicitly hedged on the causal attribution: he writes it 'has perhaps more to do with' scarcity memory. The load-bearing claim — invariance across income — is not hedged and is entirely unmeasured, which is notable because it is exactly the kind of claim a survey could test.
item.support: 'It has nothing to do with affordability; it is about sneaking in additional value to make the transaction fulfilling.'
item.confounders: Scoped to urban middle-class India by the source's own Introduction; not a claim about Indian consumers as such.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 35-36 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
item.question: Hopkins describes two different verification controls in chapter 11. What failure does each one catch, and why does he need both?
item.answer: The first tests the advertiser's own assertions: chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims, because a true claim will be a big factor while an untrue one may prove a boomerang and may bar the advertising from good mediums — and he notes it is remarkable how often a maker proves wrong about assertions he has made for years. The second guards the writer's reasoning rather than the client's facts: in every line involving scientific details a censor is appointed, because a well-informed ad-writer may still draw wrong inferences from correct facts, so an authority passes on every advertisement. He needs both because they catch different failures — a false premise, and a false inference from a true premise — and testing the premise does nothing about the second.
item.support: p.35: "Often chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims... If untrue, it may prove a boomerang. And it may bar our ads from good mediums." p.36: "The ad-writer, however well-informed, may draw wrong inferences from facts. So an authority passes on every advertisement."
confounders: Treating the censor as a legal or compliance review; his stated concern is inference from facts.
Collapsing both into 'fact-checking', which loses the distinction the passage exists to make.
Reading the motive as ethical; his stated reasons are persuasive force, boomerang risk and medium admissibility.

item.source_locator: plate insert, Fevicol plate (images/00005.jpg)
item.question: An adhesive brand has no product demonstration budget and no headline. What does the reproduced Fevicol execution do instead, and what does the device require of its audience?
item.answer: It carries the whole argument in one photograph: an overcrowded Indian suburban train with dozens of men hanging off the side of a carriage, on which a 'FEVICOL — The Ultimate Adhesive' panel is mounted. There is no headline and no body copy; the adhesion claim is made by the juxtaposition alone, and the viewer infers it rather than being told. What the device requires is that the scene already be culturally familiar — it recruits an everyday sight the audience knows, so it does not travel to an audience that has not seen an Indian suburban train. That dependence is the extractor's observation from the plate, not something the source states; the book's caption asserts only that good creative work is possible for a humble category.
item.support: Caption: 'The Fevicol campaign was proof that scintillating creative advertising can happen for even a humble adhesive.' Plate inspected at 566 px.
item.confounders: The source does not date this execution and gives no outcome data for it.

item.what_it_is: A two-axis chart, credited to Greg Stevenson. The horizontal axis runs FAILS to WORKS; the vertical axis runs MAKES SENSE to SEEMS WEIRD. Roughly two dozen items are placed in the four quadrants.
item.what_the_figure_shows_that_the_text_does: Almost all of it. The text beside the figure says only that the top-right quadrant holds "advances made in pure science", that in the other quadrants human perception and emotionality are integral, and that the bicycle is a strange inclusion because physicists still cannot fully explain how bicycles work. Every other placement exists only in the picture.
item.why_it_matters: The figure is the book's thesis in one image, and several of its placements are the strongest claims on the page — that Marxism and economies of scale make sense and fail, that placebos and Red Bull seem weird and work. A text-only extraction of this section would carry the thesis and lose every example that supports it.

item.source_locator: plate insert, Air India plate (images/00012.jpg)
item.question: How does the reproduced Air India poster get an Indian carrier to claim a foreign destination, and why is the device repeatable?
item.answer: By inserting the airline's Maharaja mascot into a set of foreign icons and scaling him down. The plate shows 'London' in a heavy blue display face over four flat-illustrated Buckingham Palace guardsmen in red tunics and bearskins, with the moustachioed Maharaja in a striped turban standing among them at roughly half their height. The joke is carried entirely by the scale relationship and the uniform rhyme; there is no copy. The inferred reason it repeats is that the mascot's small stature and deferential posture make the encounter comic rather than competitive, so the carrier can claim the destination without claiming parity with it — and only the icon set has to change for a new destination.
item.support: Caption: 'one of the most widely recognized advertising icons for many decades'. Plate inspected.
item.confounders: Only one destination execution is reproduced, so repeatability is inferred from a single instance plus the source's statement that the icon ran for decades. The mascot is a mid-century caricature of an Indian aristocratic type, which the source does not discuss.

source_terms: They learn their appealing claims by tests—by comparing results from various headlines.
Gradually they accumulate a list of claims important enough to use. All those claims appear in every ad thereafter.
in usual lines a number of claims appeal to a large percentage. Then present those claims in every ad for their effect on that percentage.
item.claim: The set of claims an advertisement carries is built by a two-stage procedure: claims are first qualified individually by comparing results from various headlines, and the ones that prove important enough are then added to a standing list which appears in every advertisement thereafter. Testing selects the members; it does not select one winner to run alone. The source frames this as what the best advertisers do, and as the reason their advertisements stop changing.

mechanism.text: Different facts convince different people, so a claim that loses a headline comparison can still be the fact that converts a share of readers once they are reading. Headline testing measures pulling power; the standing list preserves converting power.

source_terms: Affiliation and dominion are different ways to measure status
Dominion is a vertical experience, above or below. Affiliation is a horizontal one: Who's standing next to me?

item.claim: Godin splits status into two different things being counted. Dominion asks who has more power, whose side is winning, what is mine and not yours — a vertical measure. Affiliation asks who knows you, who trusts you, what your circle is like, where you stand within the tribe — a horizontal one. The operational point is the priority: which measure applies is the customer's, not the marketer's, and the way you see the world matters far less than the worldview of those you seek to serve. He notes the two behave differently under abundance — affiliation welcomes the network effect because more affiliation benefits everyone affiliated, while dominion is scarcity-bound because someone must be below.

mechanism.text: A signal that raises standing on one measure is inert or hostile on the other: an invitation to belong is worthless to someone counting who is winning, and a claim to dominate repels someone counting who is in sync.

scope.conditions: audiences whose status measure can be observed from what they attend to

caveats.text: Godin says the same person applies different measures in different settings — his example is a child who cares only about winning on the field and only about who sits next to him on the bus. So the pair describes a situation, not a personality type, and treating it as a segmentation would misread it.
The claim that modern urban, internet, arts and innovation culture is built primarily on affiliation rather than dominion is a broad cultural assertion of 2018 with no support.

source_stated_remedies: If you want to market to someone who measures dominion or affiliation, you'll need to be aware of what's being measured and why

item.source_locator: Essay 'The Power of the Imperfect Solution'
item.question: State the Imperfect Solution thesis, separate the part with general force from the part with none, and say why the separation matters.
item.answer: The thesis is that the Indian disposition to accept the almost-good-enough — usually deplored as *chalta hai* — encodes a defensible position about time: solutions are temporary equilibria, imperfection is a permanent condition conferred by time, and holding a solution perfect costs ever-increasing effort until it becomes unsustainable. The part with general force is the maintenance-cost mechanism: keeping any solution against a changing environment requires continuing effort that rises as the environment diverges from the one the solution was built for. The part with none is the cultural attribution — 'the Indian mind' versus 'Western analysis' — which is a pair of essayistic generalisations for which no evidence of any kind is offered. The separation matters because this is the object in the book most at risk of being universalised: it records that DESAI ARGUES this, and is not evidence that Indians or Westerners think in these ways.
item.support: 'keeping a solution perfect will take an ever increasing amount of effort that eventually becomes unsustainable'
item.confounders: The author anticipates the charge of arguing for passivity and answers it rhetorically rather than with evidence.

source_terms: lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot
the great Indian rope trick of numbers
item.claim: Bijapurkar states the structural claim on which most of the book rests: "Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot," where developed-market marketers "are used to working with an exactly opposite demand structure — a few people consuming a lot each, adding up to a lot." She draws the consequence explicitly: "neither the pricing paradigms nor the cost structures of their usual, tried and tested global business models are appropriate for India's demand structure." She names the counter-intuitive consequence the "great Indian rope trick of numbers" — a small penetration of a large population produces a large absolute market, so lower-income groups can out-consume higher-income groups in absolute terms.

mechanism.text: Business models encode assumptions about consumption per head. A retail format sized for a catchment that consumes a lot per head will not reach viability in a catchment that consumes little per head, regardless of how many people are in it — which is why, on her account, the first organised retail forays failed and why a small-format chain with an aggregated back end succeeded by "mimicking the structure of the customer demand".

scope.conditions: Stated for India and for emerging markets more generally, on data to 2008. Bijapurkar draws the general form from the BRIC comparison — economies "individually poor but collectively rich" — and cites Goldman Sachs's *Dreaming with the BRICs*.

caveats.text: the two-wheeler evidence was inspected and it holds. Figure 4.1 (rural two-wheeler market) shows penetration falling 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across income groups while household counts rise 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, giving two-wheeler numbers of 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group therefore does have about 1.6 times the units of the high-income group, exactly as the text claims. Source: Indian Readership Survey 2008

source_terms: overpainting
hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze
secular darshan
item.claim: Patel documents overpainting — applying oil or gouache over a photographic still, often with a knife in thick textured strokes — as the defining technique of Indian film poster art in the 1970s and '80s, names its principal practitioner (Diwakar Karkare, trained at the Bombay School of Art, who introduced it on Daag in 1973), and states what it was for: it "provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion." She traces its lineage to nineteenth-century Indian painted photography, where studios employed up to six artists to paint a photograph, and reports that the surviving practice — memorial photographs of the deceased — produces "hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze through the sharp reworking of the eyes."

mechanism.text: A photograph fixes what was in front of the camera; paint laid over it can select, exaggerate and intensify without discarding the photographic base. The result is not more faithful but more legible as feeling: Patel calls this "enhancing of reality" and says it is what Karkare aimed at. Combined with centrality of placement and a returned gaze, she argues it produces an image that closes the psychological gap between subject and viewer.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters of the 1970s and '80s specifically. Patel dates its displacement precisely: through much of the 1990s overpainting "was gradually almost replaced by computer-generated imagery," and Karkare closed Studio Diwakar in 1988 because he believed computer technology was displacing the artist and the new designs required no real artistic input.

caveats.text: the technique is historically closed by the source's own account; it is documentation of a superseded craft, not a current method

Patel's application of 'darshan' here is explicitly downgraded to a 'secular darshan', which is a weaker claim than the one Dwyer discusses in chapters 1-2. The two authors are not asserting the same thing

source_terms:
The trick is to be able to analyze, as specifically as possible, what the most prevalent formal conditions are among all those that might be present.
"What kind of images am I using?" "Is geometry important in the shapes or relationship?" "Is there spatial depth, and, if so, what creates it—transparency, scale change, overlap?" "Do I sense movement, and, if so, is it lateral, vertical, frenzied, calm, and repeated?"
The answers to these questions are the system's rules.
item.claim: An irregular system's rules are not designed in advance; they are read off the work that already exists. The stated method is to analyse as specifically as possible which formal conditions are the most prevalent among all those present, and the source gives the diagnostic questions verbatim: what kind of images am I using; is geometry important in the shapes or relationships; is there spatial depth and, if so, what creates it — transparency, scale change, overlap; do I sense movement and, if so, is it lateral, vertical, frenzied, calm, repeated. The answers to those questions are the system's rules. Each rule may then be reinterpreted in different instances according to the variables inherent in it and to different extremes — if cropping images into an irregular trapezoid is a rule, the trapezoids may all be one size and shape, or vary in size, or vary in the measures of their sides, or extend to parallelograms and triangles.

mechanism.text: An intuitive layout has properties before it has rules. Naming the dominant properties turns what was arrived at by instinct into something repeatable, which is what makes a system possible without a grid.

scope.conditions: defining a system for a project already composed by intuitive means

caveats.text: The procedure is retrospective by design — the rules are extracted from work already made. This inverts the chapter-1 order in which a structure is derived before the pages are built, and it is the same author describing a different order of work rather than contradicting himself.
The four questions are a starting list offered as "a great way to begin", not a closed checklist, and the source gives no test for whether the answers found are the prevalent conditions.

source_stated_remedies: analyse as specifically as possible which formal conditions are most prevalent
ask what images, whether geometry matters, whether there is depth and what creates it, and whether there is movement and of what kind
take the answers as the system's rules and define the permitted variables of each

item.claim: Advertisements that are not keyed can cost their owners many times what results need cost. The source gives one case: a five-dollar article whose advertisement produced replies at 85 cents each; a second advertisement, submitted by someone who thought it better, produced replies at $14.20 each; a third produced replies at an average of 41 cents each over two years. The source invites the reader to consider that difference across 250,000 replies per year, says thousands of advertisers spend large sums on a guess, and concludes that they are paying for sales from 2 to 35 times what they need cost.

The 250,000 replies per year is offered as a multiplier to consider, not as the volume any of the three actually ran at.

The "2 to 35 times" range is the ratio between these three figures (85 cents and $14.20 against 41 cents), so it is a restatement of the same single case rather than an independent finding across advertisers.

item.claim: Desai's finding across the thirty-year window is asymmetric: the surface of the matrimonial format changed considerably — appearance descriptors multiplied, individuals expressed needs with more specificity, the chaperoned ten-minute meeting stretched to two or three meetings with chaperoning becoming optional — while the underlying model did not. Advertisements are still placed by parents, the parties are still called "boy" and "girl" whatever their age, personality is still barely mentioned, and the transaction is still between stations in life rather than between individuals. Caste mention, on his study's evidence, did not decline at all.

item.answer: On a line then before him, sample inquiries obtained by mail averaged 70 cents each, and the same advertisement brought inquiries at 18 to 22 cents each when the coupons were presented at a local store; he adds that often four times as many will present a coupon at a store as will mail it. On another line, where three routes were offered — write, telephone, or call at a store — 70 per cent of inquiries came by telephone. His explanation is friction, not motivation: most people write few letters, writing is an effort, they may have no stamps in the house, and most will pay carfare to get a sample rather than two cents postage. It is stronger than most of the book because it holds the advertisement constant — "the same ad" — varies one factor, and reports a returned cost on both arms. It is still one unnamed line, with no market, period, volume, or statement of whether the arms ran simultaneously.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3, printed p. 171; Ch. 4, printed pp. 187-192
item.question: Describe overpainting as this source documents it: the technique, who introduced it, what it was for, and where it came from.
item.answer: The technique is applying oil or gouache over a photographic still, often with a knife in thick textured strokes, and it is documented as the defining technique of Indian film poster art in the 1970s and '80s. Its principal practitioner is named — Diwakar Karkare, trained at the Bombay School of Art, who introduced it on Daag in 1973. Its purpose is stated: it 'provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion'. Its lineage is traced to nineteenth-century Indian painted photography, where studios employed up to six artists to paint a single photograph, and to the one surviving branch of that practice, memorial photographs of the deceased, which produce 'hyper-reality, a solidification of certain features and an intensification of the gaze through the sharp reworking of the eyes'. The knife-laid impasto over photographic underlay was confirmed by direct inspection of the plates in this pass.
item.support: it 'provided a means for artists to place their own interpretation over the photographic image, primarily allowing them to express and emphasize emotion.'
item.confounders: Overpainting is not retouching. The point is not to correct the photograph but to add an interpretation the photograph cannot supply.
