item.source_locator: Ch. 3, printed pp. 134-142; Ch. 4, printed pp. 190-199
item.question: What is the distinction between naturalist techniques and the schemata that carried them, and what did Indian practice take up?
item.answer: The techniques are perspective, anatomy, modelling and the rendering of light and shadow. The schemata are the institutionally sanctioned 'post-sacred' systems of signification through which those techniques entered the colonial context: romanticism and the picturesque, neoclassicism, bourgeois realism, ethnographic documentation. Jain reports Geeta Kapur's observation, and builds on it, that realism was construed in nineteenth-century Indian discourse 'to mean an ENABLING TECHNIQUE rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation within a specific historical context'. THE TECHNIQUES WERE TAKEN UP AND THE SCHEMATA LARGELY WERE NOT. She records the vernacular word some artists used instead of the English 'realism' — sajivta, 'livingness' or 'lifelikeness' — and what it puts at issue: 'at issue here is not the reality of the gods, but how alive they are'. So naturalist rendering here is in the service of presence rather than of documentary truth, which is why a picture can be highly modelled and make no claim to have depicted an event.
item.support: realism as 'an enabling technique rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation'
item.confounders: The assumption that naturalist technique brings a realist truth-claim with it is exactly what this passage denies, and it is a common way of misreading images that borrow a technique across traditions.

source_terms: naturalism and other pictorial technologies served to reconfigure or recontextualize existing forms and thereby expand the domain of commodity address
item.claim: Jain argues that the deployment of new image-making techniques, including technological mass reproduction and elements of Western naturalism, "helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies — that is, to 'naturalize' an expanded category of the popular." Her worked case is M. V. Dhurandhar's 1932 Woodward's Gripe Water calendar, which she reads as deploying two distinct registers of signification at once: a perspectival, narrative, allegorical register aimed at a modernising Indian and European resident elite, and an indexical, frontal, iconic register that institutes a divine presence. She states the general point: "commodity aesthetics provided a ground for reformulations of community and locality, in this case by drawing colonial residents and the Indian elite into a common frame of address," driven by "the opposing expansive and conservative imperatives of mass production: to solicit the largest possible audience while also drawing on familiar frames of reference."
item.interpretation_basis: The reading of the Dhurandhar calendar as doubled in address, and the generalisation from it to the expansive function of naturalism, are Jain's. She advances the position explicitly against accounts that treat Indian popular aesthetics as an iconic realm resistant to Western naturalism.

mechanism.text: Mass production pulls in two directions at once: it must reach as many people as possible, and it must remain legible within frames those people already hold. A single artefact that carries two registers can satisfy both, addressing constituencies that would otherwise require separate artefacts — which is why technique expansion and audience expansion travel together.

scope.conditions: Indian commercial imagery from roughly the 1880s to the mid-twentieth century. Jain marks the Dhurandhar case as exceptional — "it represents something of an aberration, a path not taken" — because the constituency it addressed did not last.

caveats.text: the central worked example is one the author calls an aberration and a path not taken. The mechanism is argued from a case she says did not persist, which is unusual and should be visible to anyone using the object

Jain is arguing against Pinney's and Rajadhyaksha's readings by name. The object records her position in a disagreement among specialists, not a settled result

item.claim: Patel's organising claim for chapter 3 is that Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing "the aesthetic vocabulary of the period." She sets out the sequence: text-only newspaper notices and handbills (1896 onward); the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique applied to Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to Ajanta revival and used when a studio wanted to signal that a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity, which "did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s" in India because it was seen as Western cultural imperialism; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; and computer-aided design from the 1990s.

mechanism.text: Patel's stated mechanism is that a style already carries associations before a poster uses it, so choosing a style is a way of saying something the image itself does not have to depict. She states it explicitly for the art-school style: it was "referred to whenever there was a need to communicate more than the basic information about a film," and in these instances "the mode of representation was often used to reflect or reinforce underlying messages about current cultural and political issues."

scope.conditions: Indian film advertising 1896-2002. Every phase is dated by the source. The claim is a periodisation, not a description of a standing style.

caveats.text: THIS IS THE OBJECT THAT PROTECTS THE REST FROM BEING FLATTENED. The source's own thesis is that the style changed repeatedly and that each change tracked a change in its environment. item.claim: Dwyer reports Barry King's distinction between two forms of acting — impersonation, where the actor transforms body and voice, and personification, where the actor's persona retains significant similarities across performances — and states that the latter is found most often in Hindi cinema. item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.source_locator: Ch. "Working the frame", sub-heading "Make every inch count" (spine 15)
item.question: Carroll's remedy for a composition that is not quite working is to change position "even very slightly". Why does such a small movement do anything at all, on his account?
item.answer: Because the elements in the frame do not move together. They lie at different distances from the camera, so as the camera shifts they move relative to one another at different rates. A small change of viewpoint therefore re-arranges the relationships inside the frame without changing the subject at all — which is why the instrument is a couple of steps rather than a different picture. His instruction is to change position slightly and keep an eye on how all the elements move around in relation to each other.
item.support: Working the frame spread: a little lower, a touch to the left, a couple of steps back; these minor adjustments make the fencepost vertical, frame the taxi rather than cut it in two, and ensure nothing is creeping into the frame; change position even very slightly and watch how the elements move in relation to each other.
confounders: explaining it as a change of perspective distortion or focal length; neither changes here
assuming the point is to find a better subject rather than a better arrangement of the same one

item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Advertising and the Communication of Meaning', opening of 'The Star Image', printed p. 183
item.question: Patel's account of why a poster opens with a face has two stages. Separate them, and say which one survives outside the culture.
item.answer: Stage one is pre-cultural and stage two is not, and she separates them explicitly. First, an image of a human face is 'instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all': of any mix of images the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a particular star, which arouses expectations built up over that star's career. Only the first survives outside the culture, and she states the boundary in the same breath — 'an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response'. The practical consequence is that a face still buys the glance anywhere; what the glance then delivers is entirely dependent on the viewer holding the star's history.
item.support: 'an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response.'
item.confounders: Collapsing the two stages produces the false generalisation that 'putting a face on it works' — which is true only of the attention effect, not of anything the face is supposed to mean.

item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Indian Cinema', section 'Attraction: the Star', printed p. 33
item.question: This source describes darshan as a structure of looking. What is unusual about the direction of power in it, and how far does the author herself extend the claim?
item.answer: The look runs both ways and the power sits with the image rather than with the viewer: the beholder TAKES darshan (darshan lena) and the object GIVES darshan (darshan dena), and the image 'authorizes the look (rather than merely being its object), thereby benefiting the beholder'. That inverts the usual direction of power in accounts of spectatorship, where the gaze belongs to the one who looks. Dwyer reports its cinematic use — the star appears in tableau scenes that invite darshan, which hierarchises the look and lends the star the associations of kings and gods, the traditional granters of darshan. Her own extension is narrow and she draws the line herself: she reports this as Prasad's and Vasudevan's argument, says Vasudevan's contention about stasis and tableaux is one she finds persuasive, and then bounds it — while it may operate within the film to produce the star, she cannot otherwise see any culturally specific ways in which the star is produced.
item.support: the image 'authorizes the look (rather than merely being its object), thereby benefiting the beholder.'
item.confounders: The common summary is that Indian audiences 'worship' film stars. The source's claim is narrower and formal — about how a look is structured and where it is authorised from — and Dwyer explicitly declines the broader version.

item.label: indian_advertising_clearance_as_a_multi_gate_route
item.description: The clearance route an Indian advertisement had to pass, as the book describes it: broadcaster pre-approval of the storyboard, broadcaster approval of the finished film, self-regulatory review by ASCI on complaint, and separate production clearances (Animal Welfare Board; cinema censor certificate for theatrical shorts). Each gate can reject work the previous gate passed.

whole_system_claim.text: Clearance in Indian advertising is not one decision but a series of independent ones held by different bodies at different moments, and passing an earlier gate carries no guarantee at a later one — so clearance risk is distributed across the whole production timeline rather than concentrated before it starts.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The author describes each of these bodies, but he describes them as episodes in one chapter's narrative rather than as a route. The claim that they constitute a sequence with independent gates is the extractor's. What justifies it is the Sweetex case he reports first-hand, in which storyboard approval demonstrably did not bind the finished-film decision, and the KamaSutra case, in which Doordarshan withdrew a storyboard approval it had already given. The independence of the gates is a fact he evidences twice; that it is a general structure is our reading.

dependencies.nature: broadcaster clearance and self-regulatory review are independent; passing one does not settle the other

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. The existence and remit of each body is stated by the source and the independence of the first two gates is evidenced twice from the author's own experience. What is the extractor's is the ordering into one route and the claim that this is the general structure rather than a set of episodes. Note also that the regime described is substantially historical: the Doordarshan monopoly gates no longer operate as described, and the ASCI figures are as at 2016. The system should be consumed as a shape, not as a current compliance path.

source_terms: The question is not 'What sort of market for this [global] strategy?', but 'What sort of strategy for this [local] market?'
made for India
item.claim: Bijapurkar's organising argument is that firms approaching this market habitually ask the question the wrong way round. They arrive with a tried-and-tested strategy and ask what size of market exists for it; the answer is usually "not much"; and the firm concludes the market is underdeveloped and will return later. She states that this "throws the baby out with the bathwater," and that the right question is "what should be my local, customized strategy for the Indian market" given my competencies and comparative advantages.

mechanism.text: Asking what market exists for a fixed offer makes the offer's parameters — its price, its performance point, its cost structure, its business model — into constraints on the answer. Since those parameters were set for a different demand structure, the addressable market is bounded by an accident of history rather than by the market's actual size, and the firm reads a constraint it imposed as a fact about the market.

scope.conditions: Stated for firms entering or operating in India, principally multinationals, over the period 1991-2009. Bijapurkar bounds her own advocacy: she is arguing for reframing, not claiming that a reframed strategy will succeed.

caveats.text: the worked case is a glucometer company that declined to enter around 1999, told through a single unnamed account with no follow-up. The reader is never told what the company did next or whether the alternative model she proposes would have worked. This is the book's characteristic evidential shape and it recurs
the author is a consultant arguing for the value of the work she sells, which is customized market strategy. That is not a disqualification, but the interest is real and the book does not disclose it

source_terms: We need hierarchy because it helps simplify our world by making it deterministic. Science is better than commerce so why tax your mind about what to choose? It standardizes the world on a single linear dimension and helps you know your place without any ambiguity.
The individual and her desires are extracted from the equation; we study what we deserve rather than what we want.
item.claim: Desai argues that the pervasiveness of hierarchy in Indian institutional life functions to simplify: it collapses many dimensions onto one linear ordering, which removes ambiguity about one's place and removes the individual's preference from the decision entirely — "we study what we deserve rather than what we want". His instances are the Science/Commerce/Arts ordering in education, which he notes is justified neither by career prospects nor by difficulty, and the graded exemptions from airport frisking.

item.question: In the St Peter's picture Freeman credits the energy of the frame to something more specific than "diagonals are dynamic". What is the actual mechanism he names, and what does his own counterfactual concede?
item.answer: The mechanism is opposition, not diagonality. He points out that the diagonals in that frame are entirely a creation of camera angle and lens, and that rotating the camera about its viewing axis turns every vertical in the building into a diagonal running counter to the already-diagonal shafts of sunlight. It is that counter-running of two diagonal sets he credits with the energy. His counterfactual is honest about the cost: had the camera been levelled, the shafts of light would have been longer, but the picture would have been less dynamic and more rigidly architectural. Something is given up as well as gained.

item.claim: A dissolve is a gradual change from the end of one shot into the beginning of the next, achieved by superimposing both while ramping one down in opacity and the other up, so the images are seen overlapping. Unlike the cut it attracts attention to itself on purpose. Its chief use is to play with time — condensing a long event into a montage, moving into a flashback, or slowing events with slow motion so the audience has time to absorb them. Also called a lap dissolve, a lap, or a video mix.

mechanism.text: Simultaneous downward and upward ramping of opacity over a period of time, so that both images are on screen together while one replaces the other.

item.question: An advertiser of many years spends $700,000 a year and says he does not know whether his advertising is worth anything. What does Hopkins propose, what does the proposal measure, and what is his diagnosis of how the situation arose?
item.answer: He proposes ending an advertisement with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes in that he read the advertisement through, predicting that the scarcity of replies will amaze the advertiser — he claims he could prove the advertising utterly unprofitable in one week. What it measures is READING, not selling, which is a narrower question than the one asked, and he does not distinguish them. His diagnosis is default attribution: advertising is taken as prima facie evidence that the man who pays believes in it, so he takes it like a secret tonic others have endorsed, and if the business thrives the tonic gets the credit while otherwise the failure is put down to fate. His contrast is the big store, where every line is charged to the proper department and every inch must justify its cost the next day. Note that he predicts the result in the same sentence as the proposal and reports no run of it.

item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a segmentation whose axis is not spending power but VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost. item.question: What is the objection to 'the Indian middle class' as a planning input, and why is the author's own position in the story evidentially interesting?
item.answer: That the category has no agreed definition, so its size varies enormously with whichever definition is chosen, and a number quoted without its definition is therefore uninterpretable — yet it is routinely used as a planning input, with capacity built against it. The objection is methodological rather than empirical: she is not arguing the middle class is smaller than claimed, but that 'how big is it' is not a well-formed question until the definition and the population base are stated. WHAT MAKES HER POSITION EVIDENTIALLY INTERESTING is that she discloses her own role in creating the myth she now attacks — she was part of the industry that produced and circulated the number. That is testimony against interest, which is why the record treats the disclosure as STRENGTHENING the object rather than as a caveat on it: an insider naming a construction she helped build is a more reliable witness to how it was built than an outside critic. The affluence-layer material she offers instead was recovered from Table 5.1 in this pass, which exists only as an image in this copy: income percentiles, household counts and per-tier ownership of colour TV, refrigerator, two-wheeler, car, landline, washing machine and PC, sourced to IRS 2008.
item.support: Ch. 5; and the author's own account of her role in the middle-class myth.
item.confounders: The lesson is not 'the middle class is a myth' but 'a segment label without a stated definition and population base is not a planning input'. The first is a claim about India; the second is a rule about labels.

item.question: A documentary series is shot entirely head-on and squared up, and the photographer says this makes it more objective. How would Freeman respond, and what would he grant?
item.answer: He would call the belief a delusion, and he uses that word. His position is that the treatment certainly looks as if you are approaching the subject head-on and without fancy dramatic angles, which is why it has become the treatment of choice for documenting things, people and places — but the look of objectivity is itself a compositional effect, not a property of the method. What he would grant is that the treatment is genuinely useful and that many serious photographers have used it, naming Sander, Strand and the Bechers. source_terms: Remember that windows are light sources and that they can be filtered just like any other light source.
our lights are probably weaker than the sun, and we would prefer not to dim them even more with the light absorbed by the filter
A better solution would be to put orange theatrical gels on the outside of the window and then shoot with a tungsten white balance.
item.claim: A window is a light source and can be gelled like any other, a possibility the source says motion picture and video photographers use routinely and still photographers tend to overlook. In a room lit by tungsten photographic lights and by daylight through windows, the quick fix is blue gels on the photographic lights and a daylight balance. The better fix inverts it: orange theatrical gel on the outside of the window and a tungsten balance. Both achieve the same colour match. The second is preferred because the photographic lights are probably weaker than the sun, so filtering them costs output where it can least be spared, whereas filtering the window attenuates the stronger source and balances the two intensities as well as their colours.

mechanism.text: A colour-correction filter absorbs light as well as shifting its balance, so which source is filtered determines which source is attenuated; putting the loss on the stronger source improves the intensity ratio at the same time as the colour match.

scope.conditions: interiors with both photographic lighting and daylight

caveats.text: an instance of the general matching principle with an added criterion — where two ways of matching exist, prefer the one that also improves the intensity balance
the source attributes the practice to motion picture and video photographers, which is a claim about another craft's habits rather than about optics

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Other Kinds of Geometric Structure (spine 6)
item.question: An arrangement shows no repetition or pattern among its parts. Does Samara consider it a structure? Give his reasoning.
item.answer: Yes. His starting point is that inserting any form into a space — even a solitary one — creates structure, meaning a set of visual relationships between its contour, the shape of its outer boundary, and its axis, the imaginary line separating its halves, and those of other forms. He then says explicitly that any structure may be fluid and irregular in proportion or interval, and that simply because an arrangement presents no perceptible repetition or pattern among its parts does not discredit it as a structure. He notes that because of our orientation to Earth we typically perceive forms as expressing two primary axes, horizontal and vertical, but offers nature as the counter-catalogue — radial flower petals, the irregular axes of constellations, hexagonal crystal lattices, the helical whorl of DNA.
item.support: "Other Kinds of Geometric Structure": any inserted form creates structure via contour and axis; orthogonal perception attributed to our orientation to Earth; nature's non-orthogonal structures; the explicit statement that absence of perceptible repetition does not discredit a structure.

source_terms: The Law of Shape
A brand's logotype should be designed to fit the eyes. Both eyes.
Legibility is the most important consideration in selecting a typeface used in a logotype.
The meaning lies in the word, or words, not in the visual symbol.
item.claim: Law 16. Three connected claims about visual identity. First shape: because human eyes are mounted side by side, the ideal logotype is horizontal, roughly two and a quarter units wide to one high, and a vertical logotype is at a severe disadvantage, especially on a retail frontage. Second typography: legibility is the most important consideration, over any expressive quality, because a typeface's mood only becomes noticeable through exaggeration and exaggeration costs legibility — a trade the authors say is not worth making. Third symbol: the trademark is overrated, the meaning lies in the word, and it is the name that gives the symbol meaning rather than the reverse. A symbol may come to stand for a name through long association, but the authors say the advantages of using it alone are slim, and that if history has not already given a brand one of the few simple effective symbols it is probably too late to create one.

mechanism.text: For shape, binocular geometry: two eyes side by side make a horizontal field, so a horizontal mark takes maximum advantage of it. For typography, a stated vicious cycle: to make the mood of a face noticeable to an average prospect you must exaggerate it, and exaggeration destroys readability, so the name cannot be read and therefore cannot be remembered. For the symbol, a "rebus" effect: the mark can stand for the name only after the name has given it meaning.

scope.conditions: the horizontal claim is said to hold wherever a logotype is used and to matter most on retail premises

caveats.text: the 2.25:1 proportion is given with no derivation and no evidence; the binocular argument is stated as though it settled the ratio, which it does not
the typography claim rests on a paraphrase of David Ogilvy and on the authors' own rhetorical questions about which typeface Rolex or Rolls-Royce uses; no legibility measurement is cited

item.question: Carroll allows telephoto lenses in some circumstances and warns about them in others. What is the condition that separates the two, and what does he say the lens does to the space in the picture?
item.answer: The condition is whether you could have got close. Telephoto lenses are essential where you are unable to get physically close — his examples are sports and wildlife — but when you are able to get close and choose not to, the images can start to feel predatory. So the fault is not in the lens but in a decision the picture records. To the space, the lens gives the illusion of compressing depth: everything seems flatter, a receding avenue reads as a flat vertical strip rather than leading into the distance, and buildings behave like layered cut-out shapes, which he says makes images look more graphic. He calls the compression an illusion and explains it no further.

item.interpretation_basis: The reading of the siren, and the general claim that status requires reception, are the author's interpretation of observed behaviour. Nothing is measured.

mechanism.text: If a status signal's function is to place others at a distance, then a signal nobody perceives accomplishes nothing. Signal design therefore optimises for unavoidable reception rather than for accuracy or elegance.

caveats.text: the general claim about status signalling is presented as a universal, but it is argued entirely from Indian institutional examples, and this record does not extend it beyond them
the reading of the siren is a rhetorical high point of the essay; the transferable content is the reception requirement, not the metaphor

item.claim: Sullivan's stated starting procedure is to write the thing you want to say flatly and without art, then make it memorable afterwards. He suggests literally beginning a headline with "This is an ad about …" and continuing, on the grounds that even if the result is unusable the writer has focused. He reports Thomas Kemeny's version — start literal, finish lateral — and endorses the image: you begin in a straight direction and then add spin, the way a knight in chess moves forward and then jukes sideways at the end.

mechanism.text: Clarity is established before art is attempted, so the spin has something to be a spin on. The flat statement fixes what must survive, which is what stops the clever version from losing the selling idea in the act of expressing it.

caveats.text: presented as the author's own practice and one of several processes he offers, not as the only route

source_terms: an enabling technique rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation
sajivta
item.claim: Jain reports Geeta Kapur's observation, and builds on it, that "realism" was construed in nineteenth-century Indian discourse "to mean an ENABLING TECHNIQUE rather than a philosophically accredited style of representation within a specific historical context." She draws the distinction out: there is a difference between naturalist TECHNIQUES — perspective, anatomy, modelling, the rendering of light and shadow — and the institutionally sanctioned "post-sacred" schemata of signification through which they entered the colonial context: romanticism and the picturesque, neoclassicism, bourgeois realism, ethnographic documentation. The techniques were taken up; the schemata largely were not. She records the vernacular word some artists used instead of the English "realism" — sajivta, "livingness" or "lifelikeness" — and states what it puts at issue: "at issue here is not the reality of the gods, but how alive they are: how the image brings them to life."

mechanism.text: A technique and the worldview that historically carried it are separable, because a technique is a way of making marks and a worldview is a set of commitments about what marks are for. Where the receiving context has its own commitments, the technique can be adopted to serve those instead. Jain's instance: naturalist modelling was taken up not in its techno-rationalist aspect but in its "personalizing, affective, libidinal aspect, making the divine accessible to devotees as an empathetic presence."

scope.conditions: Nineteenth and twentieth century Indian commercial image-making, principally chromolithography, Nathdwara and the calendar industry.

caveats.text: Jain positions this against Christopher Pinney's account of a 'naturalist blip' between 1878 and 1927 and against readings that align naturalism with disenchantment. She is arguing with named colleagues, and the object should be read as her position in a live scholarly disagreement rather than as settled fact
the separability claim is historical and interpretive. No mechanism is tested; the evidence is the pattern of what was and was not adopted

the same chapter shows the separation is not clean in practice: artists trained in anatomy report frustration at being unable to use it, and 'realism' in their discourse is, in Jain's words, 'an often contradictory, highly overdetermined term'

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Advanced explicitly against other scholars' positions; the source marks the disagreement.

source_terms: triggering a hierarchy of responses
the primary field of expressive action
item.claim: Patel argues that the star portrait is the natural opening component of a poster because it activates a "hierarchy of responses" in two distinct stages that she separates explicitly. First, an image of a human face is "instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all" — of any mix of images, the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a star, which arouses expectations built up over time. She states the boundary in the same breath: "an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response."

mechanism.text: Patel grounds the first stage in the claim that the structuring of human relationships from the earliest stages of life is based on physical appearance and facial recognition, and that the face is "the primary field of expressive action" where all forms of emotion can be made visible, so it holds attention at a deeper level than other visual images. The second stage is not perceptual but cultural: it depends on the viewer holding the star's accumulated text.

scope.conditions: Stated for film posters, Indian and Western alike ("the majority of film posters (both Indian and Western) use portraits"). Stage one is offered as general; stage two is expressly bounded to viewers inside the culture.

caveats.text: THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ABOUT THIS OBJECT IS THE SEPARATION IT MAKES. The source itself divides a putatively universal attentional effect from a culturally-specific recognition effect, and states that the second does not travel. Collapsing the two would be the error the source is guarding against

the first stage is asserted from developmental and expressive premises with no measurement; Patel reports no eye-tracking, no attention study and no test of any kind. It is a plausible mechanism, not a demonstrated one
the source is a 2002 art-historical book, not a perception study, and should not be cited as evidence for a face-attention effect

source_terms: darshan
darshan lena

item.claim: Dwyer describes darshan as a structure of spectation drawn from Hindu religious practice in which the look runs both ways: the beholder TAKES darshan (darshan lena) and the object GIVES darshan (darshan dena). The distinctive feature she draws out is that the image, not the person looking, holds the power — the image "authorizes the look (rather than merely being its object), thereby benefiting the beholder." She reports that this is used in Hindi cinema to construct the star: the star appears in tableau scenes that invite darshan, which hierarchises the look and lends the star the associations of the traditional granters of darshan, kings and gods.

mechanism.text: A look that is authorised by its object rather than by its subject inverts the usual direction of power in spectatorship. Stasis and the tableau hold the figure still and frontal long enough for the exchange to be legible as an exchange rather than as narrative action, which is why Dwyer (following Vasudevan) ties darshan to stasis and tableaux rather than to continuity editing.

scope.conditions: Stated for Hindi commercial cinema and for viewers who hold the code. Dwyer is careful that this is a contested topic: she reports it as Prasad's and Vasudevan's argument, says Vasudevan's contention that stasis and tableaux permit hierarchical darshan is one "I find persuasive," and immediately bounds her own agreement — "while it may operate within the film to produce the star, I cannot otherwise see any culturally specific ways in which the star is produced."

caveats.text: Dwyer explicitly limits her endorsement: she accepts darshan as operating INSIDE the film to produce the star and otherwise finds the Hindi star produced no differently from the Hollywood star. An extraction that reported darshan as a general theory of Indian spectatorship would overstate what she signs up to
the source describes a reading practice available to viewers who hold the code; it reports no measurement that viewers in fact respond this way
Patel, in chapter 4, applies the term to poster design but explicitly downgrades it there, calling it a 'secular darshan' — the two authors do not use the term at equal strength

source_terms: See here, sir, [god] isn't looking at us, and if he is not looking at us how will he bestow benevolence on us (kripa kaise karenge)?
Bold colors, bold figures, front looking - these are the most important things.
item.claim: Jain records, from the Meerut calendar artist Yogendra Rastogi, an explicit production constraint and the reason given for it: the figure must look out of the frame at the viewer, whatever the figure is doing. Rastogi's examples are secular as well as divine — a woman putting on a slipper for a footwear advertisement, a woman rolling a beedi, a woman washing clothes for a soap advertisement, "she has to look at you"; "that child who is studying, if he's reading his eyes will be downcast, and if his eyes are downcast the calendar will not sell." The stated reason is devotional: a viewer will say that if the deity is not looking at us it cannot bestow benevolence. Jain reports the corresponding compositional consequence — an intense emphasis in calendar art on the face and eyes, with eyes typically painted last as part of the "finishing" strokes.

mechanism.text: Darshan is a two-way seeing: the devotee must not merely see the deity but BE SEEN by it in order to receive its blessing. An image in which the figure's gaze is directed inside the depicted world cannot support that exchange, because the second direction of the look is missing. Frontality is therefore not a stylistic preference but the condition on which the image can do the thing it is bought to do — which is why it overrides the naturalistic requirement that a figure look where its action is directed.

scope.conditions: Stated for the Indian calendar and framing-picture industry as the author encountered it, 1994-2001, and for images intended to circulate in the bazaar. Jain is careful that this is partly a DISCURSIVE category: "these imperatives of the bazaar are not always or necessarily reflected in the images themselves: these are primarily discursive categories, part of the bazaar's self-understanding." She then says there IS in fact an intense emphasis on face and eyes, so the practice as well as the discourse is attested.

caveats.text: Jain states in the same passage that the imperative is 'not always or necessarily reflected in the images themselves' and is 'part of the bazaar's self-understanding'. Reporting it as an observed universal of the artefacts would go further than she does

the reason given is a practitioner's account of what HIS CUSTOMERS believe. No consumer study supports it. The constraint is well attested as a constraint the industry works under; the belief attributed to consumers is reported, not measured

item.claim: Dwyer reports Geeta Kapur's formal category of "frontality" in the Indian popular arts and Kapur's use of "iconicity" — not in the Peircean sense of resemblance, but as a meaningful condensation of symbolic meanings into ONE STATIC IMAGE, which need not be religious or mythological. Frontality here is not merely filming from a right-angle plane or direct address to camera but also operates through the spectator's knowledge of narrative and mise-en-scene. Dwyer adds that frontality may be seen as a freezing of space, and sometimes of time, into a tableau, which positions characters and objects in relation to one another and gives the spectator "the opportunity to see meaning represented, emotions and moral states rendered in clear visible signs."

mechanism.text: Freezing space and time suspends the narrative demand that a shot advance an action, which frees the composition to carry a state instead of an event. Because the state is rendered in arranged visible signs rather than in inferred psychology, it can be read without the viewer reconstructing an interior. This is why the same device serves both the icon and melodrama.

scope.conditions: Attributed to Geeta Kapur for the Indian popular arts generally (word, image, design and the performative act, cinema included) and traced by Dwyer through Phalke, early photography, miniature painting, the Company style and Ravi Varma. Dwyer notes the limit herself: most of these studies "draw on early films and those from the 1950s and do not trace more recent changes in styles of looking."

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Systematizing the Organic (spine 6)
item.question: You have designed eight spreads intuitively and now need rules so the rest of the book can be built by someone else. What is Samara's procedure, and what is unusual about the order it works in?
item.answer: Analyse, as specifically as possible, which formal conditions are the most prevalent among all those present, using questions he supplies: what kind of images am I using; is geometry important in the shapes or relationships; is there spatial depth and, if so, what creates it — transparency, scale change, overlap; do I sense movement and, if so, is it lateral, vertical, frenzied, calm, repeated. The answers to those questions are the system's rules. Each rule is then given its permitted variables and their range — if cropping images into an irregular trapezoid is a rule, the trapezoids might all be one size and shape, or vary in size, or vary in the measures of their sides, or extend to parallelograms and triangles. What is unusual is the direction: the rules are read off work that already exists rather than being specified before it, which inverts the order in which a grid is normally derived. He also says a discrepancy should be treated as a prompt to reinvestigate the rules — edited out, or promoted into a new rule that must then be resolved among the existing elements.
item.support: "Systematizing the Organic": analysing the most prevalent formal conditions; the four diagnostic questions; the answers as the system's rules; the trapezoid example of graded variation; treating a discrepancy as an incentive to reinvestigate the rules.
confounders: specifying rules in advance, which is the opposite of the procedure described
treating the four questions as a closed checklist; he calls them a way to begin
assuming a discrepancy must always be removed — he allows it to become a new rule

item.question: What structure does this source propose for a national agency operating across locations, and which part of the claim is the interesting one?
item.answer: Two parts: a shared knowledge and resource pool that defines the culture and holds output quality up at any location, plus a locally knowledgeable team that understands local nuance and client expectation. He offers it as the claim that what applies to a global company across countries applies equally to a national company across locations within one country. The interesting part is that premise — that India is internally multicultural to a degree comparable with cross-border operation — and he asserts rather than argues it. The two-part structure itself is asserted, not derived, and his cases (the Madras office's Konica film and India's first brand music video for TI Cycles) illustrate rather than test it. The chapter's most developed material is in fact about the durability of client relationships, not about the structure it opens by stating.

source_terms: the sari is heavily laden with cultural meanings of nostalgia, tradition, womanhood, nationalism and social status

item.claim: Dwyer states that "the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions," and then traces those functions. She reports a real-world grammar that the audience brings: a widely understood grammar of wearing the sari, with specific occasions requiring different saris by season, time of day and degree of formality, and a colour code (red, green and yellow for festive occasions; white or pale for widows; black largely a Western fashion). She then reports the cinematic use built on it — in older films contrasting the heroine with the vamp, the heroine almost invariably wore a sari as an emblem of chastity and goodness; the unmarried heroine wears Western clothes before marriage and changes into salwar-khamees or a sari after it; mothers and mother-figures always wear traditional sober saris.

mechanism.text: The garment carries meaning before it reaches the film, so the film does not have to construct the meaning; it selects from a code the viewer already holds. This is why costume can mark marital status, age, class, region, religion and moral position without dialogue, and why the same garment changes what it says when worn by a different character type.

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. item.claim: The chapter's central mechanism is to make stocking the dealer's own commercial decision by pre-announcing demand he can see. A coupon good at any store for a full-size package is placed in the advertising; before it appears, a proof of the advertisement is mailed to dealers, in the national version accompanied by the list of magazines to be used and their circulations, with the argument that many of his customers are bound to present that coupon and each coupon means a cash sale at full profit. The source states that no average dealer will let those customers go elsewhere, that makers have sometimes attained reasonable national distribution in one week this way, that many advertisers get national distribution without employing a single salesman, and that the free packages cost less than other ways of forcing distribution while starting thousands of users besides. The alternatives are costed and rejected: gift stock to every dealer must be figured at selling price and gives a high cost per dealer that a salesman might beat, and consignment to retailers is not widely favoured because many dealers resent it, collections are difficult, and unbusinesslike methods do not win dealer respect.

mechanism.text: A dealer stocks when refusing to stock has a visible cost to him. The pre-announced coupon converts a promise about future advertising into an itemised forecast of customers arriving at his counter with cash, which is evidence rather than persuasion.

The examples are selected on their outcome. Products whose free-package offer failed to force distribution would not appear in this chapter and none does.

`historical_claim`, strongly. This is a mechanism built on bearer coupons redeemable at any retailer, a dealer population reachable by mailed proofs, and published magazine circulation figures. It is recorded as 1923 practice and is NOT translated into any modern equivalent.

item.claim: Bijapurkar names a repeating pattern she says has recurred many times since 1991: an initial starburst of demand caused by a confluence of one-time events — release of pent-up demand, a category first strongly promoted, a distribution boom, a price threshold crossed by a sachet or an instalment scheme — followed by extrapolation of those early rates into the future, followed by stagnation when the market "hits a rock table and growth grinds to a halt". She reports the consequence of the 1990s instance: analysts extrapolated 20-30 per cent volume growth, "the myth of the Great Indian Middle Class was born", large capacity investments followed, and the consumption machine failed to materialise. She names what she says is required at the rock table: "not a mop but actually a powerful drill fashioned from a good market strategy", and specifically to search for weak areas rather than flog the sales team with targets based on historical growth.

mechanism.text: A starburst is produced by a stock being released, not by a flow being established. Because the observed growth rate during release looks identical to the growth rate of an expanding flow, extrapolation cannot distinguish them from the rate alone — and the error is only visible after the stock is exhausted, by which point capacity has been committed.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets 1991-2009. Bijapurkar applies the same caution prospectively to the rural demand of 2005-09 in chapter 11, which is a genuine test of the pattern's use.

caveats.text: THE STRONGEST THING ABOUT THIS OBJECT IS THAT THE AUTHOR APPLIES IT AGAINST HER OWN INTEREST. In chapter 11 she turns the same caution on the 'rural renaissance' optimism of 2009 — 'such talk makes me very nervous. It has too many overtones of the Great Indian Middle Class story, where we called victory at least a decade too early' — and enumerates the one-time events behind the rural boom: good monsoons, high support prices, and a one-time write-off of Rs 60,000 crore of farm loans in 2007-8. That is a falsifiable prospective use of her own pattern

source_terms: Research shows that it is more difficult to hold your audience if you use voice-over. It is better to have the actors talk on camera.

It pays to reinforce your promise by setting it in type and superimposing it over the video, while your soundtrack speaks the words. But make sure that the words in your supers are exactly the same as your spoken words. Any divergence confuses the viewer.
Research shows that this is neither a positive nor a negative factor. It does no harm and it does no measurable good.
item.claim: The source gives four separate findings about sound and its relation to picture. Voice-over holds the audience less well than actors talking on camera, and he reports a manufacturer who made two commercials identical except for this and found the on-camera version sold more. Supers — the promise set in type over the video while the soundtrack speaks it — pay, but the words must be exactly the same as the spoken words, because any divergence confuses the viewer. Background music is neither positive nor negative: it does no harm and no measurable good. Sound effects, by contrast, can make a positive difference, his instance being a commercial built around the sound of coffee percolating that ran five years. Jingles are below average at changing brand preference, and no jingle should go on air until people who have not read the script can decipher the words.

mechanism.text: Where speech and type deliver the same promise they reinforce; where they diverge the viewer has to reconcile two messages and is confused. No mechanism is offered for why music is inert and sound effects are not.

scope.conditions: commercials of the period

caveats.text: the voice-over comparison is the closest thing to a controlled pair in the chapter: two commercials identical in every respect except the one variable, tested, with a direction reported. The magnitude, the product and the test method are not given
the music finding is a null result stated as a null result, which is unusual in this book and worth keeping for that reason
the source's argument against background music is rhetorical — asking whether great preachers allow organists to play under their sermons — rather than evidential

source_stated_problems: Any divergence confuses the viewer.
source_stated_remedies: have the actors talk on camera
make the words in the supers exactly the same as the spoken words
test a jingle on people who have not read the script

positive.description: a coffee commercial constructed around the sound of percolation, reported to have run five years

intra_source_relations.note: the jingle judgement is in the chapter's brand-preference measure
the supers rule is a defence against miscomprehension

oppositional structures
splitting

item.claim: Patel argues that Indian film is understood through the familiarity of its characters, which are depicted as social types defined by their differences from each other — good against bad, rich against poor, weak against strong, traditional against modern — yielding recurring roles such as the long-suffering mother, the wife, the vamp, the good brother, the bad brother and the villain. Because the same actor is cast in the same role type across films, the public is familiar with both actor and type and transfers meaning between them. Posters therefore "use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film." She works one poster through: in a Deewaar poster, Bachchan's persona is recognised, the older woman reads as the long-suffering mother, her presence implies a filial relation between the two male portraits, and the audience's familiarity with the lost-and-found theme supplies the rest.

mechanism.text: A type is a compression: one figure stands for a whole set of expected relations and moral positions. When several types are placed together, the relations BETWEEN them are inferred by the viewer rather than depicted, so a still image can carry a narrative structure it never shows. This works only for a viewer holding the code.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters, mainly pre-1990. Patel states the limit and the change: female character types "commonly feature on (usually pre-1990) film posters," and since the beginning of the 1990s the oppositional structures and dramatic distinction in female character types "are no longer manifested through the type of clothes worn."

caveats.text: the source dates the code's decay: the oppositional female types stop being marked by clothing after about 1990, and representation of women in modern Western clothing ceases to signal immorality. The code is period-bound and the source says when it ended

Patel is explicit that these types are 'not universally recognized' and when depicted on posters 'are only fully understood by those with a knowledge of that culture'. This is the source's own boundary and is the single most transferable thing in the object

INSPECTED: illus. 109 and illus. 110 (Deewaar, 1975) were opened and read directly. The pyramidal arrangement with Bachchan uppermost, the mother figure and the softer-featured second male are all present as described, and the split colouring of Bachchan's face in illus. 110 — one half in warm reds, the other in blues — is plainly visible. Patel's reading of these two plates is confirmed against the plates themselves

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: No corpus is enumerated; the reading of individual posters is the evidence offered.

positive: Deewaar (1975) posters, illus. 109 and 110
Devdas (1955), where two women both wear saris but one has her hair neatly tied back and the other loose, marking the difference in type

source_terms: In every ad consider only new customers. People using your product are not going to read your ads. They have already read and decided.
You might advertise month after month to present users that the product they use is poison, and they would never know it.
So never waste one line of your space to say something to present users, unless you can say it in headlines.
Bear in mind always that you address an unconverted prospect.
item.claim: Advertising space should be allocated entirely to unconverted prospects. Existing users do not read the advertising for a product they already use, having read and decided already, so a line addressed to them is a line wasted. The source allows exactly one exception — something aimed at present users may be said in a headline, where non-readers still see it — and otherwise forbids it outright.

mechanism.text: The decision already taken removes the motive to read. Body copy is only reached by people who are still deciding; headlines are the only part of the advertisement a non-reader is exposed to.

scope.conditions: periodical advertising for a product with an existing user base

caveats.text: Stated as a universal with no evidence at all. The vivid form — that users would not notice being told month after month that their product is poison — is rhetoric, not a reported observation, and no readership measurement is offered anywhere in the chapter.

`historical_claim` and `culturally_bounded`: this is a claim about periodical readership behaviour in 1923, under conditions where the advertiser had no way to address existing and prospective customers separately. The economic argument is explicitly about the cost of paid space, so it is contingent on that constraint. It is recorded here as the source's position about its own era and is NOT translated into any claim about retention or lifecycle communication in any other medium.
The headline exception is a real qualification and is easy to lose. Hopkins does not say never speak to users; he says never spend body copy on them.

source_stated_problems: never waste one line of your space to say something to present users
source_stated_remedies: In every ad consider only new customers.
Bear in mind always that you address an unconverted prospect.

source_terms: Shooting the series level and consistently is important, otherwise the shot may not work at all
If you drop even slightly from frame to frame, as can easily happen if you shoot handheld, you would need to crop so severely that you could lose the skyline.

item.claim: The panorama sequence must be shot level and consistently. Dropping even slightly between frames, which happens easily handheld, forces a crop severe enough to lose the skyline altogether. Frames should overlap by about a half for safety; a simple method is to note something on the leading edge of one frame and put it in the middle of the next. Stitching software's content recognition is now good enough that a tripod is not required, provided the levelling is attended to.

mechanism.text: A drifting sequence produces a stitched image whose usable rectangle is the intersection of all the frames, so any vertical drift is subtracted from the final height everywhere.

scope.conditions: handheld multi-frame stitched panoramas

source_terms: awe-inspiring articles were 30 percent more likely to make the Most E-Mailed list
awe is the sense of wonder and amazement that occurs when someone is inspired by great knowledge, beauty, sublimity, or might
item.claim: The source reports his own measurement that awe-inspiring articles were 30 percent more likely to make the New York Times Most E-Mailed list. The finding matters for a structural reason he states: science articles were the anomaly in his data, out-sharing politics, fashion and business despite scoring low on both social currency and practical value, and awe is what explained them. Awe can therefore carry content that possesses none of the other drivers — the case that opens the chapter is a piece on schlieren photography of a cough, rated low on usefulness and low on interest, which readers shared anyway.

mechanism.text: Awe is the experience of confronting something greater than oneself; it expands the frame of reference and drives self-transcendence, and it involves surprise, unexpectedness or mystery. As a high-arousal positive emotion it activates, and activation produces sharing.

scope.conditions: New York Times articles over a six-month period in 2008-2009

caveats.text: Berger's OWN study, with Katherine Milkman. Design as described: a web crawler scanned the New York Times home page every fifteen minutes for six months, recording almost seven thousand articles with author, section, page placement and whether each made the Most E-Mailed list. Research assistants then scored articles on the constructs. This is a whole population over a window, not a sample of hits, which is the standard the Introduction demanded.
The definition of awe is NOT Berger's. He attributes it to psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt.

The predictor is HUMAN-RATED awe, applied by research assistants after the fact. The measurement is of raters' judgements about articles, not of readers' emotional states, and the source does not distinguish the two.

Correlational and single-outlet. All figures are the raised probability of appearing on one newspaper's Most E-Mailed list, an artefact of one publication in one period, and the source does not claim they transfer to other outlets or channels.
The Susan Boyle video is an illustration, not data. Its 100 million views in nine days are reported without any comparison content.

source_stated_problems: there was still one topic that stood out like a sore thumb: science articles

positive.description: 'The Mysterious Cough, Caught on Film', rated low on social currency and practical value and heavily shared
an article suggesting gorillas may grieve their dead

counter.description: articles about holiday shopping bargains, scored as evoking little or no awe

source_terms: if Social Currency is about information senders and how sharing makes them look, Practical Value is mostly about the information receiver
News you can use
sharing is caring
item.claim: The source distinguishes his fifth driver from his first by whose interests it serves. Social Currency is about the sender and how sharing makes them look; Practical Value is about the receiver, and it transmits because people want to help — saving someone time or money or trouble. He concedes the sender still benefits, since helping feels good and reflects well, but insists the core of the mechanism is other-directed. His cases are chosen to be unglamorous on purpose: an eighty-six-year-old's video about removing silk from corn, viewed more than five million times and skewing to viewers over fifty-five, and hikers on a mountain trail discussing vacuum cleaner models, which he uses to show that none of the earlier drivers explains the conversation.

mechanism.text: Passing on something useful is a low-cost way to help someone, and it strengthens the bond between sender and receiver — the receiver sees they were thought of. The source's analogy is a modern barn raising: a form of mutual help that distance has made rare in physical form and that useful information restores.

scope.conditions: information that saves the receiver time, money or trouble

caveats.text: No measurement supports the sender-versus-receiver distinction. It is an interpretive framing offered by the author, and the same act — sharing a useful thing — is compatible with either motive. The source concedes both motives operate and does not separate them.

The two opening cases are anecdotes, one of them personal. That practical value is what explains them is asserted by elimination — the author rules out the other drivers himself — rather than measured.

The one measurement bearing on this is the New York Times finding reported in the Emotion chapter, where more useful articles were 30 percent more likely to make the Most E-Mailed list. That is Berger's own, and it establishes the association, not the helping motive behind it.

The source ranks this driver as the easiest of the six to apply, on the reasoning that almost anything has something useful about it. This is his judgement, offered without a comparison across drivers.

source_stated_problems: the harder part is cutting through the clutter
source_stated_remedies: package our knowledge and expertise so that people learn about us while they pass it along

positive.description: Ken Craig's 'Clean Ears Everytime', a two-minute corn-shucking demonstration, most watched by people over fifty-five
hikers on a mountain trail comparing vacuum cleaner models

source_terms: pester power worked best for products that were not high value and were aimed at children

researchers also found that the child could have a 'veto' in other products like soaps, shampoos, toothpaste etc. In the case of durables like cars, motorbikes, television sets etc., pester power played a smaller role
item.claim: The influence a child exerts on a household purchase is not uniform. The source reports researchers finding three bands: strongest for low-value products aimed at the child (snacks, sweets, drinks); a *veto* rather than a positive choice in shared household categories such as soap, shampoo and toothpaste; and smallest in durables such as cars, motorbikes and television sets, where it was nonetheless said to be rising because the child sometimes held more product knowledge than the parent.

scope.conditions: Indian middle-class households, 1990s onward, as reported by unnamed consumer researchers. The bands are stated qualitatively; no magnitudes are given.

the author immediately speculates about whether better-educated mothers will reduce or increase pester power, and marks it as speculation ('I wonder if')

source_terms: melodrama
exteriority
glamorous realism
item.claim: Dwyer argues that melodrama "foregrounds language, as it makes all feelings exterior," with characters verbalising their feelings, and that it likewise affects the image: it uses close-ups to increase the effect of emotional depth, and heightens the exterior display of emotion through storms, remote places and other symbolic representations of a character's interior feelings. She draws the consequence for settings directly: settings can be "a form of making the characters' state of mind external, following the melodramatic style of exteriority," and she reports Yash Chopra's own term for the resulting look, "glamorous realism," a style in which reality is glossed over to make it more attractive.

mechanism.text: In melodrama the emphasis is not on the psychology of a unique individual but on characters in situations that push emotion to extremes. Because the interior is not the unit of interest, interior state must be placed outside the character to be read at all — in speech, in weather, in place, in the arrangement of the set. Setting therefore stops being a container for action and becomes a bearer of state.

scope.conditions: Stated for the melodramatic mode, which Dwyer says is "often found in societies where the pre-modern is giving way to the modern," and which she distinguishes from the more realist mode of some Hindi films (Bimal Roy, IPTA-influenced work). It is a mode-level claim, not a claim about all Hindi cinema.

caveats.text: Dwyer explicitly separates the melodramatic from the realist mode within Hindi cinema and names films in each. Treating exteriority as a property of Hindi cinema as such would ignore a distinction the source insists on
the mechanism is drawn from Western melodrama theory (Brooks, Neale, Ang) and applied; the source offers no Indian-specific evidence for the mechanism itself

positive: the Awara (1951) dream sequence, where the film's themes are condensed into and projected onto the sets themselves

source_terms: Often chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims. An advertiser, in all good faith, makes an impressive assertion. If it is true, it will form a big factor in advertising. If untrue, it may prove a boomerang. And it may bar our ads from good mediums.
It is remarkable how often a maker proves wrong on assertions he has made for years.
In every line involving scientific details a censor is appointed. The ad-writer, however well-informed, may draw wrong inferences from facts. So an authority passes on every advertisement.
item.claim: The source describes two distinct verification controls. The first tests the advertiser's own assertions before they are used: chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims, because a true claim will be a big factor while an untrue one may boomerang and may bar the advertising from good mediums — and, the source notes, it is remarkable how often a maker proves wrong about assertions he has been making for years. The second guards the writer's reasoning rather than the client's facts: in every line involving scientific details a censor is appointed, because a well-informed writer may still draw wrong inferences from correct facts, and an authority passes on every advertisement.

mechanism.text: Two different failures need two different controls. A false premise is caught by testing the premise; a false inference from a true premise is not, and needs a domain authority reviewing the finished argument.

scope.conditions: lines involving scientific or technical detail

caveats.text: Presented as standing agency practice with no instance. No claim is named that a chemist overturned, and no advertisement is named that a censor stopped. What is being recorded is the design of the control, not evidence that it worked.

The stated motive is mixed and the source does not separate the strands: truth is valued partly for its persuasive force, partly to avoid a boomerang, and partly because good mediums would otherwise refuse the advertising. The last is an admissions constraint of the 1923 magazine trade, not an ethical position.
The distinction between verifying a fact and reviewing an inference drawn from it is the genuinely reusable part, and the source states it explicitly.

source_stated_problems: It is remarkable how often a maker proves wrong on assertions he has made for years.
The ad-writer, however well-informed, may draw wrong inferences from facts.
source_stated_remedies: Often chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims.
In every line involving scientific details a censor is appointed.

item.source_locator: Ch. 'I am a Complan Girl…', Colgate sachet passage
item.question: A brand plans to extend the sachet format from shampoo into toothpaste. What does this source predict, what is the proposed mechanism, and how confident is the author?
item.answer: It predicts failure, and reports that Colgate's sachet attempt did fail. The proposed mechanism is that a sachet prices a single occasion, which suits occasion-shaped consumption and not continuous consumption: shampooing was an occasional act in many Indian homes so a sachet could be bought for a special occasion, whereas a consumer ready to adopt a daily-use category would buy the full pack instead. The author's confidence is explicitly low — he writes 'I suspect', proposes no test, and extends the same conjecture to hair oil 'probably for the same reason' without new evidence. The underlying usage-frequency premise is asserted, not measured.
item.support: 'I suspect consumers did not see toothpaste as an occasional use product.'
item.confounders: This is the author's conjecture about an observed commercial pattern, not a reported study. Do not upgrade 'I suspect' to a finding.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 10 'Traveling Light', section 'Filtering Daylight'
item.question: An interior is lit by tungsten photographic lights and by daylight through a window. Two gelling strategies both match the colours. Which does the book prefer, and on what ground that has nothing to do with colour?
item.answer: It prefers gelling the window. Blue gels on the photographic lights, shot at a daylight balance, would match the colours — but the photographic lights are probably weaker than the sun already, and filtering them absorbs light where it can least be spared. Orange theatrical gel on the OUTSIDE of the window, shot at a tungsten balance, achieves the same colour match and also better balances the intensity of the two sources, because the loss is now imposed on the stronger one. The general point the authors make first is the one still photographers overlook: a window is a light source and can be filtered like any other, which motion picture and video photographers do routinely.
item.support: Ch. 10, 'Filtering Daylight', which sets out both strategies and the intensity argument for choosing between them.
confounders: choosing on colour accuracy alone, where the two strategies are equivalent

item.rationale: The Law of the Generic and its constructive counterpart give a discriminable, textual, checkable property that a naming benchmark can be built on: whether a candidate name is a common descriptive phrase, or an ordinary word displaced from its usual context, or a truncation. The source supplies both sides of the discrimination with worked pairs — General Video Rental against Blockbuster, Low-Cost Car Rental against Budget, Intelligent Chip Company against Intel — and a set of near-identical generics that a benchmark item can use as distractors. The value is that the discrimination can be scored without knowing whether the source's claim about outcomes is true, which is exactly the property a benchmark item needs.

applicability.when: building a benchmark that tests whether a system can classify a proposed brand name against this source's distinction, and can produce a displaced or truncated alternative to a generic one
applicability.limits: The benchmark tests agreement with Ries & Ries, not correctness. The source establishes nothing about whether generic names actually perform worse — its historical objection is handled by asserting that the General/Standard/National companies succeeded in spite of their names, which means neither outcome can disconfirm the rule. A system scoring well here has learned this source's taxonomy and nothing more. It must never be reported as naming skill.

item.source_locator: Essay 'Hierarchies Unlimited'
item.question: What function does this source argue hierarchy serves, and what is the cost it names?
item.answer: Simplification. Hierarchy collapses many incommensurable dimensions onto one linear ordering, which makes every comparison decidable and lets a person know their place without ambiguity — 'Science is better than commerce so why tax your mind about what to choose?' His instances are the Science/Commerce/Arts ordering in education, which he notes is justified neither by career prospects nor by difficulty, and the graded exemptions from airport frisking. The cost he names is that individual preference has no place in the ordering and so drops out of the decision entirely: 'we study what we deserve rather than what we want.'
item.support: 'It standardizes the world on a single linear dimension and helps you know your place without any ambiguity.'
item.confounders: Essayistic interpretation argued from selected institutional examples. It records what Desai argues, not an established account of Indian social structure — and he himself predicts the linear hierarchy will recede.

source_terms: His replies were costing 85 cents each
But his cost per reply was $14.20, on an article which sold for $5. Then he tried our ad., and the cost per reply was 42 cents.
We prepared an ad. which the advertiser rejected, it seemed so unattractive.
countless advertisers without a trace on cost are judging ads. by appearance
item.claim: The source reports the book's clearest documented comparison. An advertiser selling a five-dollar article by mail had replies costing 85 cents and sales about $2.50, and was becoming unprofitable. The source's agency prepared an advertisement the advertiser rejected as too unattractive. A rival agency's larger, more alluring advertisement was run instead and produced replies at $14.20 each on a five-dollar article. The advertiser then ran the rejected advertisement and replies cost 42 cents, a level the source says held for years on some 250,000 replies a year, halving his previous cost. The source's conclusion is not about layout but about decision-making: advertisers without a trace on cost judge advertisements by appearance, and they lose on the same scale as this man did.

mechanism.text: Appearance and response are not correlated, and appearance is the only signal available to a decider with no cost trace. So in the absence of measurement the selection criterion is systematically wrong rather than merely noisy, and errors of very large magnitude go undetected.

scope.conditions: direct-response advertising where cost per reply is computable

caveats.text: A 34-fold spread between two advertisements is extreme and is reported with no description of either advertisement beyond attractive and unattractive, no dates, and no account of media, offer or seasonality, any of which may have differed.
The source is a party to the comparison — it won the account — and is recounting the episode decades later in a book about its own judgement.
The figures are internally consistent with the surrounding claim of halving an 85-cent cost to 42 cents, which is some support for the arithmetic if not for the attribution.

People do not know their costs, and they will not be guided by those who do.
