item.source_locator: Essay 'Hierarchies Unlimited'
item.question: This source says a status signal must be received to exist. What is the argument, and what is its exemplary case?
item.answer: That status is a relation requiring the weaker party's awareness rather than a property held privately: the 'do you know who I am' question emphasises the KNOWING, because power that keeps nobody at a distance does no work — 'Power is real only when the weaker person is aware of his relative status.' The consequence is that signal design optimises for unavoidable reception rather than for accuracy or elegance. The exemplary case is the vehicle siren, which 'converts an abstract noun into an insistent compelling whining verb' — a device that turns standing into a signal others cannot avoid receiving.
item.support: 'Power is real only when the weaker person is aware of his relative status.'
item.confounders: Stated as a universal but argued entirely from Indian institutional examples; the extraction does not extend it beyond them. The siren reading is the essay's rhetorical high point — the transferable content is the reception requirement, not the metaphor.

source_terms: Take a profitable mail-order ad. and set it in twice the space... you will double the cost of replies and sales.
All pictures have a selling value. None are used for decoration.
In national advertising the average cost is at least $10 per word.
Cut out every word which is not worth that $10. Never repeat.
item.claim: The source converts layout into arithmetic. Doubling the space of a profitable mail-order advertisement — through larger type, decoration or a border — makes it more attractive and doubles the cost per reply and per sale. It states this economy principle became practically universal after thousands of tests on hundreds of lines, and that it proves waste of space is folly in any line, including large type, borders and pictures that do not help to sell. It puts the same rule on words: national advertising costs at least $10 a word, so every word not worth $10 must be cut and nothing repeated. Its comparison is with a salesman who wastes time at perhaps $1 an hour while an advertisement doing the same wastes $10 a word. It concludes that the difference between profit and loss in advertising is usually small, most success comes from efficiency and most failure from waste.

mechanism.text: Space is bought by the unit, so any element occupying space without selling raises the denominator of cost per response without raising the numerator. Attractiveness is not a free good; it is purchased with space that must then earn its price.

item.question: Hopkins says the best advertisers learn their appealing claims by comparing headline results. What do they then do with the claims that did not win, and why does this not contradict testing?
item.answer: They keep them. The winners of the headline comparisons are not run alone; claims that prove important enough are added to a standing list, and all of them then appear in every advertisement thereafter. His reason is that different facts convince different people, so a claim that loses a headline comparison can still be the fact that converts a share of readers once they are reading. The headline test measures pulling power; the standing list preserves converting power. He gives no threshold for "important enough", which is the decision the procedure actually turns on.

item.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
item.source_locator: SC 1.4.4 Resize Text; SC 1.4.10 Reflow
item.question: Distinguish SC 1.4.4 Resize Text from SC 1.4.10 Reflow. What is each measuring, and what does each except?
item.answer: SC 1.4.4 is about magnitude: text must be resizable without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality, and it excepts captions and images of text. SC 1.4.10 is about layout under constraint: content must be presentable without loss of information or functionality and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions, at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels for vertically scrolling content or a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels for horizontally scrolling content. It excepts parts of the content that require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning, and names examples — images required for understanding such as maps and diagrams, video, games, presentations, data tables (not individual cells), and interfaces where a toolbar must stay in view. The Reflow numbers are zoom-derived: the note states 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a 1280 CSS pixel viewport at 400% zoom. A CSS pixel is itself defined as a visual angle of about 0.0213 degrees, not a hardware pixel. Both are Level AA.
item.support: Normative — SC 1.4.4, SC 1.4.10 and its Notes 1 and 2, and Glossary: "CSS pixel".
confounders: treating 320 CSS pixels as a phone screen width rather than as a zoom-derived viewport equivalence
assuming Reflow forbids all horizontal scrolling, when it forbids scrolling in two dimensions and excepts content needing two-dimensional layout

item.description: Six devices observed by inspecting the book's plate insert, in which the advertisement's argument is carried by the image and its construction rather than by copy: a familiar everyday scene recruited as the demonstration; a single abstract symbol under an instruction headline; a mascot inserted into a foreign icon set at reduced scale; a fixed form with one variable joke slot; a sung word typeset as the picture; and vernacular appropriation carried simultaneously by word, script and setting.

source_terms: Another way in which samples pay is by keying your advertisements. They register the interest you create. Thus you can compare one with another ad, headline, plan and method.
Without a key to guide you, your returns are very apt to cost you twice what they need cost. And we know that some ads on the same product will cost ten times what others cost.

A sample gets action. The reader of your ad may not be convinced to the point of buying. But he is ready to learn more... So he cuts out a coupon, lays it aside, and later mails it or presents it. Without that coupon he would soon forget.
That reader might not again read one of your ads in six months. Your impression would be lost.
item.claim: For an advertiser who is not selling by mail, the sample offer is the instrument that makes measurement possible at all: it keys the advertisement, registers the interest created, and lets one advertisement, headline, plan or method be compared with another. The source attaches magnitudes to the absence of that key — without it returns are very apt to cost twice what they need cost, and some advertisements on the same product are known to cost ten times what others cost. The offer does a second job at the same time: it converts an interested but unconvinced reader into a name and address, because the reader who is not ready to buy is ready to learn more, and the coupon carries the intention past the moment it would otherwise be forgotten.

mechanism.text: An advertisement produces no observable event of its own. The sample coupon manufactures one, and that event both carries the identity of the advertisement that produced it and preserves a prospect whose interest would otherwise decay before the next exposure.

scope.conditions: general (non-mail-order) advertisers who have no direct sale to trace

source_terms: Information that is discontinuous benefits from being organized into a grid of multiple columns.

Although their widths must always correspond to those of one or more columns (edge to edge), both images and chunks of text may be of any depth, and positioned freely within the margins from top to bottom of the page
item.claim: Discontinuous information benefits from multiple columns. The column grid is flexible because columns can be dependent on one another for running text, independent for small blocks, or crossed over to make wider measures, so different kinds of information can be separated — for instance running text and large images in some columns and captions in an adjacent one. Widths must always correspond edge to edge to one or more columns, but depth is free: images and chunks of text may be any depth and positioned anywhere between the margins. Horizontal alignment is optional and is bought by adding flowlines; the more constants required, the more flowlines.

mechanism.text: Width is constrained and depth is not, because columns fix lateral alignment while vertical position is only fixed when a flowline is introduced to fix it.

item.source_locator: Ch. 'No Squeeze, No Wheeze, No Navel Please!', Sweetex passage
item.question: An agency has its storyboard approved by the broadcaster and shoots the film. What does this source's first-hand case say about what that approval guarantees, and what is the mechanism?
item.answer: It guarantees nothing about the finished film. Under Doordarshan, clearance ran as two independent gates: the storyboard before production and the film afterwards. The author's own Sweetex campaign cleared the storyboard and was then rejected on the finished film for showing the model's navel in an opening close-up, forcing a reshoot at the advertiser's cost. The mechanism he gives is that a storyboard is a pictorial abstraction which does not fix framing, duration or emphasis, so the censor assessing the film is assessing material the storyboard never showed and can reach a different verdict on the same concept. The book evidences the same independence twice: Doordarshan also withdrew a storyboard approval it had already given to KamaSutra.

item.confounders: This is a Doordarshan-era regime the author says kept changing; it is not a description of current Indian practice.

item.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Indian Cinema', printed pp. 29 and 32-33
item.question: What constraint does personification place on an image, and why is that a constraint on the picture rather than on the performance?
item.answer: Personification is the form of acting in which the actor's persona retains significant similarities across performances, as against impersonation, in which the actor transforms body and voice — Barry King's distinction, which Dwyer reports and says is found most often in Hindi cinema. The constraint she draws is stated of the image, not of the acting: personification 'creates and maintains the star's text, RESTRICTING THE WAY IN WHICH AN IMAGE CAN BE PRESENTED', and melodrama reinforces this because 'the star must appear as a star, not as a character playing a role'. It is a constraint on the picture because the persona is what the audience is buying and what the next film inherits: an image that submerges the star in the character damages an asset that exists across films, whatever it does for this one.
item.support: personification 'creates and maintains the star's text, restricting the way in which an image can be presented'
item.confounders: This is not a claim that the acting is poor or unvaried. It is a claim about what the image is obliged to preserve.

item.source_locator: Essay 'Mother Pious Lady'
item.question: A team observes that the vocabulary of a long-running format has changed considerably over twenty years and concludes the practice has modernised. What does this source's measured finding say about that inference?
item.answer: That the inference does not follow. Across thirty years of matrimonial advertisements the surface changed considerably — appearance descriptors multiplied, individuals expressed needs with more specificity, the chaperoned ten-minute meeting stretched to two or three meetings with chaperoning becoming optional — while the underlying model did not move at all. Advertisements are still placed by parents, the parties are still called 'boy' and 'girl' whatever their age, personality is still barely mentioned, and the transaction is still between stations in life rather than between individuals. Caste mention, on the study's evidence, did not decline. Surface features respond to changing expression while the model that determines what the convention is FOR can persist unchanged underneath.
item.support: 'the essential nature of the system has not changed… The underlying mental model is still that of marriage as a relationship between stations in life and not individuals.'
item.confounders: The study's method is entirely unreported, so the finding's strength rests on the author's authority alone. The book predates the migration of Indian matrimonial matching to websites.

item.source_locator: Ch. 'The [In] Complete Man', Emami/HUL passage
item.question: A category leader has known for years from its own data that men use its women's product, and does nothing; a small entrant opens the category and the leader follows within months. What explanation does this source give, and what alternative does the author leave open?
item.answer: The explanation is that the incumbent's accumulated equity is an asset its own actions can damage, so its expected cost of a category-extending move includes a risk a newcomer with nothing to lose does not bear — the asymmetry can hand first-mover advantage to the smaller firm. The author's instance is Emami's Fair & Handsome in 2005 against Hindustan Unilever, which he says had long known men were using Fair & Lovely. He explicitly leaves open an alternative he never rules out: 'Was it just a lucky break?' A single successful entrant is consistent with luck, and the case is survivorship-shaped — newcomers who took the same risk and failed are not counted.
item.support: 'A newcomer has no such fears. They have nothing to lose.'
item.confounders: A separate named practitioner asserts in the same chapter that Indian male grooming was created single-handedly by marketing with no governmental or societal support — a strong causal claim with no evidence behind it here.

item.question: What does the reproduced 'Thanda matlab Coca-Cola' plate show that the book's text does not say, and why does it matter?

source_terms: A grid, in essence, is what happens inside the margins of an individual page, within the body.
Every grid contains the same basic parts, no matter how complex the grid becomes. These parts can be combined as needed or omitted from the overall structure at the designer’s discretion
item.claim: A grid is what happens inside the margins, within the body, and every grid however complex is built from the same parts: columns (vertical alignments separated by column gutters, any number, equal or unequal in width); flowlines (alignments breaking the space into horizontal bands, one or several); rows (many flowlines at regular repeated intervals from head to foot margin, separated by row gutters); modules (the units created where columns and rows intersect — or, seen the other way, the units whose grouping produces columns and rows); spatial zones (groups of columns, rows or modules forming distinct fields to which a role can be assigned); and markers (placement indicators for text that always occupies one location, such as running heads, section titles and folios). Any part may be combined or omitted at the designer's discretion, and the proportions of the parts depend on the designer's needs.

item.claim: Because a reader decides for or against the proposition in a single reading, and that decision operates against ever reading a second time, every important claim must be present in the advertisement the reader happens to see. source_terms: Direct marketing is action oriented. And it is measured. Brand marketing is culturally oriented. And it can't be measured
The danger is in being confused
If you're buying direct marketing ads, measure everything ... If you're buying brand marketing ads, be patient. Refuse to measure
If you can't see the funnel, don't buy the ads
you definitely, certainly, and surely don't have enough time and money to build a brand for everyone. You can't. Don't try
item.claim: Godin's most operational claim is a separation. Direct marketing is action-oriented and is measured; brand marketing is culturally oriented and cannot be measured. The disciplines that follow are opposites and he states both as instructions: if you are buying direct ads, measure everything — what attention costs, what a click costs, what an order costs — and if you cannot measure it, it does not count; if you are buying brand ads, be patient, refuse to measure, be consistent, and if you cannot afford to be consistent and patient, do not buy them at all. The danger he names is not doing either badly but confusing the two, which is what makes a shift to a measured environment destroy a business built on unmeasurable brand advertising. He adds the gate: if you cannot see the funnel, do not buy the ads, and if you can see it and it costs too much, fix the funnel first. And he insists brand marketing is subject to the same narrowing rule as everything else — you cannot afford to build a brand for everyone.

mechanism.text: The two do different work on different timescales, so they require opposite decision rules. Applying measurement to culturally-oriented spending kills it before it accumulates; declining to measure action-oriented spending removes the only control it has.

scope.conditions: any organisation buying attention rather than earning it

item.question: Berger describes an anomaly in his data that led him to awe. What was the anomaly, how did he build the dataset, and what did awe turn out to be worth?
item.answer: The anomaly was science articles. They out-shared politics, fashion and business news while scoring low on both social currency and practical value — his opening case is a piece on a photographic technique that renders a cough visible, which readers rated as neither useful nor especially interesting and shared anyway. The dataset was built with a web crawler, suggested by Katherine Milkman after he had been clipping most-emailed lists out of newspapers by hand: it scanned the New York Times home page every fifteen minutes for six months and recorded almost seven thousand articles with author, section and page placement, plus which made the Most E-Mailed list. Research assistants then scored articles for the constructs. More interesting articles were 25 percent more likely to make the list, more useful articles 30 percent, and awe-inspiring articles 30 percent. Awe is what explained the science anomaly.

Limits: correlational and single-outlet; the predictor is human-rated awe applied after the fact, which measures raters' judgements about articles rather than readers' states. The DEFINITION of awe is not his — he credits psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Embracing the suck' (spine 13)
item.question: A client's product has an obvious, well-known weakness, and the brief asks you to work around it. What does Sullivan recommend instead, and what does he say about client-mandated elements the team wants to bury?
item.answer: Take the weakness and use it to accentuate the product's main strength — what he calls embracing the suck. His modern example is a cough syrup whose campaign compared its own taste to public restroom puddle water and signed off "It tastes awful. It works." He treats admitting weakness as a way of disarming distrust, alongside admitting the commercial has an agenda at all, and reports a pizza brand opening a campaign by replaying focus-group video of its own customers saying the product was bad before promising to fix it. He extends the same move to a different case: when what sucks is not the product but a client mandate — a weak tagline, a jingle, a spokesperson — tackle it directly rather than doing something you think is cool and burying the mandated element in a corner or in the last ten seconds, because, quoting Jason Elm, good ideas often spill out of the very thing your instincts tell you to avoid.

She reports the corresponding narrowing of what "culture" is taken to mean: circumscribed, globally portable signs of heterogeneity — language, dress, food, music, art, rituals, festivals — grafted onto the protocols of a putatively universal modernity, which allows cultural difference to be relegated to leisure and harnessed to niche marketing.

item.claim: Holding the advertisement constant and changing only how the reader is asked to respond changes the cost of an inquiry several-fold. The source reports a line then in hand where sample inquiries obtained by mail averaged 70 cents each while the same advertisement produced inquiries at 18 to 22 cents each when the coupon was presented at a local store, and states generally that often four times as many will present a coupon at a store as will mail it. A second reported case: where three routes were offered — write, telephone, or call at a store — 70 per cent of inquiries came by telephone. The 70 cents against 18-22 cents comparison holds the advertisement constant — "the same ad" — and varies one factor, so `controlled_comparison` is warranted, and both arms report a returned cost, so `empirical_within_source` is warranted. What is missing is everything identifying: no product, no market, no period, no volume, and no statement of whether the two arms ran simultaneously or in comparable places.
The 70-per-cent telephone figure is a reported distribution, not a cost, and it is reported for one unnamed line. It shows which route people chose, not what each route cost.

The specific finding is about the relative friction of mail, telephone and a walk to a shop in 1923, including the assumption that households may not have stamps. The finding does not transfer; the FORM of the finding — that the response mechanism can dominate the copy in cost per response — is what the source actually establishes here, and even that is established on one line.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, 'Just How Much Purchasing Power'; Table 4.1, Figure 4.1
item.question: State the demand-structure claim this book rests on, and give the worked case that shows why it changes which segment matters.
item.answer: The claim: 'Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot' — so total demand can sit overwhelmingly in a segment with low per-head consumption, simply because the segment is very large. The worked case is rural two-wheelers, and its arithmetic was checked directly against Figure 4.1 in this pass: penetration runs 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across four income groups, household counts 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, and two-wheeler numbers 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group has about one-fourth the penetration of the high-income group and about nine times the households, and ends up with about 1.6 times the sales — 6.4 divided by 3.8 is 1.68, which matches the text. What it changes is which segment a firm should care about: a penetration-led reading picks the top group, and the volume sits below it. item.question: What does the book instruct an analyst to do about the word 'India', and why is that more than a definitional nicety?
item.answer: To stop using it as a market construct and build one: 'the onus is on them to define what their India is, and translate the geographic idea into a well-defined' population. It is more than a nicety because every quantitative claim in the book depends on which India is being counted, and the differences are not marginal — the top 30 per cent and the bottom 60 per cent of the same country behave as different markets with different price-performance frontiers, different information access and different purchase units, and a single national figure averages them into a population that does not exist. It also closes the loop on the book's other arguments: the middle-class trap, the youth sampling error and the analogy school are all instances of reasoning about an undefined or misdefined population, and this is the general instruction they share. item.claim: Jain argues that speech about an image is itself performative, so that critique is not a neutral observation of an image's power but an intervention in it: "the very act of paying attention to an image and framing it in a particular way is an encounter or actualization that changes the character of the image." item.source_locator: Ch. 4, sections 'Character Types' and 'Female Character Types', printed pp. 194-204
item.question: How does a poster carrying three portraits and no text convey a plot, on this account?
item.answer: Through a compression code the viewer already holds. Indian film is understood through the familiarity of its characters, depicted as social types defined by their differences from each other — good against bad, rich against poor, weak against strong, traditional against modern — yielding recurring roles: the long-suffering mother, the wife, the vamp, the good brother, the bad brother, the villain. Because the same actor is repeatedly cast in the same type, the public is familiar with both actor and type and transfers meaning between them, so posters 'use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film'. Patel works one through: in a Deewaar poster Bachchan's persona is recognised, the older woman reads as the long-suffering mother, her presence implies a filial relation between the two male portraits, and the theme of brothers divided is delivered without a word of text. THE CODE IS THE VIEWER'S, NOT THE POSTER'S — a viewer without it sees three faces.
item.support: posters 'use the viewer's familiarity with character types as a code with which to convey a greater sense of the theme of the film.'
item.confounders: The compression looks like an economical design decision and is actually a dependency: it works only where the casting convention that built the types has been running long enough for the audience to hold them.

item.source_locator: Ch. 6, 'Value Orientation'
item.question: What is the axis of the segmentation this book proposes, and how does it differ from segmenting by spending power?
item.answer: The axis is VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost — not how much they can spend. Her five groups run from the rich as benefit maximizers, oriented to 'money is no object if the benefit is right', through to those for whom cost dominates absolutely. The difference from spending-power segmentation is that the two cut the population differently and predict different things: an income band tells you what a buyer CAN spend and says nothing about the trade-off they will make, so two households at the same income can sit in different orientations, and one household's orientation can differ by category. It also explains behaviour that looks irrational on an income reading — a low-income buyer deferring a purchase to get a better product rather than accepting a cheaper worse one is anomalous by income and ordinary by orientation. NOTHING HERE IS BOUND IN THE CANON RECORD and the reason is stated: this classifies Indian consumer households in 2008, using NCAER-derived material, and this project classifies neither consumers nor households. What is interesting is the SHAPE of the classification, not its content.
item.support: the rich as benefit maximizers — 'money is no object if the benefit is right'

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.source_locator: printed pp. 45-46 (Chapter 14, 'Getting Distribution')
item.question: Describe the pre-announced coupon mechanism and say exactly why a dealer stocks under it.
item.answer: A coupon good at any store for a full-size package is placed in the advertising, and before it appears a proof of that advertisement is mailed to dealers — in the national version with the list of magazines to be used and their circulations. Each dealer is shown that many of his customers are bound to present that coupon, and that each coupon means a cash sale at full profit. He stocks because refusing has a visible cost to him: no average dealer will let those customers go elsewhere. What makes it work rather than a promise of advertising is that it converts a future promise into an itemised forecast of paying customers arriving at his counter — evidence rather than persuasion. item.claim: A structure's intervals may be sourced from outside the page. The intervals between musical notes or chords — the octave established by the seven unique tonal pitches of Western music — have been used by book designers to divide pages since the Middle Ages, and rhythmic or thematic alternation schemes borrowed from musical composition can be applied to the distances between elements in a layout, in patterns such as A/B/A or A/B/A/C where each letter stands for one measurement. item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', the bath-mat and 'Man Drinks Fat' comparison in 'What Makes for an Effective Trigger?', and the reusable-bag passage in 'Consider the Context' (spine 7)
item.question: A public safety film is vivid, memorable, and viewers report thinking about it often. Berger would still call it a failed trigger. Why, and what is his contrasting case?
item.answer: Because the trigger fires where the person cannot act. His example is a New Zealand spot about bathroom slips that is so memorable he says he thinks of it every time he showers in a room without a mat — and, as he puts it, you cannot buy a bath mat in a bathroom. The message is physically removed from the desired behaviour, so it must survive unaided until the action becomes possible, which is the failure the trigger was supposed to prevent. His contrast is a New York City health video showing fat pouring from a soda can, which fires the message at precisely the moment someone is about to drink one. He gives the same structure for reusable shopping bags: the supermarket is a strong cue for the bags and a badly timed one, since the bags are at home. The useful cue is the shopping list, seen before leaving the house. He adds the corollary that the longer the delay between exposure and action, the more the trigger matters — and that market research measuring immediate reaction is measuring the wrong moment.
item.support: Berger's argument. NO measurement supports the proximity condition: both films are analysed by the author from the armchair and neither is compared on outcomes. The reusable-bag case, which states the condition most cleanly, is an invented illustration.
confounders: treating memorability as evidence the trigger works; on his account the bath-mat spot is memorable and useless
proposing a more striking execution rather than moving the cue to the point of action
confusing this with the frequency condition; a bathroom is encountered daily, so the spot passes on frequency and fails on proximity

item.question: The source names a form it calls the most distinctive of its medium and then does not study it. Which form, why not, and what does that do to every claim in the book about the medium as a whole?

Patel identifies them in the Introduction as 'the most distinct feature of film advertising', with their large-scale vibrant images and bright colours, and also as the most ephemeral, destroyed once a film finishes its run: 'since there is little surviving evidence of the type of imagery depicted on early hoardings, this study is based primarily upon handbills, posters and booklets, which, despite their fragility, have survived'. WHAT THAT DOES IS MAKE THE EVIDENCE BASE A SURVIVAL SAMPLE, AND NOT A RANDOM ONE: the form that survived is the small, printed, collectable one, and the form that did not is the large, painted, public one. So any statement here about what Indian film advertising looked like is a statement about what its durable printed forms looked like. The source states the gap plainly, which is why it is a bound on the evidence rather than a hidden defect — and it is the medium's gap, not a digitisation loss, since a reader of the 2002 print edition was in exactly the same position.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3 'The Art of Advertising', printed pp. 101-182; thesis stated at p. 101
item.question: What is chapter 3's organising claim about how film-advertising style changed, and why does the Art Deco phase matter to that claim?
item.answer: That Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'. The sequence given: text-only newspaper notices and handbills from 1896; the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique on Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to the Ajanta revival, used when a studio wanted to signal a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; computer-aided design from the 1990s. Art Deco matters because of how it ended: it 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s' in India because it came to be seen as Western cultural imperialism. That is a style displaced by a political meaning attaching to it rather than by a better style, which is the strongest evidence for the chapter's claim that these are period vocabularies rather than steps toward a solution.
item.support: each phase borrows 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'; Art Deco 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s'
item.confounders: Read as a progression toward better design, the sequence supports a 'this is how you make a film poster' conclusion. Read as the source states it, it supports the opposite: no phase here is the answer.

item.source_locator: Conclusion, printed pp. 215-218
item.question: This book ends by dating its own subject. What does it say, what reasons does it give, and what does that oblige a reader to do with the rest of the book?
item.answer: The authors state that the 'filmi' style which 'defined the visual culture of the Hindi film up to the 1990s (and which has been the focus of this book) is a thing of the past and is considered to be the very antithesis of the new "look"'. Three reasons are given: a younger generation of film-makers 'raised on Hollywood but firmly grounded in Bollywood'; a new middle-class consumerist lifestyle; and the growing importance of the diasporic market, where returns per ticket are far higher because of the exchange rate. They also record an irony — as filmi style is discarded by the industry, it is the means by which the industry is finally gaining Western recognition. The costume grammar, the poster conventions, the character types and the location logic are described as the practice of a period that the authors say had ended by their own publication in 2002 — a quarter-century before this extraction. Any claim that these ARE the conventions of Indian film imagery contradicts the source it cites.
item.support: the filmi style 'is a thing of the past and is considered to be the very antithesis of the new "look"'
item.confounders: This is the single most-ignored passage in the book, and ignoring it turns a historical study into a style guide.

item.question: Give the author's rules for using Indian household income survey data, and say precisely whose work this is.
item.answer: Her rules, given as an enumerated set on the ground that surveyed income is systematically understated: do not use it literally; use it for RELATIVE distribution — who is richer than whom, and by roughly how much — rather than for absolute level; and reconcile the survey distribution against an independent aggregate, which is what her own analysis does by linking surveyed income distributions to national accounts. She did not field a survey; she reconciled other people's surveys against GDP. This is the only object in the record marked as carrying the source's own empirical work, and it is marked as mixed for exactly that reason. Two of the tables the argument rests on, 5.2 and 5.3, exist only as images in this copy and were read directly — 5.3 is the source of the text's US$367 billion bottom-of-pyramid figure, showing 690 million people against total GDP of US$367.4 billion.

item.source_locator: Ch. 8, 'How to Read and Predict Change'
item.question: What is the molting/morphing distinction, what detection problem does it create, and what evidence supports it?
item.answer: MOLTING change sheds the old for the new like a snake's skin; MORPHING change is slow and from within, 'like an amoeba which, with every tiny particle it ingests, infinitesimally changes shape'. She argues Indian change is of the second kind and gives a physics analogy for why it still matters: since Force = Mass x Acceleration, 'a small acceleration (small changes over long periods of time) can also unleash a large force of change, if the mass that is changing is very large'. The detection problem follows directly: morphing change 'is not visible through the usual run of the mill "usage and attitude" type surveys that most companies ritualistically engage in', because each annual reading falls inside the noise — hence the executive who watches annually, finds nothing worth mentioning, and five years later finds the market distinctly different and asks 'when did we blink and not see this happening?'. Her proposed unit of observation is the CHANGE CONFLUENCE: a collection of individually insignificant shifts that together cross a threshold. THE EVIDENCE IS THE WEAK PART AND MUST BE SAID: the framework is illustrated by consulting cases with no client name, no date, no sample size and no outcome, plus a reported executive experience. The mechanism is clear; nothing measures it.
item.support: morphing change 'is not visible through the usual run of the mill "usage and attitude" type surveys'
item.confounders: The Force = Mass x Acceleration line is an analogy, not a model; nothing in the book quantifies either term.

item.rationale: Bijapurkar states, with unusual precision for a book of this kind, the discipline for using an instrument that is consistently biased: it is "reliable but not valid", so it can be used for ranking and for change over time and must not be used for levels, and the operational form is to work with percentiles rather than absolute bands or verbal labels. This project reasons from instruments with known error — the benchmark-qualified text evaluator carries a stated false-pass and false-fail rate on every row — and the general discipline of asking which comparisons an instrument's error permits is exactly the one that already governs how that evaluator's output is reported. This binds the general form of that discipline, and specifically the failure mode that an instrument expressed in absolute units invites use for the one question it cannot answer.

applicability.limits: The 59.6 per cent figure, the named surveys and the Indian context are all specific and dated, and none of them transfers. item.claim: Bijapurkar's most sustained methodological argument is against using "the Indian middle class" as a business-planning input, on the ground that the category has no agreed definition and that its size is therefore a function of who is defining it. She assembles the range: Hansa Research's finding from interviewing senior marketing professionals that "everyone of them had a unique definition" and that "no one really has a fix on this nebulous entity"; estimates from 100 million to 500 million; roughly 50 million by a global-brand affordability lens, 250-300 million by an FMCG lens, 375 million by NCAER's consuming class, 300 million by a middle-majority-of-income lens, 230 million by Butel's own-transport-entertainment-communication lens, shrinking to 30 million if a computer is added. She states the consequence: "despite being notional and subjective, if treated as a gospel, it leads to non-exploitation of opportunity and lazy strategy," and quotes Dr A. S. Ganguli that arbitrary downward estimates "do not truly reflect a state of restricted opportunity, but rather non-exploration of opportunities".

item.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
item.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the opening cases and the barn-raising passage (spine 10)
item.question: Berger's fifth driver overlaps heavily with his first — both explain why people pass things on. How does he distinguish them, and what does he choose as his opening cases to make the point?
item.answer: He distinguishes them by whose interests the sharing serves. Social Currency is about the SENDER and how sharing makes them look; Practical Value is about the RECEIVER, and it transmits because people want to help — saving someone time or money or trouble. He concedes the sender still benefits, since helping feels good and reflects well, but says the core of the mechanism is other-directed, and his analogy is a barn raising: mutual help that distance has made rare in physical form and that useful information restores. His opening cases are chosen to be unglamorous on purpose, because glamour would let social currency explain them: an eighty-six- year-old's video about removing silk from corn, watched more than five million times and skewing to viewers over fifty-five, and hikers on a mountain trail discussing vacuum cleaner models. He goes through the other drivers explicitly to show none of them accounts for the vacuum conversation.
item.support: No measurement supports the sender-versus-receiver distinction; it is an interpretive framing, and the same act is compatible with either motive, which Berger concedes without separating them. The one measurement bearing on the driver is his own New York Times finding, reported in the previous chapter, that more useful articles were 30 percent more likely to make the Most E-Mailed list — which establishes the association, not the helping motive behind it. He ranks this driver the easiest of the six to apply, as a judgement without a cross-driver comparison.

item.source_locator: Ch. 3, 'The Dangerous Delusion of Pent-up Demand'
item.question: Describe the boom-extrapolation-stagnation cycle, and identify the distinction that makes it a mechanism rather than an observation.
item.answer: A repeating pattern she says has recurred many times since 1991: an initial starburst of demand caused by a confluence of one-time events — release of pent-up demand, a category first strongly promoted, a distribution boom, a price threshold crossed by a sachet or an instalment scheme — followed by extrapolation of those early rates into the future, followed by stagnation when the market 'hits a rock table and growth grinds to a halt'. THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES IT A MECHANISM IS STOCK VERSUS FLOW: a starburst is produced by a STOCK being released, not by a FLOW being established, and a stock is finite by definition, so the early rate was never a rate that could continue. That is why the pattern is predictable rather than merely recurrent. She reports the 1990s instance — analysts extrapolated 20-30 per cent volume growth, 'the myth of the Great Indian Middle Class was born', large capacity investments followed, and the consumption machine failed to materialise — and what she says is required at the rock table: 'not a mop but actually a powerful drill fashioned from a good market strategy', specifically searching for weak areas rather than flogging the sales team with targets based on historical growth. THE OUTCOME CLAIMS ARE NOT EVIDENCED: no series is supplied for the extrapolation or the stagnation.
item.support: growth 'hits a rock table and growth grinds to a halt'
item.confounders: Told as a story about the 1990s it is a period anecdote. The stock-versus-flow distinction is what makes it apply anywhere, and it is the part most often dropped.

item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a framework for reading change in this market, built on a distinction she draws: MOLTING change, in which the old is shed for the new like a snake's skin, against MORPHING change, slow and from within, "like an amoeba which, with every tiny particle it ingests, infinitesimally changes shape." She argues Indian change is of the second kind and gives the reason in a physics analogy: since Force = Mass x Acceleration, "a small acceleration (small changes over long periods of time) can also unleash a large force of change, if the mass that is changing is very large." She names the detection problem it creates — "this change is not visible through the usual run of the mill 'usage and attitude' type surveys that most companies ritualistically engage in" — and reports the executive's experience: watching for change annually and finding none worth mentioning, then five years later finding the market distinctly different and asking "when did we blink and not see this happening?" Her proposed unit of observation is the CHANGE CONFLUENCE: a collection of individually insignificant changes occurring simultaneously, which together reshape a market.

mechanism.text: An instrument that reports a rate per period will report a small number every period when the per-period change is small, regardless of how large the accumulated change becomes or how large the population it applies to. The change is therefore invisible to the instrument and visible only in the cumulative state, which is why it is discovered retrospectively.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets. The Force = Mass x Acceleration formulation is an analogy, and the author uses it as one.

item.claim: Abandoning the grid does not require abandoning structure. The source names two routes. Deconstruction is one: taking apart or subverting a grid to generate new spatial relationships. The other is the large class of structures not based on repeating, modular or even orthogonal geometry — those derived from nature, such as crystals, molecules and the branches of trees, and those derived from mathematical or formal relationships, such as nested or concentric ones. Because appreciating a particular structure instigates an association with physical experience, non-grid structures also impart metaphorical or narrative understanding, and familiarity with a variety of arrangement possibilities gives the designer greater latitude to architect a project's space and serve the content's needs.

mechanism.text: Structure is a class and the grid is a member of it. Removing the member does not remove the class, and the associations a structure carries come from what it resembles in physical experience rather than from its regularity.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section "a 'superhuman' realism", printed pp. 191-193
item.question: State the frontal-gaze constraint as this source records it, including what happens when it collides with the action being depicted, and separate the constraint from the reason given for it.
item.answer: The constraint, from the Meerut calendar artist Yogendra Rastogi, is that the figure must look out of the frame at the viewer WHATEVER THE FIGURE IS DOING — and his examples are secular as well as divine: a woman putting on a slipper for a footwear advertisement, a woman rolling a beedi, a woman washing clothes for a soap advertisement, 'she has to look at you'. Where it collides with the action he is explicit about which wins: 'that child who is studying, if he's reading his eyes will be downcast, and if his eyes are downcast the calendar will not sell.' The depicted action loses. The compositional consequence Jain reports is an intense emphasis on face and eyes, with the eyes typically painted last as part of the finishing strokes. THE REASON IS A SEPARATE THING FROM THE CONSTRAINT and must not be absorbed into it: the reason given is devotional — a viewer will say that if the deity is not looking at us it cannot bestow benevolence. The constraint is attested by practice across a trade and was confirmed by direct inspection of the plates in this pass; the reason is a practitioner's theory of his own customers.
item.support: 'she has to look at you'; 'if his eyes are downcast the calendar will not sell.'
item.confounders: The tempting compression is 'Indian religious images face the viewer because of darshan'. The trade behaviour is well attested; the causal story is testimony, and it is offered about customers the informant is not.

source_terms: the increasing number of working women is not driving change as much as the increasing number of housewives who have acquired the 'working woman' mindset
womanism
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific measurement error. The popular theory held that household consumption was changing because more women worked outside the home. She reports the data against it: only 23 per cent of housewives in urban India had a job outside the home, and "as households get richer, the proportion of women in the workforce falls" — 20 per cent of SEC A housewives working outside, sliding through B and C, rising again to almost 40 per cent toward SEC E. She then reports why the proxy failed even where it applied: "the 'this as well as that' working woman continues to play the traditional role at home, and in many ways is the last to change practices inside the home, even as she blazes new trails outside," so "her personal spending and saving patterns on personal products will change quite dramatically, but not her household behaviour." Her conclusion is the correction: the change is driven not by more women working but by more housewives acquiring a working-woman mindset, a shift she calls womanism and describes as "a change in the mindset of women rather than in behaviour."

mechanism.text: The proxy assumed employment outside the home would change practices inside it. It does not, because the two roles are held simultaneously rather than exchanged. So the metric that was easy to count tracked a variable that was not the operative one, and marketers watching it "are perhaps missing the big changes inside the home."

scope.conditions: Indian households on IRS 2008 data, urban and rural.

caveats.text: THE TRANSFERABLE PART IS THE ERROR SHAPE, NOT THE FINDING. A countable proxy adopted because it is countable, tracking a variable that is not the operative one, is a general research failure. The Indian specifics are 2008-vintage

the corrective concept, womanism, is explicitly a mindset shift that the author says is 'not easy to see' and shows up in attitude rather than behaviour. It is therefore hard to measure and the book offers no instrument for it, which limits its operational use

the supporting evidence beyond the workforce-participation data is drawn from advertising-agency and market-research studies (FCB ULKA, IMRB, McCann, Research International) reported without sample sizes or dates, and from the author's own reading of matrimonial advertisements

INSPECTED: Figure 10.2, the incidence of housewives working outside the home by SEC, was opened. The U-shape is clearly visible in both the urban and rural panels — falling from A1 through B2 and rising through D to E2 in urban, rising monotonically R1 to R4 in rural — which supports the claim as stated. Source given as IRS

source_terms: we will use the term complex surface to mean a single surface that requires both diffuse and direct reflection to define it properly
Only direct reflection can tell the viewer that the wood is glossy, but diffuse reflection is essential to reveal the color and the grain of the wood beneath the gloss.
item.claim: The source defines a complex surface as a single surface that needs both diffuse and direct reflection to be defined properly. Glossy wood is the given example: only direct reflection can say the wood is glossy, and only diffuse reflection can show the colour and grain beneath the gloss. The two cannot occupy the same area, so the surface is divided. The source lit a polished wooden box with a source large enough to fill the whole family of angles, then blocked part of it with a gobo, so that one part of the surface shows the gloss by direct reflection and the other shows the wood's true colour and grain by diffuse reflection. The source notes that the diffusely lit area is the only place where the true colour of the wood is clearly apparent.

mechanism.text: Direct reflection is an image of the source and therefore reports finish; diffuse reflection reports pigment. A surface carrying both properties can only report both by devoting different regions of itself to different reflection types, which a partly blocked large source achieves.

scope.conditions: single surfaces carrying both a finish and an underlying colour or pattern

caveats.text: the source's own term, introduced with a definition; label_origin recorded as source_verbatim for the term 'complex surface'
the division is spatial, and the source does not claim a rule for where the boundary should fall; in its example the gloss occupies camera-left and the grain camera-right

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, 'Premium, Popular and Discount'; Figure 4.2
item.question: Marketers observed richer consumers buying popular-segment products and called it down-trading. What does this source say was actually happening, and what is the general shape of the error?
item.answer: That the direction of the inference was wrong. The observation was read as a consumer trait — 'many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy' — and her correction is that 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', so the popular and discount segments in many cases now offered equivalent or better benefits at a lower price. She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced 'rogue' marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. Her instances are automotive — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B-segment car with premium features — and her conclusion is that 'the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant'. THE GENERAL SHAPE is attributing a change in observed behaviour to a change in the people, when what changed was the set of options they faced. Figure 4.2 was opened in this pass and carries no data: it is a price-against-performance schematic, so it illustrates the argument and is not evidence for it. No switching data is supplied anywhere.
item.support: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer'
item.confounders: Character explanations are attractive because they need no data and predict everything. This is the book's clearest instance, and its correction is also unmeasured.

item.source_locator: Ch. 9, 'This as Well as That'; Tables 9.1, 9.2
item.question: Separate the transferable mechanism in the 'this as well as that' argument from the framing it is wrapped in, and say why the separation matters.
item.answer: THE MECHANISM is a clean and general account of hybrid adoption: a bundled practice is adopted by outsourcing the disliked component and retaining the valued one — which is why a successful entrant unbundles rather than substitutes, and why the expected zero-sum contest between tradition and modernity, with modernity winning, did not occur. That is testable in principle and applies wherever an incumbent practice is a bundle. THE FRAMING treats this as an Indian cultural 'DNA' with 'high tolerance of ambiguity', evidenced by avatars in the Hindu pantheon and by Brahmins in Bengal being permitted fish. That framing is essentialist, is not evidenced, and does no work the mechanism does not already do. THE SEPARATION MATTERS FOR TWO REASONS. First, the framing makes the mechanism sound like a fact about Indians, which stops it being applied anywhere else and makes it unfalsifiable where it is applied. Second, the framing's own evidence is Table 9.2, which was opened in this pass: a two-column contrast of asserted values — patriarchy against egalitarianism, ambiguity and low dissonance against clarity and linearity, socially defined roles against individually chosen roles — WITH NO SOURCE LINE AND NO DATA. The text says 'as can be seen in Table 9.2' and stops. It is the author's summary of her own position presented in the visual form of evidence.
item.support: Table 9.2, read directly: a two-column contrast of asserted values with no source and no data.
item.confounders: A table with no source line still reads as data because of its form. This is the clearest instance in the batch of a layout carrying an authority its content does not have.

item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
item.source_locator: printed p. 106 (Chapter Nine, the unnamed present) and printed p. 164 (Chapter Fifteen)
item.question: Hopkins names curiosity as the strongest activating factor he knows and derives a specific rule from it. State the rule and the selection argument behind it, and give the condition he attaches.
item.answer: The rule is that an undisclosed reward outperforms a described one. His argument is about selection rather than about excitement: describe a gift and some will decide they want it while more will decide they do not, whereas everybody wants a secret gift — description gives the reader enough information to refuse, and withholding it removes the ground for refusal. He applies the same logic to campaign concepts, citing foods shot from guns, grains pictured at eight times normal size, and a pamphlet about convict-cut Indian wood hauled to the Ganges by elephants, all built to make the reader want to see the thing. His condition is hard: the undisclosed gift must not disappoint, must be something every recipient wants, and should be somewhat better than expected; and the offer should be handled quietly rather than blazoned. No comparative figure for described versus undisclosed rewards appears anywhere in the book.
item.support: Printed p. 106 for the wrapped unlabelled presents in grocers' windows and the curiosity claim; printed p. 164 for the undescribed gift on the sales manager's card. He also states in the same material a period belief that curiosity is especially strong with women, which is 1920s framing and is not extracted here as a claim about buyers.
confounders: reading it as a general endorsement of mystery or teasing; his mechanism is specifically about removing grounds for refusal
ignoring the disappointment condition, without which the device damages the seller on delivery

source_terms: Narrative Constructs
Pictorialization and Metaphorical Allusion
the layout becomes a kind of illustration
As content progresses or pursues a different direction from page to page or screen to screen, the "subject" depicted by the layout changes, but the governing logic remains the same.
item.claim: An idea embedded in the project's content can itself be visualised as the compositional structure of the page or screen. The source names two variants. In narrative pictorialisation the layout and its parts are made to look like something discussed in the text — elements arranged to give the impression of objects swept up in a flood, or to construct a literal image of a car or other machine; in simplest terms the layout becomes a kind of illustration. As the content progresses or changes direction from page to page, the subject the layout depicts changes while the governing logic stays the same. In metaphorical allusion the layout structure and the visual language of the forms it arranges refer to some tangential idea that supports or manipulates perception of the meaning — a promotion for a film festival splicing repeated images to refer to film editing. Both variants follow the idea of visual storytelling, relying on depictive strategies to deliver narrative meaning that either describes the content or reframes and augments it.

mechanism.text: Chapter 2 has already established that a viewer reads a structure as the thing it resembles. Pictorialisation and allusion are the deliberate exploitation of that reading: the arrangement is made to resemble something so that the resemblance carries meaning.

scope.conditions: content that contains an idea capable of being depicted

caveats.text: The whole method depends on the viewer recognising the resemblance. The source offers no account of what happens when they do not.
Each example is a layout whose resemblance exists only in the image. The strategy is recorded; no judgement is made here about whether any of the cited layouts achieves it.

make the layout look like something discussed in the text, holding the governing logic constant as the depicted subject changes

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, 'Premium, Popular and Discount'; Ch. 10, 'Women'
item.question: A product's usage among 25-34 year-olds has fallen for three quarters and the team concludes that this cohort is becoming less brand-loyal. Apply this source, and say what it cannot settle.
item.answer: The source's response is that a change in a measured series has been attributed to a change in the PEOPLE without testing whether what changed was the OPTIONS, and it supplies two worked cases of exactly that error. In the down-trading case the observation was read as 'the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy', and the actual cause was supply-side: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', after tax and duty changes forced small manufacturers into open competition and produced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. In the working-women case a plausible driver was adopted and never checked, and the data ran the other way through the affluent segment. The rule to apply here: BEFORE ACCEPTING A DEMAND-SIDE EXPLANATION FOR A MOVED SERIES, ESTABLISH WHAT CHANGED ON THE SUPPLY SIDE — what entered the category, what changed price, what changed in distribution, and what a competitor did in the same three quarters. Character explanations should be the residual, not the first hypothesis, because they need no data and predict everything. What this source CANNOT settle is whether the loyalty explanation is wrong in this case. It supplies no test, no threshold and no metric — two cases in which a demand-side reading was wrong establish that the check is worth running, not what it will return.
item.support: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer'
item.confounders: Both of the source's cases are ones where the supply-side explanation won, which is a selected sample of two. The asymmetry it justifies is one of ORDER — check supply first — not a presumption about the answer.

source_terms: the analogy school
emerging markets are not what the developed markets were in their infancy
Consumers exist in real time
item.claim: Bijapurkar attacks what she calls "the analogy school" — the practice of predicting a market's evolution by studying a more developed market assumed to be analogous, plotting per-capita GDP against per-capita consumption across countries and reading the gap as opportunity. Her core objection is stated flatly: "the assumption that Indian consumers today are like American consumers twenty years ago, is deeply flawed. CONSUMERS EXIST IN REAL TIME and are confronted by all the forces of today, not yesterday. Moreover, they are products of their own unique consumer history and culture." She gives the reinforcing observation: "never before in the history of humanity have so many poor and illiterate people been subjected to so much real time exposure to the developed world," so a global health discourse about colas or fast food reaches a nascent market at the same moment it reaches a mature one. She adds a second objection — emerging markets need not be virgin markets — with the "experienced hire versus fresh hire" analogy: Consumer India already had a dense array of home-grown options at many price-performance points, which raises the bar for entrants.

mechanism.text: An analogy across time assumes the two markets faced the same information and the same alternatives at the same stage. Neither holds: information now arrives simultaneously everywhere, and the later market's alternatives include technologies the earlier market did not have at that stage. So the later market can skip stages the analogy requires it to pass through, and the analogy's prediction fails in the direction of over-predicting the skipped stage.

scope.conditions: Stated for India against developed-market analogies, over 1991-2009.

caveats.text: her strongest instance is a leapfrogging prediction that was correct and is checkable: 'Intel will have to stop worrying about when PC penetration in India will hit the same levels as it did in developed markets earlier - it will need to fight in an India revolutionized by feature-rich cellphones, which are getting far more deeply entrenched than PCs in a much shorter span of time.' Written before 2009, this is a specific, falsifiable forecast and it held

the argument is asymmetric. She offers cases where analogy over-predicted (colas, breakfast cereals, PCs) and none where it under-predicted or was right. An argument against a forecasting method built only from its failures is weaker than it appears

her positive alternative — 'painstakingly construct it from first principles, by studying age cohorts, by looking at cultural drivers of change and by understanding the process of change and the DNA of the society' — is a research programme, not a method, and no worked instance of it producing a forecast is given

item.rationale: Two constraints in this source are unusually well suited to production reasoning because they are STATED AS CONSTRAINTS BY THE PEOPLE SUBJECT TO THEM, they have reasons attached, and they are checkable against the artefact. A figure must return the viewer's gaze even where the depicted action would direct it elsewhere; a divine body must not carry musculature or an alert, agentive posture. What is bound is the existence and shape of such constraints for work intended for this tradition — that a request for an image in this idiom carries requirements which override naturalistic plausibility and which a generator working from generic naturalist priors will violate by default.

item.claim: Sullivan describes a failure that passes every check: the obedient idea, which is on strategy, correctly targeted, and does nothing. He says he sees many of them as a creative director and as a teacher, and characterises them as work that dutifully ticks the boxes about what an advertisement should be and then lies there asking to be looked at. source_terms: accuracy in following them is a particularly stringent requirement
the production of locality
item.claim: Jain reports, from artists, printers, distributors and clients alike, "a well-defined regional iconography characterizing preferences in the north, south, east, and west," operating not only at the level of which deities are favoured but at the level of their iconographic attributes and formal treatment. Her enumerated examples: Lakshmi and Shiva preferred standing in the north and seated in the south; the eyes of Shiva and Hanuman wide open in the south and often half-closed in the north; Ganesh's ears and trunk longer in the north and his face paler in Bengal; Lakshmi accompanied by an owl in Bengal and nowhere else; Radha often portrayed with her garments askew in the north while in Bengal all goddesses are covered to the point that even their ears are hidden. She states the operational consequence directly: artists develop a thorough knowledge of these codes, "as accuracy in following them is a particularly stringent requirement; most cited this as THE MAIN AREA WHERE THEY MIGHT BE ASKED TO MAKE CHANGES BEFORE A DESIGN IS APPROVED TO GO TO PRESS." She adds a second finding: because the codes are conventionalised, an artist need not inhabit or identify with the community whose images he or she is producing — enabling the "production of locality" from dispersed sites, or as she puts it, its commoditisation.

mechanism.text: Once a regional preference is codified into a finite list of attributes, it becomes transferable knowledge rather than lived membership. The artist can then satisfy it from anywhere, which is why Jain finds Venkatesh Sapar in Sholapur creating the Durgas and Krishnas that represent Bengaliness, Nirmala in Calcutta painting a "northern" Shiva-Parvati, and Yogendra Rastogi in Meerut figuring a south Indian identity through his Lakshmis.

scope.conditions: The pan-national Sivakasi-centred trade as observed 1994-2001. Jain notes the same conventions are mapped onto a discourse of taste — Bengali taste considered the most refined and softest in colour, northern and western markets preferring lighter colours, the most intense schemes used for the south.

caveats.text: the enumerated attribute-level differences are reported from informants, not from a survey of prints. Jain does not count them or test whether the prints in fact conform
'most cited this as the main area where they might be asked to make changes' is the strongest operational statement in the object and is also unquantified — 'most' of an unnamed number of artists
the taste discourse ('Bengali taste is the most refined') is a trade stereotype the industry holds, reported as such. It is not the author's finding about Bengali viewers and must not be read as one

the same section records that the participation of Muslim artists in this Hindu-dominated imagery has been characterised by degrees of 'passing' — Liaqat Ali's major input to paintings signed by Rastogi goes unsigned, and Muslim artists who do sign have adopted names that are not easily identifiable. The transferability of the codes is real and it is not evidence of communal difference being erased

Adjacency to sk_jgb_0050 recorded without a graph edge: the commoditisation of difference. The original extraction used a 'supports' relation, which SPEC-03 does not define; no permitted relation expresses it from this object's side, so it is kept as an observation rather than expressed as a fabricated edge.

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Field-attested from multiple roles in the industry, unquantified throughout.

source_stated_remedies: learn the regional attribute codes as explicit transferable knowledge rather than relying on membership

source_terms: focus on one thing
just one. Not two, three, or four.

item.claim: The source's sharpest rule is a count: an iconic design that stands out has exactly one feature doing the standing out. It states the number emphatically and twice — one, not two, three or four — and gives the mechanism through a counterfactual rather than an example. The French Property Exhibition mark focuses on a single attribute, an open door in the tricolour. The source observes that the designer could have added an Eiffel Tower, that everyone would immediately associate an Eiffel Tower with France, and that this is precisely why it would have been wrong: the viewer would then have had to process an unnecessary element, making the design less memorable.

mechanism.text: Every additional element in a mark is an additional thing the viewer must process inside the glance, and processing capacity inside a glance is the scarce resource. An element can be both relevant and harmful — the Eiffel Tower would have been relevant — because relevance does not buy back the attention it costs.

scope.conditions: marks that must register in a quick glance; the source states the clients' customers will not spend long studying the logo

caveats.text: the counterfactual is asserted, not tested — no version with the Eiffel Tower was made or shown

the source's own Tenth Church example (printed 101) is praised for carrying 'multiple conceptual themes of worship, welcome, transformation, outreach, and the cross' in one wordmark, which sits in tension with a strict reading of the one-feature rule. The tension is the source's.

an added element that is relevant but unnecessary

item.question: A generative system is asked to produce devotional images for the Indian market and is trained mostly on general naturalist photography. Which constraints in this source would it violate by default, which of them can actually be checked, and what should not be built from this material?
item.answer: Three would be violated by default, because naturalist priors run against each. The frontal gaze: a naturalist prior renders a figure attending to whatever it is doing, and the trade constraint is that the figure looks out at the viewer regardless — 'if his eyes are downcast the calendar will not sell'. The unmuscled divine body: a naturalist prior renders a figure drawing a bow with visible anatomy, and the constraint is 'there won't be any muscles, we people avoid muscles'. And saturation: a naturalist prior reproduces the reference faithfully, where the trade adds saturation deliberately. Both of the first two were confirmed by direct inspection of the plates in this pass, so they are not merely reported. WHAT CAN BE CHECKED is limited: whether a face is turned out and whether a body is modelled are inspectable properties of an output, so a human reviewer can apply them. Regional attribute codes are a harder case — Jain gives illustrative examples from informants, not a complete or dated code, and reports no survey of prints against it, so it is not a specification. WHAT SHOULD NOT BE BUILT is a scored conformity metric. Jain warns that these are 'primarily discursive categories, part of the bazaar's self-understanding' rather than observed regularities of the artefacts; her code is illustrative and undated; and the muscularity injunction was breached from the late 1980s, so a metric built on it would penalise images the tradition itself now contains. There is also no numeric form of any of this in the source: no angle, no tolerance, no test.
item.support: 'There won't be any muscles, we people avoid muscles.'
item.confounders: The constraints are unusually crisp for a cultural source, which makes them feel specifiable. Crispness of statement is not the same as having a threshold, and the source supplies none.

results.representation_note: Q&A is an alternate grounded representation of the same source. It corroborates nothing on its own.

item.claim: Sullivan names a specific and checkable failure: the piece in which the visual shows what the headline already says. He calls it a see-say advertisement and identifies it as a common rookie error, describing the symptom as every element trying way too hard and either repeating or tripping over one another. The stated requirement is that the visual should amplify the headline or reinterpret it, not restate it.

mechanism.text: Duplication wastes the second element. Because tension in a layout is produced by the distance between what is said and what is shown (see sk_whip_0048), a visual that closes that distance to zero leaves nothing for the reader to resolve and nothing for the second element to add.

caveats.text: the source's own 'clever headline, straight visual' rule requires the straight visual to add something — he describes it as amplifying emotional impact or finishing the thought — so the line between a supporting visual and a see-say is a judgement he does not operationalise

source_terms: 'Nobody reads body copy.' True or false? It depends on two things. First, on how many people are interested in the kind of product you are advertising... Second, on how many people have been enticed into your ad by your illustration and headline.

The average readership of the body copy in magazine ads is about 5 per cent. That does not sound like a lot until you remember that 5 per cent of readers of the Reader's Digest adds up to 1,500,000 men and women.
item.claim: The source refuses the flat proposition that nobody reads body copy and decomposes it into two determinants: how many people are interested in that kind of product, which the advertisement cannot change, and how many were enticed in by the illustration and headline, which it can. He gives category examples in the same breath — many women will read copy about food products, few will read copy about cigars — and puts average magazine body-copy readership at about five per cent, arguing that five per cent of a large circulation is still a very large number of people.

mechanism.text: Readership is the product of pre-existing category interest and the entry the advertisement itself creates, so the same craft applied to two categories yields different absolute readership without either advertisement being better or worse.
