item.rationale: Two documented instances of a single evaluation failure: a measured quantity moving for a reason other than the one attributed to it. In the first, a countable proxy (women working outside the home) was adopted because it was countable and tracked a variable that was not the operative one, so the forecast built on it failed. In the second, observed buying behaviour shifted because the price-performance frontier moved, and analysts attributed the shift to the buyer's character. This project attributes changes in measured outcomes to causes, and both instances are cases of attributing a movement to the wrong term.

applicability.when: attributing a change in a measured outcome to a cause, where the measurement instrument or the choice set may itself have moved
applicability.limits: Both instances are Indian, dated and told without the underlying analysis being shown. They support asking, of any attributed movement, whether the proxy tracks the operative variable and whether the choice set moved. They establish no rate at which this error occurs, supply no test, and licence no threshold. Note also that the source itself offers two unreconciled explanations for one of its own examples (see the conflict recorded in scs_rbwl_003), which is a live illustration of the difficulty rather than a solution to it.

item.recast_note: RECAST FROM AN EVALUATION BINDING. It carried `observation_unit: measurement_series`, which is not one of SPEC-04's media observation units - those run frame, shot, shot_pair, sequence, whole_asset, asset_set_over_time, and a business measurement series is none of them. The underlying lesson is real and is not about media at all: when a measured quantity moves, the movement may belong to the instrument or to the choice set rather than to the subject, and this source supplies two worked cases of it. That is a rule about how evidence may be interpreted, so it is now a governance binding with consumer `evidence_interpretation`. Nothing about a media output is evaluated by it, no threshold is adopted, and the role is `constrains` because it constrains what an attributed movement may be read as.

source_terms: Large highlights are essential to glass surface definition.
Rather than cluttering the other elements of the photograph for the attention of the viewer, it serves the constructive purpose of saying, 'This is how this glass surface looks and feels.'
Had we lit the whole diffusion sheet brightly, it would have reflected in the glass as an obvious hard-edged rectangle. This reflection would have advertised the presence of a studio light
item.claim: Defining the edges is not always enough; often the surface must be shown too, and that requires managing the highlights. Large highlights are essential, and the difference from small ones is not of degree but of function: a tiny bright spot is distracting at best and meaningless at worst, while a large highlight tells the viewer how the surface looks and feels. Producing one means filling the relevant family of angles with light, and because a rounded glass reflects much of the studio, that family can be surprisingly large. The distance from the lamp head to the diffusion sheet then becomes a design decision: close in, only the centre of the sheet is bright and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight, which the source says should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as a hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality. Strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.

mechanism.text: A direct reflection is an image of the source, so the highlight's size, shape and evenness are the source's size, shape and evenness. Making the highlight describe a surface therefore means shaping the source, and making it look unlike a studio means giving the source a shape found outside one.

scope.conditions: glassware whose surface, not only outline, must read; also useful with non-transparent secondary subjects present

caveats.text: this is the live chapter-3 mirror-image property (sk_lsm_c003_0010, sk_lsm_c003_0012) used as a design control rather than as a fact; the new content is that highlight SIZE carries surface information and that a recognisable source shape reads as artificial

item.description: A record of the book's own evidential form: lessons drawn from cases that succeeded, campaign outcomes asserted without data, and the campaign evidence itself published outside the book. Grouped so that a downstream consumer meets the bound attached to the source rather than having to rediscover it.

whole_system_claim.text: This source can support statements about what an eminent Indian practitioner believes and recommends, and about the mechanisms he articulates. It cannot support any claim that a practice causes an outcome, because every case it offers is one that succeeded, no outcome is evidenced, and the work itself is not reproduced.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Entirely the extractor's. Pandey makes no methodological statement about his own book. The grouping is a statement about the representation and its evidential limits, not about advertising, and it is recorded here rather than left in prose because the same bound applies to every object in the file and would otherwise have to be restated on each.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. Unusually for a system, what it asserts is checkable against the file itself: the claim is that this book's cases all succeeded and its outcomes are unevidenced, and a reader can verify that by reading the objects. What remains the extractor's is the decision to record the evidential bound as a system rather than as prose, and the judgement about what the source can and cannot support — which is a recommendation to consumers, not a finding about Pandey.

source_terms: The Law of Singularity
The most important aspect of a brand is its single-mindedness.
What's a brand? A singular idea or concept that you own inside the mind of the prospect.
item.claim: Law 22, and the book's closing definition. The most important property of a brand is single-mindedness, and a brand is a singular idea or concept owned inside a prospect's mind. The authors give the diagnostic in the form they used to open the book: ask what a name is, and if the answer is a list of contradictory attributes — a large, small, cheap, expensive car or truck — the brand is burned out. They add a boundary that matters for how a burned-out brand looks from outside: such brands can stay on the marketing scene for years because their competitors are equally line-extended, so survival is not evidence that singularity was retained. The Introduction states the same principle at the demand side: because branding rests on singularity, no brand can have universal appeal.

mechanism.text: The social function the authors assign a brand is substitution: a proper noun that can be used in place of a common phrase, so that a buyer asks for a Heineken instead of an imported beer, or a Volvo instead of a safe car. A name that stands for several things cannot perform that substitution, which is what "burned out" means in their vocabulary.

scope.conditions: stated without limit as the closing definition of the book

caveats.text: the chapter is largely a restatement of the Law of Expansion and the Law of the Word, and this lane extracted it for the closing definition and the survival caveat rather than for its examples
the survival caveat repeats the weak-competition escape clause a fourth time, and it does so in the book's final pages: a brand's continued existence is not allowed to count against the diagnosis

source_terms: Most retail category killers follow the same five-step pattern.
Narrow the focus. Stock in depth. Buy cheap. Sell cheap. Dominate the category.
item.claim: The authors set out a five-step pattern they say most retail category killers follow, in order: narrow the focus by contracting rather than expanding the category; stock the narrowed category in depth (a Toys "R" Us store carrying ten thousand toys against three thousand in a large department store); buy cheap, which they say is where the money is actually made; sell cheap, which depth of buying makes possible while holding margin; and dominate the category, which they name as the ultimate objective of any branding programme.

mechanism.text: The steps are causally chained by the authors: narrowing permits depth, depth permits buying power, buying power permits low prices at maintained margin, and the combination produces category domination. Domination is then said to make a brand extremely powerful.

source_terms: reliable but not valid
consumption is like maternity, a certainty. Income is like paternity - merely a matter of inference.
item.claim: Bijapurkar gives an explicit, enumerated set of rules for using Indian household income survey data, on the ground that it is systematically understated. Her rules: do not use it literally (the most rigorous survey, the NDSSP, accounts for only 59.6 per cent of total disposable personal income per the National Accounting Statistics); do not try to reconcile across surveys, because they define income classes differently, elicit it with different questions and index to different base years; and recognise that the data is "what statisticians would call RELIABLE BUT NOT VALID" — repeat the survey and you get the same answers, so it does not measure the real thing but is "perfectly usable for grading the population based on its relative purchasing power and for comparing the growths and declines of various income groups over time." She adds the operational consequence: work with income PERCENTILES rather than absolute bands or labels, and calibrate each percentile against what people in it actually consume. She compresses the whole into an aphorism: "consumption is like maternity, a certainty. Income is like paternity — merely a matter of inference."

mechanism.text: A consistent bias destroys level comparisons while preserving rank and change comparisons. So the same dataset that cannot answer "how much do they earn" can answer "who earns more than whom" and "which group grew" — and the failure mode is using it for the first question because it is expressed in the units of the first question.

scope.conditions: Indian household income surveys as of the 2008 data used in the revised edition. Bijapurkar attributes the understatement to cultural rather than methodological causes — "This has nothing to do with weak survey design methodology" — which is an assertion, not a demonstrated finding.

caveats.text: THIS IS THE MOST TRANSFERABLE OBJECT IN THE RECORD AND ALSO THE ONE MOST TIED TO ITS DATA. The reliable-but-not-valid distinction, and the rule of using ranks and changes rather than levels from a consistently biased instrument, generalise well beyond India. source_terms: eye path
Compositional flow, sometimes called "eye path," occurs as a viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast from the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance
For Western readers, it's wise to orient top-level elements toward the left-hand area of a layout.

Elements to be encountered next must differentiate from their contexts to a similar degree (like things attract attention) or be positioned in proximity to the place where the viewer's eye is likely to leave the first element behind.
item.claim: Where the first or most important element sits, and how it optically connects the viewer to what follows, matter as much as differentiation itself. Compositional flow — eye path — occurs as the viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast against the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance; the eye moves from the area of greatest overall contrast to the least, along a direction the designer can support by positioning axes or by using graphical forms to point. For Western readers the source advises orienting top-level elements toward the left-hand area of the layout. Each subsequent element must either differentiate from its context to a similar degree, because like things attract attention, or be placed near where the eye is likely to leave the previous element. Inserting graphical markers or anchoring points at strategic locations helps focus attention and direct the flow. The same rule is applied to a specific case: when setting type on a circular path or arc, orient its entry point toward the upper left and, if possible, so that the first words are relatively horizontal.

mechanism.text: Contrast is restated as optical resistance, so a sequence of decreasing contrast reads as a path of decreasing resistance. Order is therefore produced by a gradient rather than by position in a structure, which is why a layout with no grid can still have a reading order.

scope.conditions: Western reading conventions; explicitly scoped to Western readers by the source

caveats.text: The left-hand and upper-left advice is stated by the source as specific to Western readers and must not be generalised to readers of right-to-left or vertical scripts.
The mechanism is an account of perception offered without evidence; it is a designer's model of reading, not a reading study.
The comparison that carries the type-on-a-curve rule is a paired before/after image. Only the rule is recorded; the demonstrated difference in readability was not seen.

item.claim: The authors prescribe that a leader advertise its leadership rather than its quality, and note that very few do. Their reason is what each claim produces in the reader: "our product is better" produces the response "that's what they all say", while "our product is the leader" produces "it must be better". item.claim: In the exhibits Samara repeatedly names the same underlying condition as the thing that makes an apparently disordered layout read as crafted rather than as chaos, and the condition is restriction of the axis set. In one exhibit the designers attend to whether axes run parallel or divergent and to their junctures, distributing them along a limited selection of planar levels and directions, which he says ensures well-crafted, rhythmic cohesion instead of chaotic randomness. In another, spatial confusion and complicated interference between overlapping shapes and text are underpinned by a rigorously controlled network of geometric axes in which the edges of every element line up with, or point to, those of other elements and the junctures between them; he traces one such axis through the poster explicitly. item.interpretation_basis: Samara states each observation about its own exhibit and does not generalise them into a rule. The generalisation — that a restricted family of axes is what distinguishes intentional disorder from incompetent disorder — is the extractor's reading across several exhibit commentaries that use the same contrast in the same terms. mechanism.text: Every element has axes whether or not a grid is present. Where those axes fall into a small number of families the eye finds repetition beneath the complexity, and the arrangement reads as governed; where they do not, there is nothing to find and it reads as accidental.

scope.conditions: densely layered compositions with no visible grid

item.claim: Sullivan names two distinct headline faults with different mechanisms. The first is the invented person — a "Little Billy" — which he says readers recognise immediately as fake, and an irritating kind of fake, like the stock relatives supplied inside shop-bought picture frames. He grants an exception: where a name is the only way the concept can work, an experienced team can do it gracefully, and the difference is entirely in the execution. The second is the product or model number, which he says feels familiar to the maker because they work on the account, and functions for the reader as a speed bump: the characters are not words, so the reader must change gear mid-sentence to get through them.

mechanism.text: Two mechanisms. The fake name fails by detection — the reader identifies the fabrication and transfers the judgement to the advertiser. The model number fails by processing: an alphanumeric string interrupts the reading of a sentence because it is not read as language. item.claim: A metal box shows up to three faces, each with its own family of angles facing a different direction, all of which must be satisfied at once. Because a polished metal box produces only direct reflection and reads as black without it, the usual aim is to fill every family rather than to avoid any — the opposite of the treatment a glossy non-metallic box gets. The top is easy and is treated as flat metal. The sides are not: the family defined by the front face falls on the table, so the table is the light source for the front of the box whether or not the photographer wants it, and no reflector can serve that face without appearing in the picture. Brightly polished metal boxes almost always show the resulting defect — the line where a reflector meets the table, or the bottom of the box merging into a dark table. The source's easiest answer is a light-toned background: the background itself becomes the source for much of the visible metal, and the requirement is that the background fill the family of angles the metal reflects, not merely the area the camera sees.

mechanism.text: Each planar face reflects a different region of space to the camera. The region reflected by a vertical front face is the horizontal surface in front of it, so whatever occupies the table is that face's source.

source_terms: The Law of the Generic
One of the fastest routes to failure is giving a brand a generic name.

item.claim: Law 12. A generic name cannot separate a brand from its competitors, and the authors ground this in a claim about processing. Most brand communication happens verbally rather than visually — they say the average person spends nine times as long listening to radio and television as reading print — and even the printed word is processed through the sound it generates, so a reader cannot hear the difference between "general" and "General". Capitalising a generic word does not make it a name. They use this to explain why line extensions fare poorly: an extension typically pairs a brand name with a generic descriptor, and the descriptor cannot create the separate identity the branding process needs.

mechanism.text: Sound is the channel. Because the mind processes the printed word through its sound, the orthographic marking that distinguishes a proper noun from a common one is lost, and the generic word is heard as generic however it is set. item.claim: Sullivan ends his provocation chapter by discarding his own book — learn the rules, then break them all — and then names the one exception. item.label: how_value_is_settled_in_the_household_the_source_describes
item.description: Four claims from the book's opening essay that together describe how a purchase is judged in the middle-class household Desai writes from: value realised through use over time rather than at price; a free extra whose function is closure rather than saving; indulgence licensed by an occasion rather than by appetite; and a second, social return currency in which the same household spends ruinously without inconsistency.

whole_system_claim.text: In this account a purchase is not settled at the transaction. It is settled afterwards, by use; the transaction itself is closed by a token extra whose money value is irrelevant; appetite alone does not license spending, an occasion does; and a separate social-return budget operates alongside all of this without being felt to contradict it.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Desai states each of these in one essay, "The Dhania Factor", plus the wedding case in the same essay. He does not assemble them into an account of how value is settled, and he draws no general conclusion from the set. The synthesis is the extractor's. What justifies attempting it is that the four are stated in one continuous argument and each is offered as part of the same disposition; what makes it a synthesis rather than a report is that Desai never states that they jointly constitute a model of anything, and would probably resist the word "model".

tradeoffs.nature: extracting every paisa of use-value, against spending ruinously on a wedding — the author holds both without contradiction because the return currencies differ

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: High. Every member is directly stated by Desai in one essay, so membership is well grounded. What is entirely the extractor's is the claim that the four constitute a system for settling value — Desai writes an essay, not a model, and the Introduction explicitly describes the book as scraps sewn together rather than as a single argument. The system is also bounded twice over: to the urban middle class the author names, and to a period he himself describes as loosening. It must not be consumed as a model of Indian consumer behaviour.

item.label: the_mirror_thesis_and_the_brakes_the_author_puts_on_it
item.description: The book's organising thesis (advertising records social change) together with the two explicit qualifications the author himself supplies, and the one place where the thesis's most quantitative-sounding support turns out to be unsupplied. The members qualify each other: the thesis is what makes the book worth reading, and the brakes are what make it safe to consume.

whole_system_claim.text: Advertising may be read as evidence about which social ideas were available and salient at a time, but not as evidence about how common the depicted arrangements were, and not universally — the author records a full decade in which Indian advertising did not track the dominant social mood at all.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The author never assembles these. He states the thesis in the Introduction, records the Angry-Young-Man exception in one chapter and the depiction-is-not-prevalence brake in another, roughly two hundred pages apart, and does not connect them. The grouping is entirely the extractor's. What justifies it is that the two qualifications are the only things in the book that bound the thesis, and consuming the thesis without them would licence exactly the inference the author refuses to make.

dependencies.nature: the thesis may only be consumed with the depiction/prevalence brake attached

conflicts.nature: the author's own counter-instance contradicts his organising thesis for 1975-1985 and he does not resolve it

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: High. The members are individually well supported and directly quoted, but the claim that they form ONE mutually qualifying structure is entirely the extractor's — the author states them separately, in different chapters, and never treats the later two as bounding the first. A reader could equally regard the counter-instance as an aside. What the grouping asserts, and what must be attributed to CANON-014 rather than to Parameswaran, is that the brakes are load-bearing rather than decorative.

item.claim: The source describes the operational learning loop it ran on its most successful campaign. Every advertisement carried a keyed coupon; hundreds were tried; results were reported to it week by week, and each report arrived with the headline that had produced it, so the appeal and its response stayed attached. source_terms: In most lines, like food products, the word 'free' was appealing. It multiplied the readers of our ads.

item.claim: This is the source's clearest reported boundary condition and it contradicts one of its own rules. On food products the word free multiplied the readers of its advertisements. On a hygiene product the same device, featured at the top of the advertisement, divided results by four. Its stated explanation is positional: an advertiser offering a benefit of importance is understood as a scientist seeking to benefit, and featuring a giveaway reclassifies him as a trader seeking to sell, discrediting the very factors that produce converts. Its resolution was to keep the sample free but to remove the free offer from the position of chief appeal, so the apparent object of the advertisement was to prove at the advertiser's cost what the product could do. mechanism.text: The free offer carries a signal about the advertiser's role, and the value of that signal depends on the role the category invites him to occupy. item.claim: Godin's account of why people act as they do is a single question they ask themselves — do people like me do things like this — and he makes it primary rather than one factor among several. Culture is produced by normalisation, and normalisation is produced by choices made in answer to that question, so the loop is self-reinforcing. Two consequences follow that he states explicitly. First, the marketer cannot change "the culture", only "a culture" — one pocket of the world — which is why the smallest viable market maximises the chance of changing anything at all. Second, the first job is to define "us", and the more specific and tighter the "us" the better; he warns that defining it backwards — the people who do this are people like us — is not an answer. Even outliers, he adds, are aligning with the behaviour of outliers.

mechanism.text: Behaviour is normalised by observing others in a group one identifies with, and the resulting culture then supplies the reference for the next choice. Change therefore travels horizontally, person to person inside a defined group, rather than vertically from an organisation to an individual.

source_terms: Speed of the Get

item.claim: The time a viewer takes to understand an idea is itself a design variable, and it can be mis-set in either direction. Sullivan calls it the Speed of the Get and likens it to the fuse on a firecracker. A fuse that is too short means the idea resolves before the viewer has begun attending, and its instant, contentless bang tells them there is nothing there worth attending to. A fuse that is too long means the idea does not go off before the viewer has moved on. He holds that a quick get is the first and most important property an idea needs — more important, he says explicitly, than the creativity of the piece — and that in student work the error is almost always the long fuse, produced by over-complicating and thereby "encoding" the idea.

mechanism.text: Comprehension time competes with a viewer's willingness to spend attention at all. The viewer is not looking for the message; they will not wait, so an idea that has not resolved inside the available window simply does not resolve. At the other end, an idea that resolves instantly and completely leaves nothing for the viewer to do, so nothing is registered.

scope.conditions: advertising encountered by a viewer who did not seek it out; the permissible fuse length varies with how long the viewer dwells with the medium (see sk_whip_0060)

caveats.text: the source calls the priority of the quick get 'heresy' in his own field, which marks it as his position rather than a settled view
no measurement is offered for either bound; 'too fast' and 'too slow' are named by example and by the author's judgement of student work

item.claim: Patel documents a technology-driven change in who makes posters and what they look like. From the early 1990s, photographic stills fed into a computer could be manipulated on screen, "allowing for the smooth superimposition, juxtaposition, reduction, enlargement and colour contrasting of images and text with relative ease," and the characteristic overpainted montage of the previous two decades was replaced by images "defined by simplicity and elegance." She reports the consequence for personnel plainly: "the role of the traditional artist has been displaced by the computer specialist," naming H.R. Enterprises, run by two publicity designers who are not trained artists but have extensive computer knowledge, and Yash Raj Films' in-house Design Cell under Fayyaz Badruddin, also a computer specialist. She records the practitioners' own views on both sides: Yash Chopra prefers painted posters for their element of 'art' and greater emphasis on emotion but sees the new ones as having more modern appeal; to the new designers hand-painted posters look old-fashioned.

mechanism.text: When composition becomes cheap and non-destructive, the montage no longer has to be resolved by hand into a single painted surface, so the design constraint that produced the montage look disappears. What replaces it is not a better version of the same thing but a different object — Patel's "slick, glossy posters" that "match those produced in the West and as such they have become indicators of modernity."

item.claim: Sullivan identifies a family of signals whose presence is itself the tell. A package promising "made with real cheese" or "contains real fruit" invites the inference that something is not real, and he gives the reductio: nobody sells a phone by saying it is made with real phone. An asterisk on a price, he argues, can legitimately be read as the sentence saying "we're lying", because it announces that a briefcase of qualifications is propping the number up. Stock photography is his third case — the manufactured handshake, the executive staring thoughtfully into a screen — which he says reeks of inauthenticity, and he names the most-demanded stock image in his own count of the genre. His stated underlying principle, taken from Frank Rose, is that authenticity is scarce and value tracks scarcity.

source_terms: rules and standards
Rules are meant to eliminate discretion by those who apply them; standards are meant to grant such discretion
the costs of decisions and the costs of errors

item.claim: Rules eliminate discretion and therefore noise; standards export decision authority and therefore invite it. The source's framework for choosing reduces to two factors: the cost of making decisions and the cost of errors. Standards make every decision expensive because someone must give the open-ended term content; rules make decisions cheap but make writing the rule expensive, and are sometimes prohibitively so. On errors there is no general winner. The decisive practical question is trust: principals impose rules when they cannot rely on their agents to be competent, unbiased, and practising decision hygiene.

mechanism.text: Where many similar decisions must be made, the per-decision cost of a standard accumulates and the one-off cost of writing a rule amortises, which is why the source says repeated decisions argue for moving toward rules. It also names the failure mode: a rule that produces terrible results in particular cases gets quietly ignored — jury nullification, prosecutors declining to charge a third felony, employees disregarding stupid rules — so noise reappears where no one can hear it.

scope.conditions: The source notes rules and standards are a continuum and can be mixed — a rule constraining the pool, a standard choosing within it — and that guidelines can sit at either end.

caveats.text: The source records a reason for standards that has nothing to do with judgement quality: where a group is divided or lacks the information to write a sensible rule, a standard may be the only thing that can be agreed at all.
Rules do not automatically end noise: fact-finding under a rule is itself judgement and can be noisy or biased. The reduction depends on people actually following the rule.
The Facebook example is drawn from the company's public Community Standards and a non-public implementation document obtained by a magazine, not from a study.
The source's closing position is normative and it says so — that legal systems should do much more to control noise, and that it would "not go so far" as to make noise reduction a human right.

source_terms: the files are not direct indices of market demand but represent several layers of second-guessing and self-projection
the formal expression - and the vehicle - of a relationship
item.claim: Jain identifies a structural problem with treating this industry's catalogues as evidence of what consumers want, and states it precisely. Because Sivakasi calendars are mostly advertisements given out free rather than commodities bought by end-users, "the calendar files are not direct indices of market demand but represent several layers of second-guessing and self-projection." She enumerates the layers: the files index what publishers think will interest their clients (the people responsible for a firm's publicity); which in turn indexes not just what those clients think will please their own customers, but also HOW THOSE CLIENTS WANT THEMSELVES TO BE SEEN. She adds the consequence for what the artefact is: "if a calendar is primarily a commodity from the point of view of the publishers, from the point of view of their clients it is primarily the formal expression — and the vehicle — of a relationship."

mechanism.text: When the purchaser is not the viewer, every signal that reaches the producer has passed through at least one party whose interest is in self-presentation rather than in the viewer's preference. The catalogue therefore encodes a chain of projections, and the further from the end-user the reading is taken, the more self-presentation and the less preference it contains.

scope.conditions: The Indian calendar trade 1994-2001, where the industry used no professional market research organisation and relied instead on the direct interactions and physical mobility of individual agents and printers.

caveats.text: the chain of inference is Jain's analysis of the trade's structure, not something practitioners told her. It is a well-argued structural point about a business model, not a measured distortion

Jain notes the industry's compensating mechanism — agents and printers who are 'linked to their end-users ... by less than five or six direct, interpersonal degrees of separation' — so the layering is not a claim that the industry is blind, only that its catalogue is not a demand curve

source_terms: Is there a magic number above which 'consumption take-off' happens?
The threshold theory assumes that no smart new business models are possible
item.claim: Bijapurkar addresses the theory that consumption "takes off" above a threshold per-capita income — variously pegged at US$1,100 or US$2 a day — and gives both sides. She concedes the correlation: the top 30 per cent of India, classified as having consuming power on proven aggressive consumption behaviour, did have a per-capita GDP of US$2,216 in 2008, "so there is some sanctity to the number." She then states the objection: at category level, consumption data for FMCG items with a history of aggressive value innovation — detergents, tea, shampoo — and for two-wheelers and cellphones "shows that consumption can take off well below any 'magic number'." Her diagnosis of the theory: it "is based on the notion that prices of delivered goods and services will remain unchanged, and will conform to existing 'global' standards of existing companies ... The threshold theory assumes that no smart new business models are possible which can achieve this."

mechanism.text: A threshold expressed in income units is really a statement about the ratio of income to price. Holding price fixed makes it look like a property of the population. If price can move — through pack size, business model or cost structure — the threshold moves with it, so the "magic number" is an artefact of the assumption rather than a fact about consumers.

scope.conditions: India, categories with a history of aggressive value innovation, on 2008 data.

caveats.text: the author gives the evidence for the position she is attacking as well as against it, which is unusual in this book and strengthens the object

a triangulation ... between the image, the viewer, and the viewer's sense of what others see
item.claim: Jain argues, drawing on Michael Warner and René Girard, that iconic figures in a mass-mediated public sphere take on a distinctive "logic of appeal" through the value embodied in publicity itself: after a point it is not the figure's attributes that matter but the very fact of its popularity — "the popularity of popularity, a meta-popularity." The operation is triangular, "between the image, the viewer, and the viewer's sense of what others see, think, and feel," so that desire for the icon "is enhanced, even produced, by witnessing — or, crucially, even just imagining — the intensity and desire of others." She then states the corollary that gives the object its force: because presentation before the public gaze is what renders an image valuable and powerful, "by the same token it also renders them vulnerable to disinvestment," and desecration becomes a site of violence.
item.interpretation_basis: The theoretical apparatus is Warner's and Girard's; the application to Indian bazaar images, and the linkage to the "aesthetics of presence" and to desecration, are Jain's synthesis. She presents it as her contention — "I want to suggest that a similar notion of a triangulated gaze informs..."

mechanism.text: Where value is imputed to an object rather than produced by an identifiable maker, an individual viewer cannot verify it alone; the viewer infers it from what others appear to invest. Mass mediation makes that inference cheap and continuous, so publicness becomes self-reinforcing. The same structure runs in reverse: an object whose value rests on imagined collective investment can be attacked by attacking that investment publicly.

scope.conditions: Developed for public images in India, with the political examples drawn from the 1990s — principally the Shiv Sena's actions and the case brought against M. F. Husain in 1996.

caveats.text: this is a theoretical claim illustrated by cases, not a measured effect. No quantitative work on image popularity or desecration is reported

the mechanism is drawn from Euro-American theory (Warner on Reagan, Girard on mimetic desire) and applied to a different setting; Jain argues the application, but the underlying mechanism is not independently established here
the desecration corollary is illustrated by episodes of real political violence. It should not be handled as a marketing observation

source_terms: A large food advertiser felt that his product would be more popular in another form. He and all his advisers were certain about it. They were willing to act on this supposition without consulting the consumers, but wiser advice prevailed.
He inserted an ad in a few towns with a coupon, good at any store for a package of the new-style product. Then he wrote to the users about it. They were almost unanimous in their disapproval.
he submitted the question to a few thousand women in a similar way and 91 per cent voted for it
These tests cost about $1,000 each. The first one saved him a very costly mistake.
item.claim: The source reports a case in which unanimous internal conviction was overruled by consumers. A large food advertiser and all his advisers were certain a product would be more popular in another form and were willing to act without consulting consumers. A test was run instead — an advertisement in a few towns carrying a coupon good at any store for a package of the new-style product, followed by writing to the users who took it — and the users were almost unanimous in disapproval. When a further variant was proposed later, the previous verdict made a test look hardly worth while, but the question was submitted to a few thousand women in the same way and 91 per cent voted for it. The tests cost about $1,000 each. The source's reading is that the first saved a very costly mistake and the second will probably bring large profits.

mechanism.text: Judgement about what buyers will like is unreliable in a specific way the source names elsewhere — none of us knows enough people's desires to get an average viewpoint — and internal unanimity does not correct it, because the people agreeing share the same distance from the buyer.

scope.conditions: product-form decisions where an existing user base can be sampled and asked

caveats.text: `empirical_within_source` is warranted, narrowly. This is the only place in chapter 15 where a test is reported to have RETURNED a number: 91 per cent. But note precisely what that number is. It is a vote on a product form collected from users who redeemed a coupon — a survey result, not a measured advertising return, and not cost per customer, repeat rate or payback. Chapter 15 reports a measurement from a product-research use of the apparatus and none from the test campaign it spends its first two pages specifying.
The first test's result is reported only qualitatively — "almost unanimous in their disapproval" — with no figure to set against the 91 per cent.

Both outcomes are read as vindications after the fact and the second is explicitly a prediction: "will probably bring large profits". The claim that the first test "saved him a very costly mistake" assumes the disapproval was correct, which the test cannot establish.
The respondents are self-selected coupon redeemers, which the source does not note. The second test's population — "a few thousand women" — is described only by size.

source_stated_problems: They were willing to act on this supposition without consulting the consumers.
None of us know enough people's desires to get an average viewpoint.
source_stated_remedies: he submitted the question to a few thousand women in a similar way

source_terms: define your own India
my target India
India is merely a geographic expression
item.claim: Bijapurkar argues that "India" is not a usable market construct and that the analyst must build one: "the onus is on them to define what their India is, and translate the geographic idea into a well-defined construct of a consumer market." She develops this into the book's recurring device, "my target India", and supplies the variables from which one is assembled — consumer classes, urban versus rural, states, age cohorts and the five economies — arguing that population-stratum definitions (metro, small town, semi-urban, rural) are "no longer wise" because development has created oases that do not follow town size. She illustrates with three firms defining non-overlapping target Indias: Hindustan Unilever taking "least developed India" — deeply rural, media-dark, low-literacy — for its utensil and fabric care growth; ICICI Bank taking developed, well-off rural India for wealth management; and a typical Fortune 500 defaulting to the rich urban educated "like anywhere in the world consumer who happens to be in India."

mechanism.text: A market construct inherited as a given carries somebody else's segmentation and somebody else's idea of what varies. Constructing it deliberately from named variables forces the firm's own competencies into the definition, which is what makes two firms' target Indias differ legitimately rather than one of them being wrong.

scope.conditions: Indian market strategy, 1990s-2009.

caveats.text: the three firm examples are described without dates, revenue, outcome or source, and two are large firms whose stated strategies are matters of public record but are not cited here

the Hindustan Unilever figure — contacting 13.6 million women across 30,000 villages in eight states between 2005 and 2006 for the detergent business alone — is the most specific operational number in the chapter and is given without a source
the argument is a reframing rather than a method: it says what a target-market definition must be built from, not how to choose among the resulting definitions. The book does not claim otherwise

source_terms: Changing people's habits is very expensive.
To sell shaving soap to the peasants of Russia one would first need to change their beard-wearing habits. The cost would be excessive.
Tests which we know of have indicated that the cost of such converts may run from $20 to $25 each.
What cannot be done on a large scale profitably cannot be done on a small scale.
Yet they devote a share of their space to that object. That is only the same folly on a smaller scale.
item.claim: Some objects are simply priced out of reach of advertising, and changing an established habit is the archetype. The source reports tests indicating that converting someone to the tooth-brush habit may cost $20 to $25 per convert — partly from the difficulty and partly because much of the advertising reaches people already converted — a cost it calls unthinkable and unlikely to be recovered in a lifetime of sales. It then states the rule that makes the finding operational: what cannot be done profitably on a large scale cannot be done on a small scale, so an advertiser who concedes an object is impossible and then devotes a share of his space to it is committing the same folly in smaller units.

mechanism.text: The cost per convert does not fall with reduced commitment; only the number of converts does. A fractional budget therefore buys a fraction of an already unaffordable result, and part of the spend is wasted on the already-converted in either case.

scope.conditions: objects requiring a change in an established consumer habit, and any object shown to be unprofitable at full scale

caveats.text: `empirical_within_source` is used here and the grounds are stated precisely: the $20-$25 figure is a result Hopkins reports a test as having returned, and a subsequent decision — the maker devoting not one line to the object — is reported as following from it. What is absent is everything that would let anyone check it: no product, no advertiser, no date, no method, no sample size, no definition of "convert". It is a reported number without a reported study.

The oatmeal case is weaker: "The results were too small to discover" reports a measurement that returned nothing measurable, and the explanation offered — that everyone already knows of oatmeal and non-servers may have insurmountable objections — is speculation the source marks with "perhaps".

`historical_claim` and `culturally_bounded`: the illustrative case is beard-wearing among Russian peasants in 1923 and the working case is the state of tooth-brushing habits in the United States at that time. The reasoning is transferable in form; the specific costs are not, and are not presented here as if they were.

source_terms: To attack a rival is never good advertising. Don't point out others' faults. It is not permitted in the best mediums. It is never good policy. The selfish purpose is apparent.
Don't show the wrinkles you propose to remove, but the face as it will appear. Your customers know all about the wrinkles.
Picture what others wish to be, not what they may be now.
Tell people what to do, not what to avoid.
Assume that people will do what you ask. Say, 'Send now for this sample.' Don't say, 'Why do you neglect this offer?' That suggests that people are neglecting.
You will find that the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, if you have our experience.
item.claim: The source states a single positive-framing doctrine covering both competitors and the customer's own condition. Attacking a rival is never good advertising: it is not permitted in the best mediums, the selfish purpose is apparent, and it looks unfair. And the advertisement should depict the condition the buyer wants to arrive at rather than the defect being removed — pretty teeth not bad teeth, well-dressed people not the shabby, successful men not failures — on the stated ground that the customer already knows all about the wrinkles. The rule is extended to the instruction itself: tell people what to do rather than what to avoid, and assume compliance ("Send now for this sample") rather than imply neglect ("Why do you neglect this offer?"), which only suggests that people are neglecting. The source claims that on comparing a negative and a positive advertisement the positive outpulls the other four to one.

mechanism.text: People are attracted by sunshine, beauty, happiness, health and success, so the advertisement should point the way to those rather than the way out of their opposites. Naming a negative behaviour also implies it is normal, which invites the reader to follow the wrong crowd.

scope.conditions: the source allows one historical exception: 'before and after taking' advertisements 'never had a place save with the afflicted'

caveats.text: THE FOUR-TO-ONE CLAIM IS HEDGED BY THE SOURCE ITSELF and the hedge is easy to drop: "if you have our experience". No comparison is reported — no product, no pair of advertisements, no returns. This is an outcome claimed on the author's unshown records and explicitly conditioned on the reader's records resembling them.

Three separable claims are presented as one doctrine and only the framing claim is even nominally supported: that attacking rivals is bad policy, that depicting the desired state outperforms depicting the defect, and that assuming compliance outperforms implying neglect. The four-to-one figure is attached to the second only.

`historical_claim`: "It is not permitted in the best mediums" is a statement about 1923 magazine and newspaper acceptance policy, not an argument about effect, and it is doing part of the work of the prohibition.
The doctrine sits in some tension with the book's own use of fear and trouble elsewhere; the source resolves it by scoping the exception to the afflicted, and does not discuss it further.

That suggests that people are neglecting.

Invite them to follow the crowd.

source_terms: vernacularizing capitalism
the commodification of cultural difference
a difference-eating machine
item.claim: Jain's central structural argument is that the spread of centralised commodity manufacture into "vernacular" constituencies is a TWO-WAY process, which she calls vernacularizing capitalism: the incorporation of vernacular constituencies into a regnant capitalist order on one side, and the protean adaptation of capital's axiomatics to varying local circumstances on the other, producing multiple cultures of capitalism rather than one. Her evidence is the calendar industry's own mechanics: a centralised offset economy of scale in Sivakasi combined with local letterpress overprinting for personalisation, mobile self-employed agents, home-based artists, and annually refreshed catalogue "files" segmented by religion and region. She states the consequence against the cultural-imperialism thesis directly: "the industry has thrived on the commodification of cultural difference," and in the Conclusion, "capital in its reterritorializing aspect thrives on difference: it is a difference-eating machine."

mechanism.text: Difference is not friction for this kind of expansion, it is the product. A centralised press that can run any design at the same unit cost, plus a local process that personalises each run, lets a single industrial system address many segments without homogenising them — indeed it creates an incentive to maintain and refine the segmentation, because segmentation is what the catalogue sells.

scope.conditions: Grounded in the Indian calendar industry 1994-2001 and in the historical bazaar formation. Jain says the analysis "should also be pertinent to thinking about the cultures of capitalism more generally", but that extension is offered as a suggestion, not demonstrated.

caveats.text: the general claim about capitalism is proposed rather than shown; the demonstration is one industry in one country over roughly seven years of fieldwork

Jain explicitly refuses to romanticise the vernacular arena. She states that the bazaar ethos, 'while subaltern in relation to the regnant style of capitalist expansion, is a hegemonic formation in itself and therefore should not be romanticized in the name of the popular'. An extraction that read this as celebration of local resistance would invert her argument

Sivakasi's cost advantage rests substantially on de-mechanisation and informal piece-rate labour, and Jain records that the match industry there has been 'notoriously dependent on its exploitation of child labor' and that all three of its major industries remained largely untouched by occupational health and safety in the late 1990s. The mechanism being described has this cost and the source names it

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Well grounded for the industry studied; the generalisation beyond it is proposed.

source_terms: Pictures in advertising are very expensive. Not in the cost of good art work alone, but in the cost of space.
From one-third to one-half of an advertising campaign is often staked on the power of the pictures.
Use pictures only to attract those who may profit you. Use them only when they form a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type.
Anything expensive must be effective, else it involves much waste.
item.claim: The real price of a picture is the paid space it occupies, not the artwork fee, and on that accounting one-third to one-half of a campaign is often staked on the pictures. The source therefore states a single admission test for any picture: use it only when it forms a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type. Pictures used because they are interesting, to attract attention, or to decorate, fail the test by construction, because the advertisement's business is money-spending addressed to a restricted minority rather than pleasing, interesting or amusing a general audience.

mechanism.text: Space is the scarce, purchased resource and type and image compete for the same units of it. A picture therefore has an explicit opportunity cost — the selling argument the same space would have carried in words — and must beat it.

scope.conditions: Paid print space in 1923, priced by area, with type-set copy as the alternative use of that area. The source excludes from the discussion "the lines where the article itself should be pictured".

caveats.text: TECHNOLOGY- AND COST-CONTINGENT, and this must not be read as a durable claim about images. The whole argument is arithmetic over 1923 print economics: space sold by the column inch, halftone reproduction, and a set of media where a page of type was a live alternative to a page of picture. The conclusion follows from that cost structure. Where the cost structure differs, the arithmetic does not carry, and this lane asserts nothing about what it would give under any other one.

EXTENDS the live object sk_hop_sa_0026 (`a_picture_must_earn_the_space_it_occupies`) from chapter 4, which states the principle and reports the incubator case. Chapter 9 supplies what chapter 4 does not: the cost premise (one-third to one-half of a campaign), and an operational comparison test — better than the same space set in type — rather than a general injunction to earn the space.
"From one-third to one-half" is offered with no source, no sample and no definition of what is being measured (space share, budget share, or share of the campaigns the author has seen).

The chapter's own close contradicts its opening: pictures are "of paramount importance" on p.28 and art questions are "minor questions... mere economies, not largely affecting the results of a campaign" on p.30. The tension is recorded at sk_sa8_0009 rather than resolved.

source_stated_problems: Pictures should not be used merely because they are interesting. Or to attract attention. Or to decorate an ad.
It is certainly unwise to spend large sums on a dubious adventure.
source_stated_remedies: Use them only when they form a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type.
if none exist which apply to his line, he should work out his own by tests

item.label: exteriority_as_the_reason_setting_costume_and_location_are_asked_to_carry_meaning
item.description: Dwyer's chapter-2 material read back to the principle she states in chapter 1. If melodrama makes feeling exterior, then interior state has to be placed somewhere outside the character, and the three places this book examines are the set, the location and the costume — with the song sequence as the licensed zone in which the ordinary rules of place and time are suspended so the placement can be extreme.

whole_system_claim.text: In this body of work setting, location and costume are not backgrounds but bearers. They carry state, status and moral position because the mode does not carry them inside the character. The song sequence is where this reaches its limit: because the sequence is understood as suspending the film's own rules, it can place feeling in a location the narrative never travelled to and a costume the scene never allowed time to change into.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Dwyer states the principle of exteriority, states each of the placements, and connects exteriority to settings once (printed p. 52). She does not connect it to the prop vocabulary, to the location chronotopes, or to the costume code. Reading all of these as instances of one principle is the extractor's synthesis and is recorded as a hypothesis about how her chapter hangs together, not as an argument she makes.

dependencies.nature: the location device depends on the song's licence: Dwyer's own example of the Switzerland cut occurs inside a song
frontality and the tableau are how melodrama's exteriority becomes visible in a frame; Dwyer connects the two explicitly at printed p. 44

tradeoffs.nature: the suspension buys expressive freedom at the cost of narrative continuity. Dwyer says the audience does not mind; that assertion is not evidenced and the trade-off is therefore recorded as one the source asserts is costless, not one shown to be

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. Dwyer states the principle (exteriority) and states each of the placements, and she connects exteriority to settings once, explicitly, at printed p. 52. She does NOT connect it to the prop vocabulary, to the location chronotopes or to the costume code. Reading all four as instances of one principle is the extractor's synthesis and is the claim most at risk of tidying a two-author academic book into a coherence it does not have. It is recorded as a hypothesis about how Dwyer's chapter 2 hangs together, not as her argument.

source_terms: I have no relation with the artist, I have a relation with the picture.
Subject means same. Murugan means Murugan, Ganesh means Ganesh.
item.claim: Jain reports that consumers of these images choose by SUBJECT, not by artist: "clients, and their customers in turn, are primarily interested in the 'subject' of a calendar and are unconcerned about other issues of provenance," artists' names "almost never register in conversations between publishers and their clients," and most end-users could not name any calendar artist beyond Ravi Varma. She quotes an Old Delhi pharmaceuticals trader: "I have no relation with the artist, I have a relation with the picture." She then reports the production constraint this creates. Customers often want a picture of the same deity year after year, so artists and printers are obliged to supply a constant stream of "new" designs on the "same" subjects, while iconographic recognisability limits what can change. She quotes a Sivakasi printer: "mythological means gods. In that we cannot change anything. Only colors we can change, dress we can change. Subject means same." And J. P. Singhal: "whatever change there is, it's in the decoration."

mechanism.text: If the thing being bought is the subject and the subject is fixed by iconographic convention, then the axis along which a producer can differentiate is narrow by construction. Novelty is therefore forced into the residual dimensions — background, colour, dress, ornament — which is why the industry recycles existing designs with modifications in exactly those, and why "copy masters" exist as a role.

scope.conditions: Religious calendars in the Indian trade 1994-2001. Jain notes the constraint is looser for secular subjects, for the upmarket multi-sheet calendars, and for wedding and greeting cards, "where the demand for novelty often outweighs considerations of expense, allowing for a greater degree of creative risk taking."

caveats.text: Jain reports that this is why copyright is effectively unenforceable in the trade — 'originality' is particularly hard to establish for a religious icon, everyone copies, and so none can point a finger. The constraint and the property regime are two sides of the same fact and should not be separated
the claim about what end-users care about rests on the author's conversations, unquantified; no consumer survey is reported

the same section documents that signatures in this industry function as brand names rather than authorial marks — works continue to be produced under a dead artist's signature, artists use different signatures for different subject types, and signatures closely resembling well-known ones are adopted by others. Anyone reading a signature here as an authorship claim would be reading it wrongly

source_terms: community consumption
occasional but regular
under-dosers
item.claim: Bijapurkar reports two related design moves that decouple use from ownership where per-head consumption is low. The first is COMMUNITY CONSUMPTION: models such as cyber cafes, STD/ISD telephone booths, cable operators serving a few thousand homes each, photocopying job shops and custom-hired tractors "amortize the investment across many people and thus effectively create a 'pay as you use' model," and she states the comparison explicitly — "a few telephone owners consuming a little are not as attractive as many call booths catering to a lot of people consuming a little each." The second is the SMALL PACK at low unit price, "characterized by the success of the sachet," which produces "large numbers of people who are 'occasional but regular' consumers of things." She adds the consumption-behaviour observation behind both: Indians are "a nation of under-dosers" who will use one heaped tablespoon where the pack says two, partly from affordability and partly because "careful consumption is ingrained".

mechanism.text: Where per-head consumption is low, the barrier is the unit of purchase rather than the total demand: a large indivisible unit prices out buyers whose aggregate demand is nonetheless substantial. Reducing the purchase unit — by sharing the asset or by shrinking the pack — converts latent aggregate demand into transactions without requiring incomes to rise.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets, principally pre-2009 and pre-smartphone. The named instances — STD/ISD booths, cyber cafes, community television — are of that period and several have since disappeared.

caveats.text: SEVERAL OF THE NAMED INSTANCES NO LONGER EXIST. STD/ISD booths and cyber cafes were artefacts of a pre-mobile, pre-broadband cost structure. The book cannot know this and the object records it, because the MECHANISM — reduce the purchase unit rather than wait for incomes — outlived the instances

the shampoo sachet claim is her strongest and is supported by inspected data: Table 5.6 shows rural shampoo penetration rising from 13.3 to 68.7 per cent between 2000 and 2008, which the author footnotes as the effect of packaging innovation and lower unit sizes. The causal attribution is hers; the penetration change is IRS-sourced
the 'under-doser' claim is an unsourced generalisation about a national population, illustrated by anecdotes about ketchup and cheese, and is the weakest element in the object

the Hindustan Lever fuel-injection-pump story about achieving sachet fill precision is told without date or source and is the kind of well-travelled industry anecdote that should not be treated as documented

source_terms: sukomal
we people avoid muscles
lila
It looks ridiculous!
item.claim: Jain documents a specific and consequential production constraint, attested from several independent practitioners. Indra Sharma: "Now the body is very strong, but we will not show the anatomy. For god's body, the description is of a gentle, beautiful (sukomal) body. . . . There won't be any muscles, we people avoid muscles." The expressions must likewise be tranquil, almost meditative. Jain reports the reason given: divine agency in the Vaishnava schema is a matter of lila, sacred play, not of labour — Ram Waeerkar, first illustrator of the Amar Chitra Katha comics, "Bhagwan Krishna, Prabhu Ram . . . they have succeeded in fighting, but they are not fighters." She then reports the consequence the artists themselves run into: attempting to depict action and bodily agency within these constraints "render[s] irreconcilable the differences between narrative 'realism' and sacred textual imperatives," and quotes Waeerkar's verdict on the result: "It looks ridiculous!"

mechanism.text: Where power is held to emanate from a transcendent source rather than from a body, visible bodily force is not a sign of power but a contradiction of it. Musculature and wide-eyed alertness are the visual signature of instrumental human agency; applying them to a figure whose agency is defined as non-instrumental produces an image that is internally inconsistent, which is why the failure shows up precisely in scenes of action.

scope.conditions: Stated for Vaishnava iconography in bazaar images as practised through the period of the fieldwork, and reported by Jain as extending to the cinema — she cites N. T. Ramarao saying "I realized that keeping a muscular body won't be nice, particularly for a character like Krishna ... I took to pranayam and gave up physical exercises." Jain also records exceptions inside the schema: some muscularity is not inappropriate for Shiva given his association with tapasya, and Hanuman is muscular throughout.

caveats.text: the constraint is NOT permanent, and the source's chapter 7 is about its breach: from the late 1980s a muscular, aggressive Ram appears in bazaar prints in confluence with the Ramjanmabhumi movement, and a muscular Krishna follows. An extraction that presented the injunction as a standing rule would contradict the source's own argument

the injunction is reported as textual, but Jain notes that where textual prescriptions conflict with plausibility the prescriptions win, and where the texts are silent artists improvise — Waeerkar had to depict horse-riding in the Mahabharata despite history dating its introduction later

item.label: how_a_still_image_carries_a_narrative_to_a_viewer_who_holds_the_code
item.description: Patel's chapter-4 account of poster meaning, assembled: the face opens attention before recognition; recognition of the star brings forward a persona that was built cumulatively by star, artist and public and is carried by a few fixed features; character types compress whole sets of relations into single figures so that the relations BETWEEN them are inferred rather than depicted; and because the code does the work, text can be minimised, which is what Indian posters in fact do.

whole_system_claim.text: A poster can carry a narrative structure it never depicts, provided the viewer holds the code. Attention is won by the face without recognition; meaning is then supplied by the viewer out of an accumulated persona and a familiar typology, not out of the poster. The poster's job is therefore indexing, not describing — which is why minimal text suffices and why the same design fails outside the code.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Patel connects the first three members explicitly through her "hierarchy of responses" and her worked reading of the Deewaar poster. She does not present them as a model, does not draw the consequence for text as following from the type code, and never cites Dwyer's chapter-1 account of personification as the precondition. Assembling them into a causal chain, and adding those two members, is the extractor's. What the grouping ADDS, and what must be attributed to CANON-014, is the observation that all four devices fail together at the same boundary - the viewer who does not hold the code - which is visible across the set and not within any member.

dependencies.nature: the persona can only be indexed by a few features if personification, not impersonation, is the prevailing mode; Dwyer establishes that in chapter 1 and Patel relies on it in chapter 4 without restating it
text can be dropped only because the type code already carries the information text would have carried

tradeoffs.nature: Patel states the trade-off herself: designs that focus on one element are more universally understood but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. Reach and specificity are exchanged

item.source_warning_ref: Patel states that character types 'are not universally recognized' and are 'only fully understood by those with a knowledge of that culture' (printed p. 194); she draws the same boundary for star recognition at p. 183

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. The members are all Patel's, all from one chapter, and she does connect the first three explicitly through the "hierarchy of responses". The causal ordering is likewise the extractor's. The system is recorded as a reading of Patel's argument, not as a structure she sets out.

source_terms: Aapko Madam is se aur koi ganda topic nahin mila?
social distinction is not primarily performed through the exercise of taste
item.claim: Jain documents a systematic gap between what people in the calendar industry SAY about their audience and what they DO. Artists, publishers and printers routinely described the consumers of calendar art as "ordinary people," "the masses," "villagers," "the labor class," ascribing to them unrefined taste and religious credulity — while, as she observes, "my interviewees were more often than not sitting under the benign gaze of a printed deity, usually of the very type they were denigrating," and most had similar images in a shrine at home. She reports the countervailing testimony from the one secular artist in her sample, Ram Kumar Sharma: "The picture of Ramchandraji will be up in the home of a man of a modern progressive mind, and in that of a mythological man as well." Her reading is that the high-low distinction is deployed "at a primarily rhetorical level, as a means of performing solidarity between educated, relatively cosmopolitan constituencies while simultaneously asserting distinctness from others" — and, crucially, that this rhetoric "does not actually correspond to aesthetically enforced social distinctions."
item.interpretation_basis: The observations are the author's — informants' words, and what she saw on the walls behind them. The reading that the distinction is rhetorical rather than operative, and that it is a response to her own presence as a fine-art researcher, is her interpretation of that material. She says so: "I read it as an attempt to function within the epistemological constraints imposed by the terms of aesthetic judgment in a postcolonial field."

mechanism.text: Mass production creates a shared realm of consumption that threatens to conflate socially distinct constituencies. The rhetoric of taste is then adopted in particular contexts to reinstate a distinction that consumption no longer enforces. Because the distinction is being performed rather than practised, it appears in speech and not in behaviour.

scope.conditions: The Indian calendar industry 1994-2001, in interviews conducted by a researcher who introduced herself as a student in a department of fine arts — a framing Jain identifies as the probable trigger for the rhetoric.

caveats.text: THE INTERVIEWER'S PRESENCE IS PART OF THE FINDING AND THE SOURCE SAYS SO. Jain notes the caveats 'often surfaced at the very outset of a conversation' and concludes they were a response to her self-introduction. The data are co-produced and she treats them as such; anyone using this object must too
the sample is not enumerated. 'Many of the artists and printers with whom I spoke' is the quantifier throughout, over an unstated number of informants

the finding is advanced against Bourdieu's account of taste as the vehicle of social distinction, and Jain is explicit that she is not claiming social hierarchies are absent, only that taste is not their primary vehicle here. That is a narrower claim than it can look

source_terms: another good rule for black-on-black is to light it as if it were metal , regardless of the actual material
The best solution is to find a background material that produces less diffuse reflection than the subject. Black velvet serves this purpose
Much of the direct reflection from a black subject is likely to be polarized. If we use a polarizing filter to take the reflection off our table surface, we will probably turn the subject black too.
item.claim: Because a black subject's direct reflection has little diffuse competition, the rule for black-on-black is to capitalize on direct reflection wherever possible — in the source's words, to light it as if it were metal regardless of what it is actually made of, which means finding the family of angles and filling it. The background problem is then the hard part. Opaque black paper is the worst common choice: it receives as much light as the subject, and since the subject must be rendered dark grey rather than black to hold detail, the paper under it cannot be black either. A spotlight would keep the background darker but is ruled out, because the direct reflection wanted on the subject requires a large source. The source's answer is a background material producing less diffuse reflection than the subject — black velvet — with two stated limits: a few subjects are so black that even velvet is not blacker, and the subject's edges may merge with its own shadow. Glossy black acrylic supplies invisible light to fill those edges, but the same overhead source then fills the acrylic's family of angles and the background stops being black; the source argues its way to keeping this, saying the reflection under the subject is itself a sufficient clue that the surface is black and glossy, and concedes some readers will not accept that. The clean solution is distance: put the subject far enough from the background that lighting one does not touch the other. And the metal chapter's glass-support trick does not transfer — much of a black subject's direct reflection is polarized, so a polarizer used to clear the table would probably blacken the subject too.

mechanism.text: Black surfaces show direct reflection because their diffuse reflection is weak, which makes them behave for lighting purposes like polished metal. The glass-support trick depends on the subject and the support polarizing differently; black insulating subjects polarize like the glass, so the filter cannot discriminate.

scope.conditions: black subjects on black backgrounds

caveats.text: the same authors revising their own earlier prescription: the metal chapter's transparent-support-plus-polarizer solution is explicitly withdrawn for black subjects, on a stated optical ground. Not cross-source disagreement.
the acrylic-background argument is presented as an argument the source expects some readers to refuse, and it says so — an unusually explicit acknowledgement that it is bending its own rule
the string-support alternative is dismissed as usually needing retouching, and the source notes it may survive in a brief motion picture or video shot while being apparent in a high-quality still

source_terms: a marked iconographic shift
ugra
item.claim: Jain revisits Anuradha Kapur's account of a marked iconographic shift in popular imagery from depictions of Ram as soft, smooth-bodied, almost pudgy, smiling, benign, gentle and tranquil, to muscular versions whose mood is predominantly ugra — "angry, exercised . . . punishing" — emphasising his bow and arrows as weapons rather than as iconographic markers, appearing from the late 1980s in confluence with the Ramjanmabhumi movement. Jain accepts the shift as real and dateable but rejects Kapur's explanation of it as a consequence of colonial "realism," arguing instead that it was ENABLED by the one figure for whom musculature had long been acceptable: Hanuman, whose muscular body posed no threat to the location of agency in Ram because it was framed as that of an animal, a devotee and a servant. Jain proposes Hanuman as the site at which muscularity was naturalised in the expressive vocabulary of bazaar artists and thence became available for extension to other deities, noting that a muscular Krishna followed the muscular Ram.
item.interpretation_basis: The shift and its dating are Kapur's and are accepted by Jain. The explanation — the Hanuman route, and the reading of the change as a shift in what male power is signalled by rather than as an increase in violence — is Jain's own counter-argument, advanced explicitly against Kapur's "humanization" narrative and in dialogue with Pinney's objection to physiognomic readings.

mechanism.text: A canon does not open at the point of greatest resistance. It opens where a licensed exception already exists: Hanuman's muscularity was permitted because it was subordinated — animal, devotee, servant — so painting it did not violate the schema. Once the vocabulary was routine for one figure, extending it required no new capability, only a new permission.

scope.conditions: Indian bazaar prints from the late 1980s, in the context of a specific political movement. Jain notes that calendar Hanumans "have not always been muscular" either, so the enabling figure is itself the product of a change.

caveats.text: THIS OBJECT IS THE COUNTERWEIGHT TO sk_jgb_0030 AND MUST TRAVEL WITH IT. The iconographic injunction against muscularity is real, multiply attested, and was breached within living memory. Any use of the injunction as a timeless rule is refuted by this object, and any use of the breach as evidence that the injunction was never real is refuted by the other

the Hanuman route is a proposal, offered as 'worth examining' and as a narrative Jain generates in an explicitly rhetorical mode. She writes that chapter 7 is 'an experiment' and that its narrative 'unapologetically indexes a certain will to power'. This is the least evidentially secure object in the record and is retained because the shift itself is well attested even where the explanation is not
the material is inseparable from a history of communal violence. It is extracted as iconographic history and carries no implication about any community
