source_terms: socio-economic classification (SEC)
not just in terms of how much they consume but also in terms of what they will and will not prefer to consume
item.claim: Bijapurkar reports the SEC system — developed by the Market Research Society of India in the early 1980s, classifying urban households by the occupation and education of the chief wage earner and rural households by education and house type — and states why she prefers it to income: "through it we are able to identify consumer segments not just in terms of how much they consume but also in terms of what they will and will not prefer to consume." Her mechanism is that occupation and education shape not only earning capacity but family self-image and social status, and that "people like us / people not like us" differentiation governs behaviour. She gives the discriminating case: a junior executive with a professional qualification and a shopkeeper with a similar income will spend on different things, and the difference is sharpest for products requiring cultural rather than economic capital — newspapers, home computers, overseas holidays. She adds a precise contrast: "Television buying is more income driven, but the programmes watched are SEC driven," and that cellphones "have transcended social classes, and are driven almost totally by income."

mechanism.text: Income predicts how much can be spent; it does not predict what will be considered appropriate to spend it on. Where a purchase carries social meaning, the constraint is the buyer's sense of which goods belong to people like them, which tracks occupation and education rather than earnings — so two households with the same income diverge on exactly the categories that carry the most meaning.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer classification as standardised by the Market Research Society of India and used across consumer goods, services and financial services; population figures from IRS 2008.

caveats.text: the discriminating examples are illustrative anecdotes — Neeta the masseuse, the author's own contractor, a hotel marketing director's discounted-package story — not analysis of the survey data she cites. The survey establishes the population sizes; the behavioural claims are told through cases

the hotel anecdote, in which discounted-room guests 'did not know how to use a shower and a Western toilet properly and were far more down market than he would have liked', is reported as the marketing director's account and reproduces his framing. It is retained because it is the evidence offered for the claim, and it should be read as a practitioner's account of his own customers, not as an observation

SEVERE FRESHNESS RISK, and it is category-specific here. The claim that cellphones are income-driven while television programme choice is SEC-driven is a 2008-era observation about a media environment that no longer exists

source_terms: What suppliers consider to be a frill, consumers consider to be a necessity.
jugaad
poor consumers are far more innovative than the folks that design products and services for them
item.claim: Bijapurkar states a specific and repeated failure in designing for low-income consumers: firms "reduced the price by reducing performance and assumed that this combination would work," offering reduced functionality, reduced styling and old or obsolete products, and "the consumer, as always the wiser, rejected all of it. Marketers then blamed the consumer and the country for not being evolved, whereas, in reality, the consumer was way ahead in sophistication." Her diagnosis is a single line: "What suppliers consider to be a frill, consumers consider to be a necessity." She supports it with the constraint that produces it — these consumers are "aware of what is happening in the rest of the world — as it happens, in real time," so "a better wood stove is not good enough in the world of LPG, nor is a black-and-white television or even a colour one without a remote" — and with the observation that they will "rather defer a purchase and get a better product than settle for something of a far lower standard today."

mechanism.text: The supplier decides which attributes are inessential by reference to its own product hierarchy; the buyer decides by reference to what they have seen to exist. Where the buyer's reference set is the same global one as the supplier's premium customers, the attributes the supplier treats as removable are the ones the buyer treats as defining, and the stripped offer fails not on price but on relevance.

scope.conditions: Indian low-income consumers post-liberalisation, on 2008 data. The book positions itself explicitly against and alongside C. K. Prahalad's *Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid*, and Prahalad wrote its Foreword.

caveats.text: THE RELATIONSHIP WITH PRAHALAD SHOULD BE VISIBLE. Prahalad wrote the Foreword to this book and his BoP thesis is the interlocutor for its chapter 12. Bijapurkar is not neutral here, though she does qualify him: 'the bottom 250 million may be very hard to integrate into the mainstream market economy, as Prahalad urges in the book'
no failed product is named. The claim that firms did this and were rejected is asserted across an unnamed set of cases, in contrast with the named examples used elsewhere in the book

the positive claims — that poor consumers do more complex financial value processing than the rich, that default rates on their loans are extremely low, that they innovate their own solutions — are asserted with illustrations (missed calls, mixed petrol and kerosene for community lighting, smaller glasses at weddings, GIAN's pedal-powered washing machine) and no data

SEVERE FRESHNESS RISK. The market conditions described are pre-smartphone and pre-cheap-data. The 'missed call' practice she reports as characteristic is an artefact of a tariff structure that no longer exists

item.label: the_reasoning_errors_this_book_names_about_a_market_it_says_is_read_wrongly
item.description: The book's substantive contribution, gathered: a set of named errors in how firms and analysts reason about this market, each with a diagnosis. Ask what market exists for a fixed offer rather than what strategy the market requires. Predict evolution by analogy with another market's past. Extrapolate from a one-time demand release. Plan on a category whose size is set by your own affordability threshold. Read a consistently biased survey number as a level. Attribute a shift caused by a moving choice set to consumer character. Generalise a metropolitan high-SEC sample to a national youth population. Adopt a countable proxy that does not track the operative variable. Strip attributes the supplier thinks are frills.

whole_system_claim.text: What this source contributes that outlives its data is a catalogue of reasoning failures, each of which has the same general form: an assumption imported from elsewhere is treated as a property of the market, and the resulting number or judgement is then read with more authority than its construction supports. The Indian specifics date; the failure shapes do not.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Bijapurkar states each of these individually and states her overall thesis — that this market is systematically misread — repeatedly. She does NOT gather them as a set of reasoning errors, and several sit chapters apart. Reading them as one catalogue with a common form is the extractor's. What the grouping ADDS, and what must be attributed to CANON-014, is the observation that in every case the error is the same one at a different site: a constraint the analyst imposed is read back as a fact about the market. That is visible across the set and not within any member.

dependencies.nature: the take-off threshold is a special case of the analogy trap: it reads another market's income-to-price ratio as a property of this population

the middle-class question cannot be settled from income data, so the definitional trap and the data trap are the same problem at two removes. Bijapurkar treats them in the same chapter but does not join them
the extrapolation of the early-1990s boom is what produced the middle-class figure; the source states this connection

tradeoffs.nature: the book's prescription — customize everything, define your own market construct — buys relevance at the cost of strategy complexity, and the source records the objection in the voice of an exasperated CEO: 'Why do we need a Rolls-Royce approach to segmentation for a market so small?' It answers that there is 'regrettably, no way out of this', which is an assertion rather than an argument

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. The members are individually the author's, stated clearly and in her own words. The RISK the grouping introduces is that it makes a consultant's strategy book look like a methodology: presenting nine scattered arguments as a catalogue of errors with a common form lends them a coherence and an authority the book does not claim. It is recorded as a reading of what is durable in this source, not as her framework. The claim that all nine share one form is the extractor's and is the part most open to challenge.

Four are supported by named survey data and by tables inspected in this pass; five rest on undated, unattributed consulting anecdotes. The caveats on each member say which.

item.label: the_apparatus_for_replacing_opinion_with_knowledge
item.description: The stages by which the source says an advertising decision stops being an opinion: gather information (read the literature, canvass consumers, verify the maker's claims, commission the figures), obtain an instrument (the sample coupon, which keys a general advertiser's advertising), run the test (four or five towns, or twenty-five letter cells, or paired towns for a single variable), extrapolate (the small-scale average asserted always to hold), and apply the verdict to disputes, expenditures and personnel. Chapter 21 states what the apparatus exists to prevent: a growing business absorbing unmeasured advertising into its own success story.

whole_system_claim.text: The stages are load-bearing on each other, and the chain has one weak link that the source never strengthens. Information decides what to test; the coupon makes a general advertiser testable at all; the test returns per-customer quantities; and the whole apparatus is decision-useful only if small-scale averages hold at scale — which is the one step in the chain the source asserts without any evidence, mechanism or condition.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The grouping across chapters 11, 13, 15, 16, 19 and 21 is ours, but three of the links are the source's own. Chapter 12 names the intelligence function as a stage: "Our intelligence department is a vital factor, as told in the previous chapter." Chapter 13 states that samples pay "by keying your advertisements... Thus you can compare one with another ad, headline, plan and method", which is the coupon presented as the instrument of the test. Chapter 19 states that letter testing is done "Just as men are doing now in all scientific advertising", explicitly filing it under the same apparatus. What is entirely ours is the identification of sk_sa8_0034 as the chain's weak link — the source treats it as its firmest ground, not its weakest. That reading is recorded as ours and the reason is stated in that object's caveats.

dependencies.nature: the procedure produces a decision only under the always-hold premise
the test starts users with a sample offer, which is also what keys it
the offer must be free for the test to start users quickly and cheaply
the agent audition is the champion/challenger arrangement used on a supplier instead of a plan

tradeoffs.nature: Two different test shapes sit side by side and the source does not distinguish them. The chapter 15 test measures absolute levels in a few towns with no comparison arm; the chapters 13 and 16 tests are paired-town comparisons with an arm held back. The second answers "which is better", the first answers "is it viable", and only the second controls anything.

conflicts.nature: "Those averages always hold" against chapter 11's instruction to gather appeal percentages by class because "the percentage may differ on farms and in cities". If response varies by class, an average from four or five towns generalises only if those towns match the national class mix, which the source never mentions.

Chapter 13 warns that arguments about advertising expenditure are usually biased and names the interest behind them; chapter 15 predicts that applying the audition method would move a large percentage of all advertising — a prediction in the direct commercial interest of the author's own agency, made without noting it.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The stages are the source's; the assembly into one apparatus is ours, though the source links three of the joins itself. The critical judgement — that sk_sa8_0034 is the unsupported link on which everything else depends — is entirely ours and is the opposite of the source's own view of it. Two of the fifteen members carry a reported measurement (sk_sa8_0035's 91 per cent, sk_sa8_0036's 75 per cent) and neither is a test-campaign return; the remainder assert measurement and withhold the result. A reader should treat this system as a well-specified METHOD with almost no reported OUTPUT.
